title: Creating link groups
body_text: Creating link groups Link groups can only occur between phases that are in the same recipe and of the same recipe level. If the current level is an operation, the only valid phases for link groups are phases in the current operation. If the current level is a unit procedure, the valid phases for link groups are phases found in any operation referenced by steps in the unit procedure. If the current level is a procedure, the valid phases for link groups include all phases found in any unit procedure referenced by steps in the procedure and any operations referenced by the steps in the unit procedures. In other words, the valid phases follow the hierarchy down all the recipe levels. This means that the number of valid phases for a link group becomes greater the higher up the recipe level hierarchy you go. You can create a link group from any phases that are referenced (either directly or indirectly by drilling down into the components) by the recipe. Note: Any phase used in a link group must be based on a phase class with a number of partners greater than zero (0). Link groups are created using Recipe Studio. To create a link group, open the recipe (at the operation, unit procedure or procedure level). On the Home tab, in the Algorithm group, click Link Groups . Click Add . Enter the Link Group name and description. Select the phases from the list of valid phases (based on the current recipe component). Click OK , and then click Close . Note: You can modify, delete, and rename link groups from the Link Group dialog. Link Group Dialogs Subtopics: Synchronizing phases with link groups Related information Configuring the phase logic

title: Creating new Application Stations for Redundant Batch
main_heading: Creating new Application Stations for Redundant Batch
body_text: Creating new Application Stations for Redundant Batch The following instructions require that the new Application Stations will be used for either (or both) a redundant Batch Executive or Campaign Manager. the new Application Stations are connected to the DeltaV network, but do not have the DeltaV software installed yet. the Application Stations will be running the same DeltaV software version (and it is the same across the entire DeltaV network). the Batch Executive or Campaign Manager is not currently enabled on this node. Subtopics: Create an Application Station Install the DeltaV software on the primary Application Station (the preferred active) Install the DeltaV software on the secondary Application Station (the preferred standby) Finish the installation

title: Creating phase categories
body_text: Creating phase categories Phase categories are organizational groupings of phase classes. DeltaV Explorer uses phase categories to facilitate creating and implementing phase classes. Phase categories do not influence your control strategy in any way.

title: Creating phase classes
body_text: Creating phase classes The phase class contains the common properties for the phase logic. Create the phase class in DeltaV Explorer. For each phase class, you can configure the following class items: Number of Phase Partners Phase Messages Phase Parameters (input and report) Phase Algorithm Parameters In the Phase Class Properties dialog, enter the description. Each phase inherits its phase class properties. Phase Class Properties Dialog Every step in an operation is associated with a phase class. That association links the step to the appropriate phase logic that controls the state transitions. Each phase logic runs on a unit or unit class. When the batch executes, each step in an operation runs on the correct equipment through these associations. Subtopics: Defining phase partners Defining phase messages Defining phase parameters Related information Recipe Studio

title: Creating phase logic module-based units
body_text: Creating phase logic module-based units A PLM-based unit is an instance of a unit class. Create units using DeltaV Explorer. You can follow your plant's P&ID, if available, to define the equipment. A unit is defined by the unit class, a name, description, picture (optional) and arbitration information. Note: If you plan to use class-based recipes, use unit modules instead of units. Configuring units for batch processing takes two steps. The first step is to organize your equipment into unit classes with broad definitions (for example, reactors, mixers, storage tanks, and so on). The second step is to create units of equipment from a unit class. A unit can be a single piece of equipment or multiple pieces of equipment that, together, perform a specific task. For example, the definition for Charge Tank A includes the input valve and flow meter as well as the tank's level indicator. Subtopics: Defining unit properties - general Defining unit properties - execution Defining unit properties - displays Defining unit properties - arbitration Defining unit properties - tools

title: Creating recipes that share units
body_text: Creating recipes that share units Class-based recipes are designed to run on a unit class and not on a specific unit. Class-based recipes let you share units within a class. The operator selects the unit at runtime, depending on the other recipes in production and the available units. When designing recipes to share units, you must define each unit within the unit class to have the same phase modules. The class properties are shared with each instance (unit) of the unit class. However, each instance can define its own unit-specific information, such as the phase logic and the unit parameter definition. The unit class also acts as a placeholder and template for a specific unit. As a result, when the procedure containing the class-based operation is scheduled, the operator is prompted to select a unit from the unit class specified for the operation or unit procedure. This allows the DeltaV system to bind a specific unit to the recipe and begin production. Note: Units are assigned to process cells which are, in turn, assigned to areas. Areas are assigned to a Batch Executive. The recipe is also assigned to a Batch Executive. In order for a class-based recipe to run using class-based equipment, all units required by the recipe must be assigned to the same Batch Executive (by way of process cell and area) as the recipe. The recipe will not run if all required units are not found on the same Batch Executive. For example, suppose you want to include the MAKE_ADDITIVE operation shown in the following figure in three different procedures running on three different production lines. Running Recipes on Similar Units If the operation is instance based, you need to create three operations, one for each mixer, as shown above. Notice that, aside from the equipment defined, the operations are identical. To avoid this situation and simplify your development effort, make the operation class based. By creating a class-based recipe, you enable each operation to run on any of the three mixers because a unit class is defined instead of a unit. This approach allows you to create one generic operation instead of three specific ones, which saves time. At run time, operators can assign any mixer in the unit class to the operation, providing flexibility, as the following figure shows. Using a Class-Based Recipe

title: Creating the phase logic
body_text: Creating the phase logic Phase logic can either be a phase algorithm definition (unit phase) assigned to unit modules and used in class-based control or a phase logic module assigned to a unit and used for non-class based control. Both are state transition diagrams that define (through the logic that you write) how each phase of a recipe executes. The phase algorithm is an instance of a phase class assigned to a unit module. All of the logic is written at the phase class level and is instantiated as a unit phase on the unit module. If you are using aliasing, you must use phase algorithms and unit modules. The phase logic module is an instance of a phase class and is assigned to a PLM-based unit. The logic is written for each individual unit. If you are not using class-based design or aliasing, you can use phase logic modules. You can create and name the phase logic objects in DeltaV Explorer. However, you can only edit the phase logic in Control Studio. In either instance, the phase logic incorporates the use of phase logic parameters. Related information Control Studio Phase logic parameters

title: Creating unit class categories
body_text: Creating unit class categories Categories are organizational groupings of unit classes. DeltaV Explorer uses categories to facilitate the creating and using of unit classes. Categories do not influence your control strategy in any way.

title: Creating unit classes
body_text: Creating unit classes Unit classes define the common properties of units. Each unit in a class shares the same basic properties. Using classes allows you to configure class-based recipes that are adapted to specific instances of a unit at run time. The unit classes are defined in DeltaV Explorer. Before you begin defining units, you need to have a complete understanding of the physical layout of your plant. All unit definitions in DeltaV Explorer must match the physical equipment in your plant. Refer to your plant's P&ID drawing if necessary. The unit classes are defined under the Library/Advanced Definitions/Unit Classes section. The units are created under System Configuration/Control Strategies/Area section of DeltaV Explorer. DeltaV Explorer Hierarchy Subtopics: Defining unit parameters Defining aliases Resolve a unit alias Select which alias to use on a unit module Associating phase classes Adding equipment module classes Adding control module classes

title: Creating unit modules
body_text: Creating unit modules A unit module is an instance of a unit class and therefore inherits all the properties of the unit class, including the associated phase classes and the logic contained in those phase classes. Create the unit modules in DeltaV Explorer by dragging the unit class to a process cell. This creates the unit module and the associated phase logic, aliases and unit parameters are inherited. The unit modules should represent actual equipment in your plant. Refer to the plant P&ID for organizational and equipment information. All units from the same unit class will have the same properties defined. You can not adjust the state transition logic (phase logic) for an individual piece of equipment at the unit module level. However, you can set the values of the unit parameters at unit module level to adjust for differences in the equipment. Note: If deleting a unit module that has been assigned to a node and when the running batch might use the unit, then set the $AVAILABLE parameter to a non-zero value first or change MSTATUS to OOS. Otherwise, the batch will go to HELD if the batch tries to run on this unit. Subtopics: Defining unit module properties - general Defining unit module properties - execution Defining unit module properties - displays Defining unit module properties - arbitration Defining unit module properties - tools

title: Creating alias names in the unit classes
main_heading: Creating alias names in the unit classes
body_text: Creating alias names in the unit classes Alias names are automatically created for any control module classes/equipment module classes when they are added to a unit class. Alias names are placeholders for the actual parameter reference path strings used in the phase logic defined in a phase class. Using aliases makes the phase logic more flexible by allowing phases to be used by multiple units/equipment. You can create alias names directly in the DeltaV Explorer and then bind the alias by browsing to the parameter reference path. It is also possible to create an alias name and then drag a control module class or equipment module class to the alias name. This creates in the unit class a module block for the equipment or control module class with the alias name. Alias names can be used for all or a portion of the parameter reference path (module/function block/parameter.field). An alias can also be used to point to a unit parameter on a unit module. Examples of valid alias names and their reference paths are: #AGITATOR# = AGIT_500 #INLET_VLV# = XV_BASE_500/DC1/SP_D.CV Subtopics: Create an alias name

title: Creating the control strategy - overview
body_text: Creating the control strategy - overview In the following procedures, you will perform these steps to create the control strategy: Create and name a plant area to hold the control modules. Create the modules that specify the input, processing, output, alarms, and conditions for the process equipment, control loops, and other parts of the process. Create a Sequential Function Chart (SFC) to automate the process. Strictly speaking, you do not need to create an SFC. You can set up your process system in such a way that an operator would activate specific equipment, change setpoints, and perform other operations. However, in many cases, it is useful to define a Sequential Function Chart to automate the process (or parts of the process, such as startup or shutdown procedures) with minimal operator intervention. When creating the control modules that make up your control strategy, sometimes you will create a module from scratch (using the basic function blocks), but more often you will start with one of the predefined module templates. There are a number of ways to create the control modules. In DeltaV Explorer, you can copy a module template from the library by dragging and dropping it onto your plant area and then renaming it. In Control Studio, you can start from a module template, modify the module, and save it in your plant area under a new module name. In Control Studio, you can start from scratch by dragging and dropping function blocks and other items from palettes of predefined items, connecting the blocks, and modifying block parameters. In Configuration Assistant, you can copy a module template from the library. In the exercises in this chapter, you will learn how to use the first three methods. Note: This manual assumes that you are working on a new system or one that is in the beginning stages of configuration-not one that is controlling a process. Subtopics: The Control Studio interface

title: Creating and managing Windows groups
body_text: Creating and managing Windows groups Note: There are two types of groups: DeltaV groups and Windows groups. This section refers to the Windows groups. The DeltaV User Manager adds users to the appropriate Windows groups automatically when you add or modify user accounts. For example, users who are assigned a DeltaV account are added to the DeltaV group. Users assigned Windows Administrator privileges are added to the Administrators group. You grant users these various account types in the user account properties. In some circumstances, you might need to add a user to a group using Windows Computer Management or through Active Directory Users and Computers on a domain system. However, the preferred way to manage your DeltaV users is through DeltaV User Manager. Refer to your Windows operating system help for instructions on adding users to groups in the Windows interface. Related information DeltaV accounts Groups

title: Creating and opening graphics configurations
body_text: Creating and opening graphics configurations Layouts, displays, display sets, GEM classes, standards, and functions are created from the ribbon's New command or from their permanent folder's context menu in the Explorer view. When you create one of these configurations, it automatically opens as a Content tab in the Content Tabs view. The New ribbon command can be used from either the Home > Graphics tab or Insert > Graphics tab. To create a new language or theme, you must first open the appropriate Languages or Themes library folder as a tab and then click New Language or New Theme in the Content pane. Double-click any graphics configuration or library folder in the Explorer view to open it as a Content tab. You can then navigate between open configurations and folders by selecting their tabs; the selected tab is the active tab. When a folder is selected as the active tab, the configurations contained in that folder are listed in the Content pane. You can do the following with this list of configurations: View certain information about each configuration, such as whether it is locked for editing or marked as a work in progress. Use the context menu to cut, copy, paste, or delete configurations. Double-click a configuration to activate it in the Content pane.

title: Creating and using source linkages
body_text: Creating and using source linkages The ability to view process trend and alarm and event data with respect to a batch is a common request. Source Linkages, typically used by Batch Historian Clients, link process history data that is stored in the Continuous Historian database with batch history data that is stored in the Batch Historian database. Refer to the online help for the DeltaV Batch Historian Administrator for information on using source linkages. Related information Batch Historian administration

title: Creating an embedded composite
body_text: Creating an embedded composite In a function block diagram, you can create an embedded composite by dragging the Custom Block from the Special Items palette and clicking the Embedded Composite icon, as shown in the following figure. Creating Custom Blocks Assistant Before clicking Next , enter the name of the composite in the Block Name field. After clicking Next , select the type of algorithm you want to use for the composite. You can create a Function Block Diagram (FBD) composite or a Sequential Function Chart (SFC) composite. The name indicates the type of algorithm the composite contains. Custom Block Assistant: Selecting Number of Inputs and Outputs The number of inputs you set on this dialog determines the number of values to which you can wire from the containing FBD into the composite. In the composite, these wired values are input parameters and used as inputs to the composite's control strategy. The number of outputs determines the number of values that can be wired from the composite back to blocks in the containing FBD. In the composite, these wired output values are output parameters. All input and output parameters are visible parameters on the composite block in the containing function block diagram. In an SFC, you can insert an embedded composite by right-clicking in the right side of the Hierarchy View, and then selecting Add . A dialog appears, where you click the Embedded Composite icon, as shown in the following figure. Creating Custom Block for an SFC Assistant Then, you enter the block name and then click Next . After clicking Next , select the type of algorithm you want to use for the composite. You can create a Function Block Diagram (FBD) composite or a Sequential Function Chart (SFC) composite. The inputs and outputs are not wired in an SFC diagram, but you might want to create a number of input and output parameters for use in the composite. After setting these numbers, click Finish . The composite now appears in the hierarchy view, but not on the SFC diagram. You run the algorithm in the composite using a non-boolean action in a step, and you can reference the parameters in the composite.

title: Create a batch file for Windows Task Scheduler
main_heading: Create a batch file for Windows Task Scheduler
body_text: Create a batch file for Windows Task Scheduler The automated backup utility for the DeltaV Continuous Historian can be scheduled using the Task Scheduler in Windows. Use the Task Scheduler to create a new scheduled task that runs the HistorianBackup.exe file and manually adds optional parameters, or you can create a batch file with the optional parameters included. Note that the Continuous Historian Administration application includes a Schedule DeltaV Continuous Historian Data Backup option. Evaluate this option before deciding to use a batch file and the Task Scheduler. To create a batch file, use a text editor, such as Notepad, and type the command for the backup you wish to create, using the syntax described in this topic. Save this file to a local directory with a *.cmd file extension ( CHBackup.cmd , for example). Use the Add Scheduled Tasks wizard to establish a schedule for backing up the DeltaV Continuous Historian, using the batch file as the program you want to schedule. Example c:\DeltaV\bin\HistorianBackup \\SiteServer\CHBackups /CreateNewActive /OnlyIfModified /DeleteIfGTDays:30 /Retries:15 /LogFile:CHBackup.log In this example, the DeltaV Continuous Historian data sets are backed up with the following conditions: The data sets are backed up to the UNC path \\SiteServer\CHBackups . A new active data set is created before the backup. Only data set that are modified is backed up. Backed up data sets that are no longer in the DeltaV Continuous Historian database, that are located in \\Siteserver\CHBackups , and that are greater than 30 days old are deleted. If the backup is unsuccessful, the system executes up to 15 retries. A log file, CHBackup.log , is created the first time the scheduled backup runs and appended to each time thereafter. Note: The user creating the scheduled task must have the appropriate Windows and DeltaV security privileges to run the scheduled task, access the automated backup utility, and write the log file. Important: During a Task Scheduler backup, a Command Prompt window opens briefly with information about the backup if the logged-on user is one who has privileges to run the scheduled task. Do not close the Command Prompt window; if it is closed, the backup process terminates.

title: Creating a linked composite
body_text: Creating a linked composite In a function block diagram, you can create a linked composite by dragging the Custom Block from the Special Items palette and clicking the Linked Composite icon, as shown in the following figure: Creating a Linked Custom Composite Block Assistant After you enter the name, click Next and select whether you want to link to an existing object or a new object. The dialog looks similar to the following. Creating a Custom Linked Composite Block Assistant: Selecting Linked Object Type After you select the type of object you want to link to, click Next . Then, you can browse for any existing objects or define new objects. Once you have identified what the composite is linked to, click Finish . In an SFC, you can insert a linked composite by right-clicking in the right side of the Hierarchy View, and then clicking Add . The steps are then like the previous procedure for adding a linked composite to an FBD: Click Linked Composite and identify what the composite is linked to. The inputs and outputs are not wired in an SFC diagram. The linked composite appears in the Hierarchy View, but not on the SFC diagram. You run the algorithm in the composite using a non-boolean action in a step, and you can reference the parameters in the composite.

title: Creating a Sequential Function Chart
body_text: Creating a Sequential Function Chart Sequential Function Charts (SFCs) are types of module algorithms that are useful for controlling time-event sequences, such as startup or shutdown of a process. SFCs are made up of steps and transitions. Steps contain a set of actions. A transition allows a sequence to proceed from one step to the next when the transition condition is true. Each time the SFC scans, the system evaluates the active steps and transitions. When a transition evaluates as True, the step prior to the transition is made inactive and the step following the transition becomes active. There are no predefined module templates for SFCs since process sequences are highly individual. In defining an SFC, you may find it helpful to first define the steps in the process, and then identify the conditions that must be met before proceeding from step to step. Subtopics: The sequence for the tank process Create a named set Creating the SFC module Finish configuring the SFC module

title: Creating class-based module templates
body_text: Creating class-based module templates A class-based template provides some of the benefits of both a module class and a template. A class-based template can be based on any module class in the library. You create a class-based template by dragging a module class to a container under the Module Templates section in the DeltaV Explorer. Alternatively, you can create a template from scratch and indicate on the New module dialog that the template is to be based on a particular module class. A class-based module template is nearly identical in function to a class-based module. They are both instances of a class. Recognizing the similarities makes it easier to understand the resultant Copy/paste and propagation behaviors of class-based templates. Class-based templates allow for the customization of a class to suit a particular application. For example: A configuration contains a class called ON_OFF_VALVE. This class is capable of handling many different kinds of ON_OFF valves (with variations in the number of outputs, number of inputs, NO/NC , permissives, interlocks, etc.). A particular application of the ON_OFF valve class is a 1 output, 2 input, NC valve. A class-based template can be created from class ON_OFF_VALVE and then the parameter values in the template can be set to suit this particular application. This removes the need to customize each instance of the class. In addition, certain parameter values in the template may be protected so that they cannot be changed on copies of the template. The copies of the module template get their initial parameter values from the template but, as is the case for templates that are not class-based, changes to the parameter values in the class-based template do not propagate to the copies. By definition, the logic in a class-based template cannot be changed. Module classes propagate changes to their structure and algorithm to any templates that are based on the class and to copies of the class-based template. Changes to a class-based template do not propagate to copies of the template. Only changes to the class can propagate to instances. Related information Protecting your engineering standards

title: Creating a control module class for level indicators
main_heading: Creating a control module class for level indicators
body_text: Creating a control module class for level indicators The second control module class we will create is for level indicators that will be used in the blenders. This class will be created in the category named AnalogInput. We will create it from a Library template and then modify several parameters. For example, one parameter we will need to change is the L_TYPE parameter on the AI block. The named state will be changed to Direct (from Indirect) because values will come directly from the simulation. Subtopics: Create the control module class Modify the LEVEL_INDICATOR class

title: Creating custom engineering unit descriptors
body_text: Creating custom engineering unit descriptors When you configure the Units field of a scaling parameter such as PV_SCALE or OUT_SCALE, DeltaV software has a standard list of engineering unit (EU) descriptors from which to choose. It is possible to add your own custom EU descriptors to this list from DeltaV Explorer. When exporting and importing the entire DeltaV system for an upgrade or reinstall, select the Include the data for a DeltaV software upgrade check box on the Export and Import dialogs to save and restore custom engineering unit descriptors.

title: Creating datalinks
body_text: Creating datalinks Datalinks can be used to display data as numbers or text. For the TANK101 picture, you will create five datalinks for the following purposes: To display the current value of the tank level (parameter reference: LI-101/AI/PV) To display the current value of the loop process value (parameter reference: FIC-101/PID1/PV) To allow entry of a setpoint value for the flow loop (parameter reference: FIC-101/PID1/SP) To allow the operator to set the regulatory valve position (parameter reference: FIC-101/OUT) To allow the operator to start and stop the pump motor (parameter reference: MTR-101/DC1/SP_D) After you have created the links, your working area will look like this: Subtopics: Create a datalink for the tank level Create a datalink for the loop setpoint Create a datalink for the loop process value Create a datalink for the loop output Create a datalink for the block valve Create a datalink for the motor setpoint

title: Creating datalinks for command and state-driven algorithm modules
main_heading: Creating datalinks for command and state-driven algorithm modules
body_text: Creating datalinks for command and state-driven algorithm modules When creating datalinks to the module parameters A_* (for example, A_PV, A_ERROR, and so on) on an operator graphic, use the Data Link Stamper tool and set the Data Entry Type to None (the default). This prevents the parameter from being written to by an operator through the graphic and is the desired behavior. Do not use the DeltaV Data Entry Expert on a data link to these parameters.

title: Creating deferred parameters
body_text: Creating deferred parameters There are two ways to create a recipe parameter and defer the lower level parameter to the new higher level parameter: Create the higher level parameter directly at its recipe level and then modify the lower level parameter to defer to the higher level. or Defer the lower level parameter and let the system automatically create the higher level parameter. The second method, which is easier, is used in the following steps. Note: Recipe level parameters can have the same names or different names as parameters at the phase level. Both naming conventions are used in the following examples. For illustration purposes, the charge amount parameters will be given a new name at each new level (prefaced by OP, UP, or PRC). However, the agitate parameter, named AGITATE_TIME at the phase level, will retain the same name in all three recipe level parameters. Subtopics: Defer a phase parameter and create an operation level parameter Create the parameters at the unit procedure and procedure levels

title: Creating the logic to monitor phase conditions
main_heading: Creating the logic to monitor phase conditions
body_text: Creating the logic to monitor phase conditions The diagram below shows the initial Fail_Monitor block, BLOCK1, and the blocks we will add to monitor the failure conditions. Each of the four condition blocks is used to define the expression for a failure condition. If the condition becomes TRUE, then the OUT_D parameter of that block is set to TRUE as well. By wiring all of the OUT_D parameters into the Boolean Fan In block, we can watch for any failure condition to become active. The Boolean Fan In block makes three decisions that are extremely useful in monitoring for failure conditions. It tells us if any condition is active (OUT_D), it identifies which conditions are active (OUT_INT), and it identifies which condition became active first (FIRST_OUT). Using the FIRST_OUT parameter and the phase_failures named set, we can display the appropriate message to the operator to describe why the phase has failed. This is done by determining which message to display (in the FAIL_MESSAGE calc/logic block) and writing the correct message to the FAIL_INDEX parameter (in the BLOCK1 calc/logic block). The FAIL_INDEX parameter is the heart of the failure monitoring system. All phases are designed such that if the FAIL_INDEX parameter for that phase is anything other than 0, then the phase automatically transitions from the running logic to the holding logic. Additionally, the value of the FAIL_INDEX parameter is displayed both on the Batch Operator Interface as well as the detail display on the unit phase faceplate as the Failure State message. We will add four condition blocks that feed into a Boolean Fan In (BFI) block. When a condition is tripped, the following things happen: The failure is detected and sent to the BFI block. The value of the FIRST_OUT parameter of the BFI is sent to the Calc/Logic block named FAIL_MESSAGE. The FAIL_MESSAGE block converts the FIRST_OUT value to one of the failures defined in the phase_failures named set. The FAIL_MESSAGE parameter OUT1 is used to set the FAIL_INDEX parameter in the phase. When the FAIL_INDEX parameter is non-zero, the phase goes to the holding state and the appropriate phase_failures named state string is displayed in the Batch Operator Interface (as well as in the details display on the unit phase faceplate). Subtopics: Create the failure monitor logic

title: Creating module classes from module templates
main_heading: Creating module classes from module templates
body_text: Creating module classes from module templates You can use module templates and module classes together. For example, if your process includes multiple 2-state motors that require similar configurations you can drag a 2-state motor template to the Control Module Classes container in DeltaV Explorer and a control module class is created from the template (the template still remains). Then, edit the class to match your control requirements more precisely. Finally, drag the control module class to an equipment module class or unit class to make it part of a hierarchical class-based configuration strategy. You can also drag the control module class as many times as needed directly to areas under Control Strategies in DeltaV Explorer to create individual control module instances that are independent of unit modules or equipment modules.

title: Creating new DeltaV Operate files with Version Control enabled
main_heading: Creating new DeltaV Operate files with Version Control enabled
body_text: Creating new DeltaV Operate files with Version Control enabled New files (displays, dynamos or schedules) can only be created from DeltaV Operate. When a new file is created, the template is opened and the new file is created from the template when you select the Save As option from the File menu. This is the normal process for creating a new graphic, schedule or dynamo set. Note: Do not use Save on the templates as this can overwrite the existing template (if checked out). A dialog reminding you to use Save As is displayed when you check out a template file. When you close the new file, Version Control adds the file to the database and automatically checks the file out. This is true even if AutoCheckIn/Out is not enabled. You can see the new file in DeltaV Explorer at this time. If AutoCheckIn is not enabled, you must check the file in from DeltaV Explorer when done editing it. You cannot create a file with the same name as another file with Version Control enabled, unless that file is checked out. If you do enter an already existing name, a dialog first warns you that you are using an existing name and then you are warned that you cannot overwrite the file. You must give the file a unique name. However, if the file is checked out, you can overwrite that file. This does not create a new file, it merely overwrites the existing file. Important: Files can be copied, deleted, renamed, and edited in DeltaV Operate ONLY. When opening a file from DeltaV Explorer, DeltaV Operate is launched in configure mode.

title: Creating a new module from scratch - overview
main_heading: Creating a new module from scratch - overview
body_text: Creating a new module from scratch - overview In this procedure, you will use Control Studio to create from scratch a module to monitor the tank level. The module will have one analog input function block (to allow reading of the analog input signal) and one output, a promoted parameter. Using a promoted parameter for an output makes the value of the output easier to access systemwide. Promoted parameters are on the Special Items palette. You will also do the following: Edit the IO parameter of the analog input block to identify the Device Signal Tag for the level transmitter, LT-1. Change the OUT_SCALE parameter on the analog input block from the default value of 100 to 10,000 to reflect the 10,000-gallon capacity of the tank. Change the HI_HI_LIM value will be changed to 1000. Add history collection to the PV of the AI block so that the tank level can be trended in the Process History View application. Subtopics: Create a new module from scratch Add and modify an analog input function block Add a module-level parameter for the process output value Add history collection to the PV parameter Connect the OUT parameter to the PV parameter Assign and save the control module

title: Creating phase messages
body_text: Creating phase messages The first step in defining an operator prompt is to create the actual message that will appear on the Batch Operator Interface screen. Subtopics: Create the phase messages

title: Creating operator pictures in DeltaV Operate - overview
main_heading: Creating operator pictures in DeltaV Operate - overview
body_text: Creating operator pictures in DeltaV Operate - overview In this section you will learn how to use DeltaV Operate in configure mode to create an operator picture (TANK101) for the example process system. It is important to understand the operating environment for a DeltaV process system before you start creating pictures to be used in that environment. The DeltaV Operate application functions in two modes: Configure mode - used to create pictures Run mode - used to run pictures in the DeltaV Operate application Let's start by taking a look at the standard DeltaV operator desktop, as seen in the DeltaV Operate application in run mode. This desktop was designed specifically for use with DeltaV process systems. It is made up of three sections: the Toolbar , the main window, and the Alarm Banner. The Toolbar buttons provide single-click access to important pictures, directories, and other applications. Important: Although it is possible to add, modify, or delete buttons from the Toolbar and make other changes to the operator desktop, it is recommended that you do not do any customization until you are thoroughly familiar with the purpose and function of all its elements. The Alarm Banner at the bottom of the desktop also has important predefined functions. The large buttons are used to notify the operator of the highest priority alarms that have been activated. When an alarm is tripped, the name of the associated control module (such as XV-101) is displayed on one of the alarm buttons. By clicking one of these buttons, the operator goes directly to the appropriate process graphic for taking action on that alarm (the primary control picture or the faceplate). The Alarm Banner also includes a node monitor button to enable operators to monitor the current status of controllers and workstations. You may remember that we assigned a primary control picture to each control module as one of the finishing steps. Modules created from library templates have predefined faceplates. A little later you will learn more about the Alarm Banner and how to acknowledge alarms. The main window is where the operator views a main picture, which is typically a process graphic that provides a view of the process or equipment. A main picture is any picture created using the main template. The main template has some predefined features, such as a small toolbar (with five buttons) in the upper left corner. The template also contains some picture commands that are required by the DeltaV environment. Even in relatively small process systems, there are likely to be a number of main pictures. Each main picture is created and saved as a picture file with its own unique name. Important: The most important thing to remember about main pictures is that they must start from the predefined template named main. Only subordinate pictures, such as pop-up messages to operators, should be created without using the main template. If you create a new picture file from scratch or use a different template as a basis, much of the DeltaV Operate environment will not work.

title: Creating pictures: general guidelines
body_text: Creating pictures: general guidelines Here is a quick list of recommendations for creating pictures: Fewer than 900 data links per picture are recommended. Remember that a data link does not have to be visible on the picture to count against the total links per picture. Animations can use none, one, or many data links. (10 data links visible on a picture each with 15 data links used in animation produce a picture with 150 data links.) Use a 1 second refresh rate. See the next section for more information. In DeltaV Operate, scripting must be in Visual Basic. An excessive amount of scripting will adversely effect system performance. Read the "Optimization Guide" in the Operator Graphics manual for a comprehensive discussion of issues regarding the impact of operator graphics on system performance.

title: Creating procedures
body_text: Creating procedures Procedures are the highest level in the recipe hierarchy. A procedure includes unit procedures in the steps of its procedural function chart. The unit procedures in a procedure may (and usually do) run on more than one unit or unit class. The Properties dialog for a unit procedure step within a procedure includes an additional check box option: Acquire unit prior to starting unit procedure? A procedure may control several units simultaneously; this option lets you decide when a branch of the procedure can be started. (If the check box is checked for any unit procedure in a parallel branch, all of the required units for that unit procedure must be acquired before any unit procedures in that branch will be started.) Additionally, selecting Retain unit after completing unit procedure means that the procedure acquires the unit, and the unit is not released until the completion of another unit procedure for which this selection is clear (that is, the Retain unit after completing unit procedure check box is not selected). If this check box is clear, the unit is released as soon as the unit procedure completes. We will leave both options unselected for the purpose of this tutorial. Procedures are created in the same way as unit procedures and operations. Subtopics: Create a procedure

title: Creating the remaining logic for the FILL phase
main_heading: Creating the remaining logic for the FILL phase
body_text: Creating the remaining logic for the FILL phase Complete the logic for the FILL phase using information from the table below. Step/Transition Name Action or Condition Text Transition: NEAR_TOTAL '//#TOTALIZER_1#/TOTAL_FLOW_1/INT_VALUE'>= 0.90 * '^/FILL_AMOUNT.CV' Step: START_ACCURATE '//#TOTALIZER_1#/A_COMMAND' := 'totalizer:Totalize_accurate' Transition: TOTAL_MET '//#TOTALIZER_1#/TOTAL_FLOW_1/INT_VALUE' >= '^/FILL_AMOUNT.CV' Step: RESET '//#TOTALIZER_1#/A_COMMAND' := 'totalizer:Reset' Termination: COMPLETE TRUE The completed SFC should look like the following, except that the step actions will not show on the diagram. (We added the step actions to the diagram using the Comment tool on the graphics toolbar.)

title: Creating the SFC module
body_text: Creating the SFC module Now you are ready to create the Sequential Function Chart. Here are the things you will do in the following procedures: Create an SFC module. Add a parameter, SP, to the module to let the operator change the state from IDLE to START. Add the steps and transitions to the SFC. Subtopics: Create a Sequential Function Chart Add the SP parameter Create a step action in the SFC Create a transition in the SFC Complete the Sequential Function Chart diagram

title: Creating transitions automatically
body_text: Creating transitions automatically There is an option in Recipe Studio to automatically write a simple transition condition that checks for completion of the preceding step. To set this capability as a default for a recipe, click the Main button, click Recipe Studio Options , click Preferences , and then click Default Transition Conditions . For an individual transition, you can right-click and select Modify , and then click the Default Condition button. In an operation with default transition writing enabled, when you draw the connecting line from a step to a transition, the transition condition is automatically written as follows: phaseclass:n/BSTATUS=$phase_state:Complete The term phaseclass:n is the instance of the particular phase class being used in the operation. The parameter BSTATUS is the phase logic parameter that indicates the current status of the phase. The name $phase_state is a standard named set in the DeltaV system. Tip: To see the text of the transition condition on the diagram instead of the name or description, on the Diagram tab, in the Layout group, click Diagram Preferences . In the Show Diagram section, select Condition under Transitions .

title: Creating unit modules
body_text: Creating unit modules Unit modules are the highest level control entities in the physical hierarchy in a DeltaV batch application. Each unit module represents a piece or group of equipment used to carry out part of a batch process; a unit module executes phase logic to carry out that process. A unit module contains module blocks representing equipment modules and control modules that identify the actual equipment to be manipulated when that unit module runs. You can create unit modules by dragging a unit module class to the Process Cell (or Area) in the System Configuration/Control Strategies section of the DeltaV Explorer. When the unit module is created, all the contained equipment module classes and control module classes are instantiated. If you are not using class-based modules, the control modules associated with the unit module can be dragged into the unit module. Our sample paint application will have unit modules for one base tank (UM_BASE_400), three color tanks (UM_COLOR 100, UM_COLOR_200, and UM_COLOR_300), and two blenders (UM_BLENDER_500 and UM_BLENDER_600). After a unit module is created, we will rename each of the contained control module and equipment module instances to make the names more meaningful for the individual unit. Note that, in the DeltaV Explorer hierarchy, the name of the module block from which the module instance was created appears in parentheses after the module name to help in identifying the source. (The module block Properties dialog can be opened to see the name of the module class.) Subtopics: Create the BLENDER unit modules Create the COLOR unit modules Create the BASE unit modules

title: Creating unit procedures
body_text: Creating unit procedures Unit procedures are the second level in the procedural hierarchy. The steps in a unit procedure represent operations. All operations in a unit procedure must run on the same unit or unit class. Creating unit procedures is very similar to creating operations. The first unit procedure you will create is UP_BLEND, which will be run on the BLENDER unit class. This unit procedure will run OP_CHARGE (for charging the base and color into a blender) and OP_FINISH (for agitating the contents of and draining a blender). Use Default Transition Conditions when creating these recipes: click the Main button, and then click Recipe Studio Options , Preferences , and Default Transition Conditions . Subtopics: Create unit procedures (UP_BLEND and UP_COLOR)

title: Crossed SLS 1508 SISNet Repeater fiber optic connection
main_heading: Crossed SLS 1508 SISNet Repeater fiber optic connection
body_text: Crossed SLS 1508 SISNet Repeater fiber optic connection In this example there are four SISNet Repeater pairs. The fiber connections into the SISNet Repeater on CTLR3 have been crossed. This causes the SISNet Repeaters on CTLR3 to receive the wrong traffic, the indication of Crossed on CTLR3 indicates what the problem is and where it is occurring.

title: Crossed SLS 1508 SIS Network bridge connections
main_heading: Crossed SLS 1508 SIS Network bridge connections
body_text: Crossed SLS 1508 SIS Network bridge connections In this example, three SISNet Repeater pairs are connected through switches, one for the primary bridges and one for the secondary bridges. The connections are in a star configuration. The primary SISNet Repeater on CTLR1 is connected to the secondary switch. This causes all the SIS Network bridges on the secondary network to see primary traffic. The Rem_Peer_Status of CTLR1's repeater indicates Bridge Net Crossed. The primary SIS Network bridge on CTLR1 is seeing secondary traffic so it sets the Crossed indication but it is also not receiving any valid communication and shows the Bridge No Comms integrity error.

title: Downloading CHARMs Smart Logic Solvers SIS system components
main_heading: Downloading CHARMs Smart Logic Solvers SIS system components
body_text: Downloading CHARMs Smart Logic Solvers SIS system components SIS Controller Downloading an SIS controller does not download the CSLSs in the Local Safety Network. Downloading the SIS controller also downloads: CHARMs assigned to CIOCs that need to be downloaded. Devices assigned to WIOCs that need to be downloaded. Remote I/O cards on the Remote I/O node. CHARMs Smart Logic Solver Note: Downloading a logic solver may result in a value and/or status change of non-secure parameters. The effect on production depends on what the references for the non-secure parameters are used for. The CHARMs Smart Logic Solver (CSLS) supports only total downloads. You cannot download individual SIS modules or LS CHARMs. CRCs are maintained for the CHARM I/O configuration, each SIS module, and the overall configuration. When a download results in a difference to the overall CRC you are prompted that a download change was detected and that a full functional test of the SIF may be required. You can then check the SIS module and I/O CRCs to determine if a functional test is really required and what the scope of it may be.

title: CSLS Global Safety Networks
body_text: CSLS Global Safety Networks In CSLS safety installations consisting of more than one local safety network (LSN) it may be necessary for a CSLS to access information on another LSN. The global safety network (GSN) provides this capability. Local safety network bridges (LSNBs) are the hardware items that are connected to create the GSN. The following table lists terms and acronyms used to describe CSLS global safety network components. Terms and acronyms Term Meaning LSNB Local Safety Network Bridge The LSNB is on the LSN under the SIS Controller. It collects user-configured secure parameters from the CSLSs on the LSN it is connected to and publishes them on the GSN. The LSNB also receives data from other LSNBs on the GSN. The LSNB publishes the data to make it available to other CSLSs on the LSN. The LSNB is available only as a redundant pair. GSN Global Safety Network The GSN is the network of connected LSNBs. domain (GSN) A GSN domain is a collection of LSNBs that can share secure parameters. This release supports only one domain so all LSNBs in the configuration are in that domain. publisher Publishers are logical entities in the DeltaV database. Publishers are not configured explicitly. As secure parameters within an LSN are referenced by other LSNs, the publisher creates and populates maps of secure parameters and references. The maps can be viewed from DeltaV Explorer. safety system In the context of CSLSs, safety system is shorthand for the CSLS safety system: the collection of all SIS controllers and CSLSs and other hardware and software. The following table lists the capacities (limits) for Global Safety Network Items. Global Safety Network capacities CSLS Global Safety Network property Limit LSNB nodes per LSN 1 Publisher maps per domain 16 Publisher maps per LSNB 4 Listener LSNBs per domain No limit Boolean Secure parameters per publisher 192 Non-Boolean Secure parameters per publisher 64 Boolean Secure parameters received from the LSN per LSNB 768 Non-Boolean Secure parameters received from the LSN per LSNB 256 Boolean Secure parameters an LSNB can receive from the GSN 3072 Non-Boolean Secure parameters an LSNB can receive from the GSN 1024 The following figure shows how the Global Safety Network (GSN) fits in a CSLS system. Global Safety Network in a CSLS system Each LSN only supports one LSNB. The LSNB collects and publishs data for all the CSLSs on that LSN. The LSNBs are linked on their own global safety network. In DeltaV Explorer LSNBs appear under SIS controllers on the LSN. The following figure shows how an LSNB appears in DeltaV Explorer. Local Safety Network Bridge in DeltaV Explorer Subtopics: Local Safety Network Bridge LSNB Ethernet port connections LSNB domains and publishers LSNB secure parameters and references LSNB secure parameter mapping Remapping secure parameters LSNB configuration LSNB diagnostics

Local Safety Network Bridges LSNBs) — When it is necessary for a CSLS in one Local Safety Network to communicate secure data to a CSLS in another Local Safety Network, two or more Local Safety Networks can be connected with LSNBs to form a Global Safety Network. The following figure shows a schematic diagram of an example CSLS system implementation. The schematic shows two redundant SIS Controllers, each with its Local Safety Network. One of the networks has two redundant CSLSs and the other has one redundant CSLS. The two Local Safety Networks are connected by Local Safety Network Bridges to form a Global Safety Network. title: Logic Solver Lock and Unlock functions
main_heading: Logic Solver Lock and Unlock functions
body_text: Logic Solver Lock and Unlock functions The CSLS must be unlocked to commission, decommission, download, debug SIS modules and allow HART write commands. Locking also prevents a user-initiated logic solver switchover. The Lock and Unlock functions are software-based. You lock and unlock the CSLS in DeltaV Explorer through the CSLS context (right-click) menus. Physical key switches The physical key switches on the CSLS carrier and SIS Controller carrier can be used to allow or prevent users from using the Unlock function. The key switches require physical presence by plant personnel. The Unlock software function works in conjunction with the physical key switches as described below. CSLS physical key-switch Enable or disable the physical key switch by selecting or clearing the Enable Key-Switch checkbox on the CSLS Properties dialog (Security tab) . If the key-switch is enabled, it must be in the unlocked position for the Unlock software function to work. SIS Controller physical key-switch The Keylock Ethernet Isolation Port (EIP) module enables the physical key switch on the SIS Controller carrier. When enabled by the Keylock EIP, the key switch on the carrier inhibits the unlock function for all assigned CSLSs. This enables you manage the unlock function for several CSLSs from one location. If the Keylock EIP module is installed, key-switch functionality is enabled for the SIS Controller. There is no software means to enable or disable the functionality for the SIS Controller key switch. Typically, you would use either the key-switches on the CSLSs or the key-switch on the SIS Controller to manage the unlock inhibit functions. For example, if you have the Keylock EIP module installed on your SIS Controller carrier, turn the key switch on the SIS Controller carrier to the locked position and turn all the assigned CSLS key switches to the unlocked position during normal operations. When you need to use the Unlock software function, turn the key switch on the SIS Controller carrier to the unlocked position. If you do not have the Keylock EIP module installed in the SIS Controller carrier, turn the CSLS key switches to the locked position during normal operations (if physical presence is required at your site to inhibit the unlock software function). Turn the key switch on a particular CSLS when you want to use the Unlock software function for that CSLS. CSLS key-switch single unlock function You can use the unlock inhibit key switch on the CSLS carrier to perform a single software unlock. This enables you to allow unlock for the CSLSs without having to go back and turn the key switch to the locked (inhibit) position. It also reduces the chances of leaving the key switch in the unlocked (allow) position. To enable a single-unlock function, turn the key switch to the unlock position until the LED flashes red on the active CSLS. Then, turn the key switch back to the lock position. The LED will flash red (at a faster rate) before turning off to indicated that the CSLS is in the single unlock allowed state. You will then be able to perform one software unlock function within the next five minutes. The CSLS automatically returns to the unlock inhibited state in five minutes (or immediately after a software unlock occurs). At an appropriate time, you can lock the CSLS, knowing that the keys switch is in the locked position. Note: The single unlock functionality requires CSLS major revision 2 or higher. SIS Controller Auto Lock function The Auto Lock function automatically returns the SIS Controller to the Locked (inhibit) state after a user-configured time has expired. This prevents the controller from remaining in the Unlocked (allow) state indefinitely. When the Auto Lock function is enabled, users do not have to remember to return the controller to the Locked state. You enable and configure Auto Lock on the SIS Controller Properties dialog (Security tab) . Use the dialog to enable the Auto Lock function and to set a time after which the controller returns to the Locked state. CSLS Unlocked Alert The CSLS Unlocked Alert occurs when either the CSLS or SZ controller's key switch is in the unlock inhibit position, CSLS is unlocked and the configured time of CSLS unlocked alert has been exceeded. You enable and configure CSLS Unlocked Alert on the SIS Controller Properties dialog (Security tab) . Use the dialog to enable the function and to set a time after the alert occurs.

title: CSLS physical unlock inhibit key
body_text: CSLS physical unlock inhibit key The CHARMs Smart Logic Solver can be locked from DeltaV Explorer to prevent accidental changes to its configuration. In addition, the CSLS has a physical key switch that prevents unlocking of the CSLS from DeltaV Explorer unless the physical key is in the unlocked position. The SIS Controller also has a physical key switch that can be used to manage the Unlock function for all the CSLSs on a Local Safety Network. Related information Logic Solver Lock and Unlock functions

title: Local Safety Network Bridge
body_text: Local Safety Network Bridge LSNBs are installed on LSNs. The LSNBs connect to each other, creating the GSN. The LSNB publishes secure parameter data from CSLSs on its local safety network to the GSN. Other LSNBs on the GSN publish secure data used by CSLSs on their LSNs. The following figure shows an example of the data flow of secure parameter SECUREPARAM1 in CSLS1 that is referenced by REFPARAM1 in CSLS2. Secure parameter data flow in a Global Safety Network The database maps SECUREPARAM1 because it is referenced by a CSLS in another LSN. SECUREPARAM1 moves down LSN1 to LSNB1. LSNB1 publishes SECUREPARAM1 to the GSN. LSNB2 receives SECUREPARAM1 and publishes it to LSN2 where it is received by REFPARAM1 in CSLS2.

title: Local Safety Network Gateway and Modbus devices
main_heading: Local Safety Network Gateway and Modbus devices
body_text: Local Safety Network Gateway and Modbus devices The Local Safety Network Gateway (LSNG) provides a safety integrity level (SIL) 2 link between CSLSs and external Modbus devices. This section describes the configuration of the LSNG and how to use it to process data received from the Modbus devices. This includes explaining the parts of the configuration that are the same regardless of the Modbus devices that are connected. Other sections explain how to use specific Modbus devices with the LSNG. The only devices currently supported by the LSNG are the Autronica BS-420 and BC-420. Note: The DeltaV system only reads detector data from the Modbus device and does not drive actuators in the Modbus device. The LSNG communicates with external devices using the Modbus TCP/IP protocol. The LSNG uses the data to form secure parameters and then publish them as global data on the local safety network. If the LSNG is in a DeltaV system that includes Local Safety Network Bridges (LSNB), the data from LSNGs can be used on other LSNs. CSLSs on the network verify and consume from LSNGs in the same way they consume other secure parameter data. The LSNG operates as a Modbus master with two external devices, one on each port using simplex network connections. The LSNG initiates the Modbus TCP/IP messaging services while the corresponding devices act as Modbus slaves. The LSNG does not support Modbus serial devices behind a Modbus gateway. After an LSNG is defined in DeltaV Explorer, signals, Modbus ports, and other device-specific items can be configured. The LSNG topology is shown in the following figure. The GSN and the remainder of the DeltaV system are not shown for clarity. Local Safety Network Gateway in a DeltaV system Each Local Safety Network can have as many as four LSNGs (Three if the LSN contains an LSNB). In DeltaV Explorer LSNGs appear under SIS controllers on the LSN. The following figure shows how an LSNG appears in DeltaV Explorer. LSNG in DeltaV Explorer The LSNG is based on the LSNB and uses the same hardware. You can create LSNB and LSNG placeholders and assign LSNB hardware to either. An unassigned LSNB assigned to an LSN under a SIS Controller can be defined as either an LSNB or an LSNG from the LSNB placeholder properties dialog. LSNG Secure Parameters are mapped into publishers when their corresponding Signals are created in the LSNG configuration. Referencing them does not affect their mapping. The database maps the secure parameters for each publisher automatically to optimize publisher usage, however, it does not shift existing secure parameter mapping when one or more are deleted. This is to avoid forcing a re-download of referencing logic solvers for unchanged secure parameters. Subtopics: LSNG publishers Configure the LSNG Configure LSNG Modbus ports LSNG port connections

title: Configure the LSNG
body_text: Configure the LSNG Configuring an LSNG consists of setting a few things on the tabs of the LSNG Properties dialog. On the LSNG Properties dialog: Enter a description of the LSNG, if desired. If you have created the LSNG placeholder by dragging an LSNB from the Unassigned Safety Nodes folder, Select Gateway in the Node Type field. If you want a standby card's revision to automatically change to the correct revision when it is inserted, select the Enable Automatic Upgrades check box. Configure the Alarms and Displays tab and the Proof Testing tab as desired. Related information Bulk edit Local Safety Network Gateways

title: LSNG port connections
body_text: LSNG port connections The Dual Universal Safety Carrier that houses the LSNG has both primary and secondary Ethernet Isolation Ports (EIP) for the LSN and Modbus connections. You must connect the two Modbus devices to the top ports of each EIP and connect the primary and secondary Local Safety Networks to the bottom ports of each EIP. These ports are not interchangeable. The figure shows the Dual Universal Carrier with Ethernet Isolation Ports installed. Note: The two Modbus devices must be on separate networks. LSNG Dual Universal Safety Carrier connections

title: Configure LSNG Modbus ports
body_text: Configure LSNG Modbus ports On the LSNG Modbus Port 1 and Modbus Port 2 properties dialogs: On the General tab, enter a description of the ports, if desired. On the Advanced tab, set the IP address and Subnet mask of the ports. Note: The IP address must be on the same segment as was configured for the device in the AS configuration tool. For example, if the IP address configured in the AS configuration tool is 192.168.0.1 for the device (on this port) the IP address here could be 192.168.0.2. Note: The IP address and subnet mask you configure must allow for the standby LSNG card's automatically configured IP address. The standby card's IP address is increased by one in the most significant 0 in the subnet mask. If the standby card's address rolls over into the next subnet, then the CONFIG ERROR bit is set and the subsystem has bad status. For example, if the subnet mask is 255.255.254.0 the standby card's address has 256 added to it. If you configure the address 10.20.1.200 standby's address is 10.20.2.200 which is a configuration error because it is not in the configured subnet. It is possible to configure signals manually in DeltaV Explorer, and there may be some circumstances in which you may want to (adding or modifying a few signals) but the most efficient way is to use DeltaV Bulk Edit.

title: SIS Controller Modbus port write support
main_heading: SIS Controller Modbus port write support
body_text: SIS Controller Modbus port write support The only supported writeable register type is a coil. Coils are limited to Boolean parameters. To write to a parameter in an SIS module use a non-secure parameter. The main usages for Boolean writes into the safety system from a third-party interface are for LSCEM resets and input bypasses. For example, to reset an LSCEM block, configure a non-secure parameter reference wired to a PDET block and then to an exposed reset parameter of the LSCEM block of an SIS module as shown in the figure. Non-Secure Parameter Reference To manipulate the non-secure parameter reference from Modbus requires a control module running in the SIS Controller that contains the non-secure parameter source as shown in the figure. Non-secure Parameter source The example's Modbus register mapping would be to the non-secure parameter source in the control module - DMS_NSM1/CEM_RESET.CV mapped to coil R100. The non-secure parameter reference type is limited to Boolean, float, and integer. Normally when the reset parameter of an LSCEM block is written to the reset action is taken and then the reset parameter is cleared. To accommodate for this the Positive Directional Edge Trigger (PDET) block is required before the RESET.

title: CSLS redundancy
body_text: CSLS redundancy DeltaV SIS supports redundant CSLSs. A redundant CSLS consists of a pair of CSLSs mounted on a single CSLS Carrier. Each CSLS gets its power from each of the CSLS Carrier Power connections. The CSLSs contain the same configuration, run the safety logic in lock-step and read and write I/O. The CSLS that is active (as indicated by the Active LED) communicates with the SISCTLR on the LSN. If a CSLS detects a problem, it initiates a reset of itself. The partner CSLS continues to drive outputs and communicates with the SISCTLR as the active CSLS. You can initiate a manual switchover in Diagnostics from the CSLS Switchover context menu. The SIS_DIAGNOSTIC_SWITCHOVER security key is required by default. In the event of a manual or automatic switchover, the system generates a CSLS hardware alarm indicating: Partner Not Available, and Card Not Communicating while the former active CSLS is powering-up and obtaining configuration. In addition, a switchover event is reported in the Event Chronicle along with the CSLS Maintenance alarms. A CSLS switchover is not disruptive to the process. However, following a switchover, the formerly active CSLS may not be available for approximately two minutes. In other words, it is temporarily not available to take over as the active CSLS. Redundant CSLSs allow proof testing to occur without affecting a running process. A proof test causes a CSLS to run its power-up test while the partner CSLS is active in order to validate that there are no dangerous, undetected faults present. There are two types of proof test: manual and automatic. An automatic proof test occurs at user-specified intervals. Set the interval using the CSLS properties dialog in DeltaV Explorer. To initiate a manual proof test, use the appropriate Force Reset command on the CSLS context menu in Diagnostics.

title: Implementing CHARMs Smart Logic Solver systems
main_heading: Implementing CHARMs Smart Logic Solver systems
body_text: Implementing CHARMs Smart Logic Solver systems The following list is a suggested order to perform the tasks required to install, setup, and configure a DeltaV SIS CSLS system: Install the DeltaV hardware. Install the DeltaV software and set it up for your needs. Enable CHARMs Smart Logic Solvers in System Preferences. Create user accounts and grant at least one user the keys to DeltaV SIS locks. Assign DeltaV SIS keys and locks as needed. In DeltaV Explorer, configure the SIS Controllers and CSLSs you need. Configure LS CHARMs as required. Assign CSLSs . Commission CSLSs . Create SIS modules to execute the logic your safety strategy requires. Create operator graphics for your SIS system. Download the configuration. If necessary, use DeltaV diagnostics to troubleshoot your DeltaV SIS CSLS system. Related information CHARMs Smart Logic Solver (CSLS) SIS system example DeltaV User Manager and SIS security

title: CSLS SIS module execution
body_text: CSLS SIS module execution The CSLS processes DeltaV SIS modules differently than the DeltaV controller processes other DeltaV modules. All DeltaV SIS modules in a CSLS run at the same scan rate. The scan rate is configurable from 50 to 200 milliseconds in 50 millisecond increments. On download, the CSLS estimates the maximum possible execution time for the SIS modules based on their complexity (number of inputs, expressions, and so on). Note that the estimated maximum execution time can be much greater than the actual ExecTime reported in DeltaV Diagnostics. The estimated maximum execution time is not reported. If the configured scan rate is less than the estimated maximum execution time, the CSLS sets the scan rate to the next slower scan rate. The CSLS also sets the SIS Module not executing at configured scan rate bit in the SIS module parameter SIF_ERRORS and activates the standard CSLS alarm MAINT_ALM. DeltaV Diagnostics Explorer shows the actual scan rate in the ActualScanTime parameter at the CSLS level. To clear the alarm, change the configured scan rate to the actual scan rate and re-download. Note: The DeltaV Controller Load Estimator has a Safety Instrumented System (SIS) function blocks reference table which displays execution time and memory usage in CSLSs and controllers. The tool can help you decide how many CSLSs you need and how to best assign SIS modules to CSLSs. If the total estimated SIS module execution time exceeds 200 milliseconds, the CSLS does not apply the downloaded script and the download fails. The order of CSLS I/O and SIS module processing is also different compared to DeltaV controllers and other DeltaV modules: Prior to running the SIS modules, every CSLS stores a snapshot of all input data in an internal database. Every CSLS executes its contained SIS modules and transmits any secure parameter data. Every CSLS transmits its I/O data to other CSLSs on the LSN.

title: CHARMs Smart Logic Solver standalone safety systems
main_heading: CHARMs Smart Logic Solver standalone safety systems
body_text: CHARMs Smart Logic Solver standalone safety systems A standalone DeltaV SIS consists of one or more DeltaV SIS Controllers with their CSLSs and CHARMs that may or may not have a dedicated DeltaV ProfessionalPLUS workstation. In the event a dedicated DeltaV ProfessionalPLUS workstation is not desired, an approved ProfessionalPLUS Laptop may be utilized. The approved ProfessionalPLUS Laptop utilizes the Primary ACN port on the DeltaV SIS Controller for connectivity. This allows a single laptop to be used for multiple standalone DeltaV SIS installations. Once connected to the DeltaV SIS Controller the ProfessionalPLUS workstation or laptop functions as any other DeltaV SIS ProfessionalPLUS. After the system is configured, downloaded, and operating the ProfessionalPLUS workstation is not needed and may be disconnected. In the event that the event chronicle connection is lost (the dedicated ProfessionalPLUS workstation loses connectivity) or a laptop is employed as the ProfessionalPLUS, the CSLS and DeltaV SIS Controller buffer their alarms and events. Once the connection to the event chronicle is restored or the laptop ProfessionalPLUS is connected, the buffered alarms and events will be retrieved from the CSLS(s) and DeltaV SIS Controller(s). You can merge a standalone CSLS system into a DeltaV control system but you must ensure that there are no duplicate configuration names or addresses in the two systems.

title: CHARMs Smart Logic Solver configuration
body_text: CHARMs Smart Logic Solver configuration DeltaV SIS CHARMs Smart Logic Solver (CSLS) system hardware and DeltaV SIS software are used to install, configure, and maintain safety instrumented systems in conjunction with sensors and final elements to take a process to a safe state when hazardous conditions occur. DeltaV SIS CSLS hardware includes the following: DeltaV SIS Controllers (model SZ) — Connect to the DeltaV area control network (ACN) and isolate the CHARMs Smart Logic Solver from the rest of the system. CHARMs Smart Logic Solvers — Connect to the DeltaV SIS controllers through the Local Safety Network (LSN). CSLSs run SIS modules that contain the safety system logic. LS CHARMs (LS stands for logic solver) — The SIS-specific input and output CHAR acterizing M odules that bring field signals into the DeltaV SIS CSLS system. Safety Instrumented Functions (SIFs) are implemented in DeltaV SIS software using CSLSs that are installed on an LSN under a DeltaV SIS controller. DeltaV SIS Controllers appear in DeltaV Explorer under the Control Network subsystem. CSLSs appear in DeltaV Explorer under the Local Safety Network subsystem of a DeltaV SIS controller. CSLSs are where the safety logic configuration is downloaded and run. The DeltaV SIS Controller (SISCTLR) has a Modbus TCP connection available to support stand-alone DeltaV SIS installations. The available module types are restricted to control module or template with algorithm types of FBD or SFC. The SISCTLR supports redundancy. CSLS components are physically separate from, but integrated with, the DeltaV distributed control system (also known as a basic process control system or BPCS). Each CSLS executes SIS modules that perform the safety logic required for each SIF. Safety instrumented functions are configured in one or more SIS modules using the DeltaV engineering tools-DeltaV Explorer and Control Studio. SIS modules are downloaded to run in CSLSs. In some cases data needs to be shared between SIS modules and/or CSLSs. This data is shared through the use of Secure Parameters and Secure Parameter References. Each CSLS can publish Secure Parameters. These are Boolean with status values that the SIS module can write to and can be referenced by any other SIS module in the same or different CSLS connected to the same LSN. The simplest CSLS system consists of a single SISCTLR and single CSLS. Up to 16 CSLSs may reside on a single LSN. Larger systems require the addition of separate SISCTLRs, LSNs, and CSLSs to a maximum of 30,000 DSTs. Subtopics: CSLS SIS systems in DeltaV Explorer Secure parameters in CSLS SIS Controller configuration CHARMs Smart Logic Solver Local Safety Network (LSN) CSLS SIS module execution CSLS redundancy CSLS physical unlock inhibit key CHARMs Smart Logic Solver downloads Use of LS CHARM data in non-SIS modules LS CHARM types LS CHARM failsafe behavior SIS Controller Modbus port CHARMs Smart Logic Solver standalone safety systems Bulk editing CHARMs Smart Logic Solver objects Related information Capacity limits for CHARMs Smart Logic Solver SIS systems
