title: Version Control and CSLS SIS systems
main_heading: Version Control and CSLS SIS systems
body_text: Version Control and CSLS SIS systems When Enable Version Control for DeltaV SIS is selected in the Version Control Configuration dialog CHARMs Smart Logic Solvers (CSLS) are added to Version Control Audit Trail (VCAT). Enabling VCAT for DeltaV SIS does not include SIS Controllers in version control. Note: To include SIS Controllers select Enable Version Control on the Version Control Configuration dialog. Some notes about Version Control and CSLS SIS components when VCAT is enabled: Changes to a Modbus Port object (property values, add/update/delete or register mappings and so on) check out the parent SIS Controller. Any changes made to LS CHARMs check out the parent CSLS rather than the LS CHARM itself. Adding modules to the DeltaV SIS Controller does not check out the DeltaV SIS Controller. The module has the checkout status. Adding modules to an AREA does not check out the AREA. The module has the checkout status. Adding SIS modules to a CSLS does not check out the CSLS. The SIS module has the checkout status. DeltaV SIS Controllers and CSLSs can be checked out and in individually. The Show All Charms and Show Only Defined CHARMs choices are disabled on the CSLS CHARMs context menu. Related information Version Control

title: Control module classes
body_text: Control module classes Control modules are the basic control elements in a batch system. Each pump, valve, or control loop is controlled by a separate control module. Each module has a unique tag and all the information for a module can be accessed through its tag name. Depending on the type, a control module can be composed of parameters, history collection strategy, alarms, conditions, algorithms, and display elements. Control module classes define the common properties of a group of control modules. You can further group control module classes into categories to help organize the classes for large systems. Control modules can be created individually from scratch. They can also be created from templates that exist in the DeltaV Library or they can be created as instances of control module classes. In this tutorial, we will create two control module classes (for valves and tank level indicators) and then create control modules from the classes. To speed up the tutorial configuration, other control module class categories and classes have already been imported. Subtopics: Create a control module class category Editing the NC_VALVE control module class Making a parameter configurable The Configure dialog in DeltaV Explorer Modifying the module class to enable simulation Creating a control module class for level indicators Related information Modules: general information

title: Custom alarm calculation
body_text: Custom alarm calculation You can perform your own alarm state calculations using any of the function blocks. Typically, you would use function blocks that support expressions, such as: Condition function block Calc/Logic function block The alarm state calculation typically uses logical and relational operators to: test the values in one or more parameters, compute a Boolean result (0 or 1), and write it to a new state parameter.

title: Custom alarm detection
body_text: Custom alarm detection To enable DeltaV alarm features, create an alarm in the same module and attach it to the Boolean state parameter that you computed. At the end of each module execution cycle, the alarms for the module are processed to detect any state changes. When the custom state computation results in a value that is non-zero, the alarm is triggered and is either displayed for the operator or logged in the event log.

title: Custom alarm presentation
body_text: Custom alarm presentation DeltaV Operate is the alarm presentation vehicle in the DeltaV system. The presentation is based on the alarm properties and the alarm type.

title: Custom batch report
body_text: Custom batch report Included in this section is a step-by-step example showing how to create a custom batch report. It describes how to create a batch report and provides a simplified version of a sample batch report to illustrate what key elements are needed. Subtopics: Create a batch report

title: Customizing the alarm list
body_text: Customizing the alarm list The alarm list is a graphics element used to show the active alarms in an operator's scope of responsibility and provide the means for operators to respond efficiently to these alarms. In Graphics Studio, the alarm list is added to a display from the Data Palette and configured in the Graphics Configuration pane. The alarm list offers various configuration options, including its look and feel, which interactions are available for operators to respond to alarms, and the context for the alarms. You can also configure the alarm list to dynamically adjust its context online, so that the same list could show alarms for a different Area, Unit, Equipment Module, Control Module, Device, or Hardware Node.

title: Customizing Batch Operator Interface screens
body_text: Customizing Batch Operator Interface screens The DeltaV Batch subsystem lets developers customize the information presented to operators in the Batch Operator Interface. By configuring the Batch Operator Interface screens individually, developers can determine what types of information operators receive. The screens are configured by accessing the System Configuration and Defaults window in the Batch Operator Interface. From the System Configuration window, you can choose from a series of 15 labeled tabs. Each of these tabs opens a window that allows you to configure the corresponding Batch Operator Interface screen or section of a Batch Operator Interface screen. To ensure that the batch production environment is fully operational, supervisory personnel should evaluate the customized Batch Operator Interface screens. Once this has been done, the batch production process can begin. You can perform the following tasks from the System Configuration and Defaults window: Display or Hide Columns Change Column and Row Sizes Order and Prioritize Sorts Change Fonts Change Filters When configuring large systems with multiple Batch Operator Interface workstations, it is easier to configure one workstation's screens and copy the configuration than it is to manually set up each workstation. Prompting for an action, confirming an action and verifying an action are configured on each Batch Executive. Enabling commands can be configured at the Batch Executive or for each Batch Operator Interface. To transfer one workstation's screens setup to another Batch Operator Interface workstation, copy the DVBClient.ini file from the configured workstation to the other workstations. Go to the C:\DeltaV\DVData\Batch folder. Select the DVBClient.ini file. Right-click and select Copy from the context menu. Go to the DeltaV\DVData\Batch folder on the other machines and paste the file. Note: You can access the other workstations' hard drives if they are all on the same DeltaV network. Use Windows' Network Neighborhood to browse for the workstation and DVData folder. Related information Filtering information in Batch Operator Interface screens The Batch Executive properties

title: Customizing the alarm banner
body_text: Customizing the alarm banner The DeltaV system allows you to manage how alarms are presented to your operator. The alarm banner in particular enables you to present alarm information to operators concisely and intuitively while minimizing nuisance alarms The alarm banner provides an overview of the operator's highest priority alarms. The alarms shown are based on the areas for which the operator is responsible and are assigned to that operator's workstation. The alarm banner also provides the ability to select an alarm and go immediately to an associated display. The DeltaV system supports 12 different alarm priorities. Each priority includes a number of user-defined characteristics. You define alarm priorities in the DeltaV Explorer under Setup/Alarm Preferences . Once the alarm priorities have been defined, all alarms in your DeltaV system of that priority will behave the same (for example, they have the same color, sound, and acknowledge characteristics). Each priority has an alarm banner option of Not Hidden , Module or Unit . This option is set in the Alarm Priority Properties dialog. Not Hidden specifies that active alarms of this priority are always shown in the alarm banner. The Unit and Module selections specify that alarms of this priority are displayed in the alarm banner only if they are the most important alarm for the associated Unit or Module. The default selection is Not Hidden . Since there is no one right approach for alarm presentation, the DeltaV system offers you the flexibility to easily define system-wide alarm presentation. The following table shows six typical alarm presentation methods. Select the method that best matches your plant operating philosophy. You can use combinations of the alarm presentation methods. Any combination of methods should follow a general philosophy. As you develop an alarm presentation philosophy, consider whether lower priority alarms should be treated differently than higher priority alarms or, consider the changes that should be made in alarm behavior as the alarm priority increases. Another approach is to think of the 12 priorities as three groups of four, where the characteristics are determined by the priority's placement within the group. Changing the default alarm presentation or a presentation method that you selected is quick and easy. Simply change each alarm priority in the DeltaV Explorer and download the Changed Setup Data to each workstation. Alarm priority changes are immediately seen on the workstations. Alarm Presentation Methods Alarm Banner Behavior Typical Use Alarm Philosophy What if a module has one alarm that is critical and another alarm that is not? What do I see in the alarm banner? 1. Show all alarms (All alarm priorities configured to Not Hidden. This is the default.) The alarm banner shows all alarms in priority order. When multiple alarms are active on the same module, multiple alarms are shown in the alarm banner for that module. Systems with a smaller number of alarms per operator. It is important for operators to see each individual alarm. The module is shown twice displaying the critical alarm and the other alarm in priority order. 2. Show alarms by module (All alarm priorities configured to Module.) The alarm banner shows alarms in priority order, by module. When multiple alarms are active on the same module, only the highest priority alarm is shown in the alarm banner for that module. Systems with a medium number of alarms per operator. Showing every alarm adds too much clutter to the alarm banner. Operators need to see which modules have alarm activity. Showing only the highest priority alarm per module is the most productive approach. The module is shown once displaying the critical alarm. 3. Show alarms by unit (All alarm priorities configured to Unit.) The alarm banner shows alarms in priority order, by unit. When multiple alarms are active within the same unit, only the highest priority alarm is shown in the alarm banner for that unit. Systems with a larger number of alarms per operator. Operators need an overview of the plant from the alarm banner. Showing only the highest priority alarm per unit is the most productive approach. The unit is shown once displaying the critical (highest priority) alarm. 4. Show critical (high priority) alarms always, other (lower priority) alarms by module Critical Alarms The alarm banner shows all critical alarms in priority order. When multiple critical alarms are active on the same module, multiple alarms are shown in the alarm banner for that module. All Other Alarms The alarm banner shows alarms in priority order, by module. When multiple alarms are active on the same module, only the highest priority alarm is shown in the alarm banner for that module. Systems with a medium number of alarms per operator, with some very critical alarms. There are some alarms that must always be presented to the operator. However, the majority of the other alarms are best presented by module. Both alarms are active and unacknowledged - the module is shown once displaying the critical alarm. Both alarms are active and only the critical alarm is unacknowledged - the module is shown once displaying the critical alarm. Both alarms are active and only the non-critical alarm is unacknowledged - the module is shown twice displaying both the critical alarm and other alarm. 5. Show critical (high priority) alarms always, other (lower priority) alarms by unit Critical Alarms The alarm banner shows all critical alarms in priority order. When multiple critical alarms are active on the same module, multiple alarms are shown in the alarm banner for that module. All Other Alarms The alarm banner shows alarms in priority order, by unit. When multiple alarms are active on the same unit, only the highest priority alarm within that unit is shown in the alarm banner for that module. Systems with a larger number of alarms per operator, with some very critical alarms. There are some alarms that must always be presented to the operator. However, the majority of the other alarms are best presented by unit. The module and the critical alarm show once. The unit and the other alarm show once. 6. Show critical (high priority) alarms by module, other (lower priority) alarms by unit Critical Alarms The alarm banner shows alarms in priority order, by module. When multiple critical alarms are active on the same module, only the highest priority alarm is shown in the alarm banner for that module. All Other Alarms The alarm banner shows alarms in priority order, by unit. When multiple alarms are active on the same unit, only the highest priority alarm within that unit is shown in the alarm banner for that module. Systems with a larger number of alarms per operator, with multiple critical alarms on modules. There are a number of critical alarms. Often there is more than one critical alarm on the same module. However, operators only need to know if a module has any critical alarm active. The majority of other alarms are best presented by unit. The module and the critical alarm show once. The unit and the other alarm show once. Subtopics: Changing the alarm icons Sounding the horn with alarms

title: Customizing the event journal file
body_text: Customizing the event journal file The operator can customize each Event Journal file by configuring specific sort and filter criteria for each file. This configuration is done from the System Configuration and Defaults screen. In addition to this standard method of filtering and sorting, these tasks can also be configured in the Event Journal screen for the file that is currently open. Related information Customizing Batch Operator Interface screens

title: Customizing the Alarm Banner display
body_text: Customizing the Alarm Banner display The Alarm Banner display provides operators the means to maintain awareness of the most important alarms in their scope of alarm responsibility and the means to respond to those alarms. DeltaV Live provides six out of the box Alarm Banner displays, a desk version and a wall version for 4x3, 16x9, and 16x10 screens. If you want an alarm banner to extend across multiple screens in a layout, you can use additional Alarm Banner displays to continue the alarm numbering. To designate where in the layout the Alarm Banner display should open, reference it from a display frame. Each Alarm Banner display contains one out of the box Alarm Banner GEM, which is linked to the Alarm Banner GEM class. If you do not want the Alarm Banner display to be included in an operator's search results, mark the display as Not discoverable in production . You can also configure alarm thresholds for each workstation using Alarm Banner properties.

title: Customizing displays for alarm presentation
body_text: Customizing displays for alarm presentation DeltaV Live provides several alarm components and features to help you customize the operator interface and manage how alarms are presented to operators so that they can maintain situational awareness of abnormal conditions and respond efficiently to their alarms. This section explains these components and features. Subtopics: Customizing the alarm list Customizing the display alarm rollup Customizing the Alarm Banner display

title: Customizing the display alarm rollup
body_text: Customizing the display alarm rollup A display alarm rollup is a graphics element used on displays to show operators a summary of alarms associated with a certain display. Alarm summary information can include a count of active alarms and the alarm priority and state for the top alarm. The alarm priority is indicated by the alarm rollup color while the alarm state is indicated by ?????. In Graphics Studio, the display alarm rollup is added to a display from the ??? palette and configured in the Graphics Configuration pane. Like the alarm list element, you can configure the appearance and alarms context for the display alarm rollup. For example, you can configure the alarm rollup to dynamically adjust its context online or appear next to its corresponding display name in a layout's navigation bar. Additionally, you can configure the alarm rollup to filter by plant hierarchy rather than primary control display. The specific section of the plant hierarchy to use for each display is determined by a <Plant Hierarchy Association> string parameter on the display, so for each display, you must associate this parameter with the correct area, unit, or equipment module. Note: When the alarm list and display alarm rollup are added to a display, some of their default parameter values reference the library functions for AlarmPriorityIcon, AlarmPriorityColor, and AlarmPriorityTextColor. Therefore, if you change the colors or icons for out of the box alarms, you should modify these functions rather than delete them and create new ones.

title: Using animation to customize graphics configurations
main_heading: Using animation to customize graphics configurations
body_text: Using animation to customize graphics configurations Displays are intended to reflect real-time conditions in the control process. Live data is constantly changing, and operators need the ability to acquire and interpret this data in ways that can improve their understanding of and reactions to what is happening in the control process. You can animate various properties of graphics configurations to transform live date into a single value of a desired type, thus providing the means for operators to see display graphics dynamically change as online values change. Layouts, displays, GEM classes, and elements all contain certain animatable properties. You can create three kinds of animations: simple animations, blink animations, or library animations. The property type determines the kind of animation you can create. These animations are configured in the Graphics Configuration pane by clicking the diamond next to the property you want to animate and selecting the desired kind of animation from the Diamond context menu. The sections below provide information about kind of animation. Creating simple animations Simple animations are created by selecting Animate from the Diamond context menu and configuring the new properties that appear. These simple animations are embedded within the element (cannot be shared) and can be applied to property types of Boolean, percentage, measurement, degree, and font. For each property type, you can create an animation compatible with that type. The property type determines which new configurable properties you need to configure. The list below describes the kind of animation you can create for each property type. Boolean Boolean animations use a logical expression supporting multiple terms to produce a True/False result. The expression references a DeltaV parameter and sets the rule for when the parameter value is true or false. For example, you can animate the Visibility property on a data link to have the data link visible only when a certain condition is met. These conditions are defined in the logical expression. To animate a Boolean property, you must define a DeltaV parameter value and in some cases, a default value. Percentage Percentage animations convert a dynamic value to a scaled result ranging from 0 to 100 percent. This type of animation includes an expression defining what to fill, fill options, and scale information. For example, you could animate a Fill Percent property on any graphics element to show it as filled or partially filled. To animate percent property, you must define what is to be filled, DeltaV scaling parameter for the fill, a default scale, and a default value. Measurement Measurement animations use linear scaling to convert a dynamic value to a result within a specified range of measurement values. For example, you can animate the Vertical Position to make a pointer on a display move up and down on a display. To animate a measurement property, you must define a DeltaV parameter reference value, DeltaV scaling parameter for the measurement, a default scale, a start and end point, and a default value. Degree Degree animations use linear scaling to convert a dynamic value to a result within a range of angular measurements (in degrees). For example, you can animate the Rotation Angle to make a needle on a radial gauge appear to swivel. To animate a degree property, you must define a DeltaV parameter value, DeltaV scaling parameter, a default scale, a minimum and maximum degree bounds, and a direction of rotation. Font Font animations are a type of Boolean animation that use a logical expression to produce an alternate Font and font characteristics when certain conditions are met. These conditions are defined in the logical expression. For example, you can animate the font on a button to become bolded red when a certain condition is met. To animate a font property, you must define an alternate font, the condition that triggers the alternate font, and a default font. When you select Animation , the property field and orange diamond indicate that an animation has been applied. Creating blink animations Blink animations, which are created only on color-type properties, allow an element to alternate between its normal color and its configured alternate color. Blink animations are created by selecting Blink Animation from the Diamond context menu and configuring the new properties that appear. When you select Blink Animation, the property field and orange diamond indicate that a blink animation has been applied. To animate a color property, you must define the condition that triggers the alternate color, the normal and alternate color, the duration for the normal and alternate color, and a default color. Creating library animations Library animations are created by selecting Library Animation from the Diamond context menu and then selecting a library function from a pop-up list. Library animations can be applied to property types of Boolean, percentage, measurement, degree, and font. For each property type, you can reference a library function of the same type. If the function you need does not exist, you can create a new library function from the Library Explorer pane. After saving the new function, return to the Graphics Configuration pane to reference this function.
