title: Do DeltaV services fail to start automatically?
main_heading: Do DeltaV services fail to start automatically?
body_text: Do DeltaV services fail to start automatically? The main problems that cause this to occur are: The DeltaV software might be installed under an account other than the one you usually log into. The installation program only adds the user who installed the DeltaV software to the DeltaV security group. To add the account under which you are trying to run DeltaV software to the security group, use the User Manager. The DeltaVAdmin password has expired. It is strongly recommended that this password be set to never expire. if the password expires and you then stop the DeltaV services or reboot a node, the services do not start and the DeltaV system does not function as expected. If the password can expire you must change the password before expiration . Use either the DeltaV Security Administration application ( Start > All Programs > DeltaV > Installation ) or the ServPwd utility (found in the \DeltaV\Bin directory) to prevent system disruption. The file permissions for the path you installed to might be too restrictive. The file permissions are inherited from the parent directory. If you install into a parent directory that has restricted access, the DeltaV system will not be able to access the files it needs to run. Change the file permissions so that the DeltaV group is allowed access to the installation directories and all of its subdirectories. There might be a problem with one of your network interface cards. In the Diagnostics program, click Tools > Windows Event Viewer > Windows Logs > System . To verify that the DeltaV program was started, click Start > Settings > Control Panel > Administrative Tools , and then double-click the Services icon.

title: Understanding fieldbus block errors
body_text: Understanding fieldbus block errors Function block errors show up as yellow question marks ( ) in Control Studio online. DeltaV function blocks, including those capable of running in fieldbus devices, report standard function block error information through the BLOCK_ERR parameter. Each block's BLOCK_ERR parameter is documented in Books Online. Function blocks that run in fieldbus devices report additional, device-specific block error information through BLOCK_ERR. You must refer to the device documentation to understand these device-specific errors. Also, more information on device block errors may be available from the device's Status/Conditions context menu item. Among the most common block errors seen with the DeltaV system are Out of Service, Input Failure/Bad PV, Configuration Error, Link Configuration Error: Out of Service: One or more of the blocks (function block, Resource block, Transducer block) is in Out of Service (OOS) mode. To see the function block mode, look at its MODE parameter in Control Studio. To see the Resource and Transducer blocks' mode, select the device in DeltaV Explorer, select Status > Conditions , and look for the mode information. Input Failure/Bad PV: Often, this is caused by an incorrect channel, incorrect choices in the XD_SCALE parameter, failures in the Transducer block, or the Transducer block is in OOS mode. Configuration Error: Most likely this is caused by an incorrect channel and/or incorrect choices in the XD_SCALE parameter. Link Configuration Error: This is often device-specific and could mean that the device does not accept a certain configuration or a link is improperly configured. For example, not all devices support a configuration in which two fieldbus links from one function block output running in one fieldbus device are connected to two inputs in another device. Refer to the device documentation's description for this block error. Device-Specific Errors The following errors refer to internal device errors that may be serious and may require service or device replacement. Refer to the device documentation if you encounter these errors: Lost NV Data Lost Static Data Memory Failure The following errors are used by the manufacturer to alert users of a possible device problem and to alert users that the device needs maintenance now or in the near future: Device Needs Maintenance Now Device Needs Maintenance Soon Related information Fieldbus device general Information Cannot download a fieldbus module

title: Drawing with connection points and tips
main_heading: Drawing with connection points and tips
body_text: Drawing with connection points and tips Lines, connectors, and arcs are often used on a display to represent process piping while other elements are used to represent process vessels. Connection points and tips provide both visual and graphical cues that help you connect lines, connectors, and arcs with these other elements. When you attach a connection tip to a connection point on another element, they snap together and form a perfectly aligned connection. If the element is moved to a different position on the Content pane, the connection remains attached and moves with it. Tip: When drawing a line or connector, hover over the element to which you are connecting to see its connection points. The following table shows which elements have connection points or connection tips: Element Has connection points Has connection tips Arc Yes Yes Chord Yes No Connector Yes Yes Display Link Yes No Ellipse Yes No Image Yes No Line Yes Yes Pie Yes No Rectangle Yes No Polygon Yes No Rounded Rectangle Yes No Text Yes No Trapezoid Yes No Triangle Yes No While a group element has no connection points or tips of its own, you can still use the connection points and tips of all the group's nested members. A GEM has connection points only if they have been added to its GEM class. Once added to a GEM class, connection points are available on any GEMs linked to it. If a linked GEM is converted to an unlinked GEM, it retains its connection points. Drawing with the Connector element The connector element draws three segments, with elbows, that are each constrained to be either horizontal or vertical. The direction of the first segment is determined by the direction you drag the connection tip when you first begin drawing with the connector. Using configurable endpoints All elements with configurable endpoints, such as arcs, lines, or connectors, have both connection points and connection tips at their start and end points. This configuration can be useful, for instance, when you need to show a long pipe flowing in one direction. These elements, each with an arrow endpoint, can be chained together to indicate the continuous flow.

title: Firewall rules for DeltaV
body_text: Firewall rules for DeltaV During the installation of DeltaV, inbound firewall rules for DeltaV and Emerson products were created and stored for the Windows firewall. These rules allow inbound communication on the port specified in the rule. All rules are disabled by default, meaning the ports are not open for inbound communications. The default Windows firewall settings allow all outbound communications on all ports (this follows the CIS (Center for Internet Security) recommendations). Firewall rules are applied only to the profiles and network interface cards specified in the Windows Firewall Advanced Settings dialog. Enable/disable the rules through the DeltaV Security Administration application. You can view the rules' properties in the Windows firewall interface. With the Windows firewall enabled, all default Windows firewall rules are applied. The DeltaV rules are in addition to the default Windows firewall rules. Important: Do not edit the DeltaV rules. If you need a specific rule, you must create a new rule and configure it as needed. Any rules created by you are your responsibility to test and validate with your DeltaV system. You can create a new rule by copying the existing DeltaV rule and modifying it. Open the Windows Firewall with Advanced Security application and select the DeltaV rule (for example, OPC: OPC UA Server). Copy and paste the rule and rename it to something meaningful. Edit the rule's properties to change what is needed; for example, a different default OPC UA Server TCP port to match what you have configured in DeltaV Explorer (for that protocol). Enable the new rule as an incoming rule on non-DeltaV networks. You are still responsible for testing and validating this change works in your DeltaV system. The firewall rules are removed when DeltaV is uninstalled.

When in a domain, you must be a domain administrator to manage the domain user accounts. Note: This may require a download of the Professional or ProfessionalPLUS workstation so that the user account is established in the DeltaV database. You should run the DeltaV Security Administration on every DeltaV workstation, performing all the tasks pertinent to the workstation (users enabled/disabled, auditing of the files and services, managing the Windows firewall rules, and so on). Launch the DeltaV Security Administration from the Start menu on a DeltaV workstation. title: Device Signal Tags (DSTs)
body_text: Device Signal Tags (DSTs) Device Tags represent instruments, valves, and other field devices. A DST consists of a Device Tag and a specific signal from that device. The licenses purchased with the system determine the number and types of DSTs allowed by the system. DSTs in DeltaV controllers are identified based on the manner in which the application is configured. Function blocks are grouped into modules. Inputs and outputs from Classic I/O, Serial I/O, Profibus I/O, AS-Interface I/O, and DeviceNet I/O referenced by the function blocks are DSTs.

When this occurs, the system will ignore the unused unit alias and filter accordingly. This requires that your equipment train is configured appropriately with #TNK# being downstream of both #MIX# and #REACT#.

title: Unit allocation and recipes with divergent and convergent recipes
main_heading: Unit allocation and recipes with divergent and convergent recipes
body_text: Unit allocation and recipes with divergent and convergent recipes The list of unit aliases in the equipment train class, the list of selectable units in the equipment train and the list of downstream units for a unit module are all 'anded' lists. This means that when a procedure using equipment trains contains a divergence or convergence, the list of possible units must be the intersection of the units. If no units intersect, the operator is prompted with a list of all units as configured in the equipment train.

title: Unit allocation and recipes with parallel steps
main_heading: Unit allocation and recipes with parallel steps
body_text: Unit allocation and recipes with parallel steps When a recipe with parallel steps runs, the system simultaneously evaluates the equipment configuration to determine the potential units. When the selection mode is Defer and the unit aliases (all different but of the same unit class) are not assigned, the operator is prompted for all the parallel steps and the list of units in all steps is identical. Therefore, it is possible for the operator to select the same unit for each step. However, when the selection mode is From_Policy, the system processes the list of units and when acquiring the units, verifies that no other step in the batch is using that unit already.

title: DeltaV Smart Switches and Media Modules
main_heading: DeltaV Smart Switches and Media Modules
body_text: DeltaV Smart Switches and Media Modules The DeltaV Smart Switches are used to construct DeltaV Control Networks according to the IEEE 802.3 Local and Metropolitan Area Networks standards. The DeltaV Smart Switches are DeltaV MD base Smart Switches and media modules DeltaV RM100 base Smart Switches and media modules DeltaV RM104 Smart Switches DeltaV FP20 8-port Smart Switches DeltaV Smart Switches are intended for plug and play use with a DeltaV system. No configuration is necessary unless you want to access a switch with Telnet, monitor a switch with a web-based switch interface from a Management station or use the DeltaV version 10.3 One-Click Lockdown application to lock the switches to prevent unauthorized devices from being connected to unused ports on the switches. In DeltaV version 11.3 and 12.3, Smart Switches are commissioned using the DeltaV Smart Switch Command Center (SSCC). In DeltaV version 13.3 and higher, Smart Switches are commissioned using the Network Device Command Center (NDCC). When you commission the switches using the NDCC (or Smart Switch Command Center (SSCC) in earlier versions), the switch is given a network address and associated with a control module so that switch hardware conditions can be interpreted as DeltaV alarms. Monitoring a switch with the web-based switch interface requires Java software that can be downloaded from the Internet. A serial interface cable is required to connect the switch’s serial port to the Management station in order to set up the switches. The serial interface cable can be purchased separately from Emerson or you can build the cable assembly. The following figure shows the pin outs for building the serial interface cable assembly. Different pin outs are used for each end of the cable. Serial Interface Cable Pin Outs Media modules with fiber-optic network ports are fixed to 100Mbit full duplex communication (except for ports that use SFP media modules that are fixed at either 100Mbit or 1 gigabit full duplex). When DeltaV Smart Switches are used in an existing network, all existing fiber-optic connections must be set to 100Mbit full duplex for the switches to communicate. For example, if DeltaV Smart Switches are installed in a network with 3Com switches, you must change the 3Com switches from the default half duplex to full duplex. Refer to Books Online for DeltaV version 10.3 for information on the One-Click Lockdown application, for information on configuring, monitoring, and accessing the switches with Telnet, and for information on downloading Java software. Refer to Books Online for DeltaV version 11.3 and 12.3 for information about the Smart Switch Command Center. Refer to Books Online for DeltaV version 13.3 for information about the Network Device Command Center (NDCC). Before installing and using DeltaV Smart Switches and media modules, refer to the important safety information in the System Administration and Maintenance manual in Books Online. title: DeltaV Smart Switches and Media Modules
main_heading: DeltaV Smart Switches and Media Modules
body_text: DeltaV Smart Switches and Media Modules The DeltaV Smart Switches are used to construct DeltaV Control Networks according to the IEEE 802.3 Local and Metropolitan Area Networks standards. The DeltaV Smart Switches are DeltaV MD base Smart Switches and media modules DeltaV RM100 base Smart Switches and media modules DeltaV RM104 Smart Switches DeltaV FP20 8-port Smart Switches DeltaV Smart Switches are intended for plug and play use with a DeltaV system. No configuration is necessary unless you want to access a switch with Telnet, monitor a switch with a web-based switch interface from a Management station or use the DeltaV version 10.3 One-Click Lockdown application to lock the switches to prevent unauthorized devices from being connected to unused ports on the switches. In DeltaV version 11.3 and 12.3, Smart Switches are commissioned using the DeltaV Smart Switch Command Center (SSCC). In DeltaV version 13.3 and higher, Smart Switches are commissioned using the Network Device Command Center (NDCC). When you commission the switches using the NDCC (or Smart Switch Command Center (SSCC) in earlier versions), the switch is given a network address and associated with a control module so that switch hardware conditions can be interpreted as DeltaV alarms. Monitoring a switch with the web-based switch interface requires Java software that can be downloaded from the Internet. A serial interface cable is required to connect the switch’s serial port to the Management station in order to set up the switches. The serial interface cable can be purchased separately from Emerson or you can build the cable assembly. The following figure shows the pin outs for building the serial interface cable assembly. Different pin outs are used for each end of the cable. When DeltaV Smart Switches are used in an existing network, all existing fiber-optic connections must be set to 100Mbit full duplex for the switches to communicate. For example, if DeltaV Smart Switches are installed in a network with 3Com switches, you must change the 3Com switches from the default half duplex to full duplex. title: DeltaV Batch concepts
body_text: DeltaV Batch concepts DeltaV Batch supports standard batch concepts and follows the ISA S88.01 , Namur NE33 Batch , and IEC 61131-3 standards. The ISA standard defines a consistent set of terminology and models to define the control requirements for batch manufacturing plants. The ISA standard and DeltaV Batch are based on procedural and physical models that emphasize good plant design and operation practices. The system features a single, completely integrated database that coordinates all batch configuration activities. Easy-to-use tools are provided for the following: Configuring physical and procedural models Creating and executing recipes Integrating batch actions with the control system Generating and storing production information in an object database DeltaV Batch is a class-based system. Many batch manufacturing plants have multiple production lines made up of the same or very similar equipment. Using classes in developing the process control system greatly simplifies the configuration process. For example, instead of fully defining the control logic for each of 100 identical or nearly identical valves, the control engineer defines the logic for the control module class and then creates 100 instances of the class (that is, control modules). It is then necessary to specify only the I/O references and any configurable parameters that differ for the individual control modules. Changes made to the class are automatically propagated to the instances, except for parameter values that have been changed at the instance level. Classes can be defined for the following: phases, control modules, equipment modules, units, and process cells. Subtopics: Batch Tutorial terminology DeltaV Batch configuration applications Related information Appendix A - DeltaV batch and S88

title: The DeltaV Batch Executive
body_text: The DeltaV Batch Executive The DeltaV Batch Executive consists of the Batch Manager service, the Batch Runtime Server, and the individual batch runner applications. One instance of a batch runner is created for every running batch. Each batch runner is responsible for taking the batch through all its states and for communicating to the Batch Manager for equipment arbitration and any other inter-runner or client-based communications. The Batch Manager is responsible for managing the batch runners. It also sends information from the runners to clients (such as the Batch Operator Interface and Campaign Manager Server) that require run-time data. In the tutorial, we will configure the Batch Executive on the same workstation on which we are doing configuration and operation. However, optimal performance of the Batch Executive is achieved by installing the Batch Executive on its own Application Station. Consult your Emerson representative before installing a Batch Executive on a workstation other than an Application Station. Note: You cannot run the Batch Executive, Recipe Simulator, or Batch Operator Interface without first enabling Batch on the node (on the Systems Preferences dialog) and then enabling the Batch Executive on the workstation (on the Batch Executive Properties dialog in the DeltaV Explorer). Options you need to configure when enabling the Batch Executive are: Remove files older than (days) - sets the maximum number of days for which batch event records are stored in the .evt file. Restart Behavior - sets the method for restarting the Batch Executive. Choices are: Query User - allows the user to select between Warm & Cold Restarts or Cancel the operation . Warm Restart - returns the Batch Executive to its last known state. Control recipes, manually controlled phases, and arbitration functions are returned to the state that existed prior to termination of the Batch Executive. The warm boot method is only used to recover batches and data after an unexpected loss of the Batch Executive. Cold Restart - starts Batch Executive with an empty batch list and with no resources allocated to the operator. Hold propagation limit - sets the level to which a Hold propagates. The choices are Phase , UOP (operation) , UPC (unit procedure) , and BPC (procedure) . Allow manual phase history to be combined with other batch history - enables the ability to combine a manual phase's history with another batch's history (for example, with the 'parent' batch). When you start the manual phase you are given the option to select a batch (by batch ID) with which the manual phase history will be combined. You can also opt to not combine histories at this point. title: Display levels
body_text: Display levels Displays can be optimized by presenting information in a way that increases situational awareness for operators. One way to create this situational awareness is to provide operators with various levels of displays, where each display level presents a different level of detail. ANSI/ISA recommends four levels of displays, with level 1, or the overview level, having the broadest scope, and level 4 having the most focused scope. These varying levels of detail allow operators to view their entire scope of responsibility and then drill down to increased levels of detail and control functionality. Each display level presents the relevant information operators need to perform their duties. Displays are designated to a particular navigation level by assigning them to a display set. The four display levels are: Level 1 (overview) displays present an at-a-glance overview of the control process within an operator’s scope of responsibility. These displays show the lowest level of process or system detail. The information presented here aids operators in identifying, processing, and comprehending the critical elements of a plant's operations. Level 2 displays allow the operator to drill down into smaller portions of the areas they are responsible for. These displays present information that aids operators in monitoring and operating the elements they are responsible for on a daily basis. For example, an operator may be responsible for operating multiple process units. Level 2 displays provide a process unit level overview for each of those units. dialog then indicates displays that are marked as a work in progress. Level 3 displays allow operators to drill down into subsystems, showing a portion of a level 2 display with an increased level of detail. Level 4 displays are used for diagnostics and show equipment or systems related to level 3 displays in greater detail, such as faceplates or detail displays.

title: Building graphics expressions
body_text: Building graphics expressions A graphics expression is a language-neutral, TypeScript expression that provides a means for the properties of graphics configurations and elements to reference either live data or values within the system and then resolve that information to a single value at the appropriate time in DeltaV Live online. The resulting value either presents itself to users as it is or presents the information in a more useful way, such as through animation. Online graphics update periodically to reflect the dynamic value determined by the expression's result. Graphics expressions can be configured for any property that supports opening the Script Assistant and a browser window. You can build these expressions by entering the expression in the property field, browsing to the desired value, or using the Script Assistant. Graphics expressions are built using the DeltaV Live-supported TypeScript operators, TypeScript-specific objects and their functions, DeltaV-specific objects and their functions, and DeltaV Live prefixes that allow you to reference various values. These expressions are evaluated using data quality information available for DeltaV parameters. If the data quality for any DeltaV parameter value in the expression is anything other than good, the data quality for the final computed value reflects the worst data quality. title: DeltaV Live online modes
body_text: DeltaV Live online modes This topic explains the two modes in which DeltaV Live can run, Window mode vs Full Desktop mode. DeltaV Live online can run in Window mode or Full Desktop mode, on either the Windows Desktop or the DeltaV Desktop. In Window mode, multiple instances of DeltaV Live can run on either desktop, with each instance behaving as a Windows application. In Full Desktop mode, only one instance of DeltaV Live can run on each desktop, with that instance taking over the entire video desktop. When configuring a workstation, you select the mode, Window or Full Desktop, in which each instance of DeltaV Live starts. You can also dedicate a workstation as a DeltaV Live-only workstation by configuring it to open in Full Desktop mode on the DeltaV Desktop. When configured as such, the workstation immediately launches DeltaV Live when the user logs on, and provides the user access to only DeltaV Live (online).

title: Publishing configurations
body_text: Publishing configurations Updates to most graphics configurations, as well as workstation configurations, are not available online prior to publishing. Publishing, a command initiated by users, authorizes graphics configurations and DeltaV Live workstations to be deployed for use online and on all DeltaV Live workstations that should have it. When a graphics configuration or workstation is published, it is marked as available for a workstation to retrieve it. Workstations that are communicating retrieve configurations as soon as they are published. Workstations that are not communicating retrieve published configurations as soon as the workstations begin communicating. Operators receive an indication that updates have arrived, but to ensure that publishing does not interrupt their normal workflow, they choose when to accept those updates. The following configurations, when created or modified, must be published for their updates to be available online: DeltaV Live workstations Languages Themes displays Display sets Contextual displays Layouts Standards Functions Note: GEM classes do not require publishing. Instead, when a GEM class is modified, the displays containing the GEMs linked to that GEM class must be published. Items within a configuration cannot be published on their own. For example, graphics elements or GEMs located within displays, or screens located within layouts, are only published as part of their containing display or layout. When you select a Publish command, the Publish dialog opens. The check boxes are automatically selected next to all items that are eligible for publishing and that meet the selected publishing command's criteria. Displays that are set as a Work in Progress appear in the Publish dialog but are not automatically selected for publishing. If you are not ready to publish an item on the list, deselect the check box next to it. Setting displays as a Work in Progress If you are not ready to publish changes you made to a display, you can set it as a Work in Progress . When you modify a GEM class, you can also notify the displays containing that class's linked GEMs that you want those displays to be set as a Work in Progress . Then, if you attempt to publish displays set as a Work in Progress, they are automatically deselected in the Publish dialog. You can still choose to publish them by selecting the appropriate check box. The Publish Pending indicator The icon indicates that a configuration has publishable changes pending, and the icon indicates that a container or folder contains at least one configuration with publishable changes pending. When a configuration has been added or modified, a publish pending indicator appears next to its name in the Explorer view, or for workstations, in the Workstation Management dialog. When a GEM class is modified, the displays containing its linked GEMs, rather than the GEM class, show a publish pending indicator. Un-Publishing configurations If you want to remove a published graphics configuration or workstation from online but not from the configuration database, you can un-publish it. Once you un-publish a configuration or workstation, it is no longer running on any workstations. Note: To delete a configuration or workstation from the configuration database, you must first un-publish it.

title: DeltaV Live (online) overview
body_text: DeltaV Live (online) overview DeltaV Live (online) is the environment from which plant operators monitor and control their plant processes. It provides a customizable interactive experience that presents both real-time and historical information for operations supervisory staff, engineers, and production management.

title: DeltaV Live workstations
body_text: DeltaV Live workstations A DeltaV Live workstation is a DeltaV workstation authorized to run DeltaV Live software and participate in DeltaV Live configuration deployment (publishing). After installing DeltaV Live, the DeltaV ProfessionalPLUS workstation is enabled by default and automatically authorized to run the DeltaV Live configuration database and all DeltaV Live applications. The ProfessionalPLUS workstation is always enabled as a DeltaV Live workstation; this status cannot be changed. Workstations that need to run DeltaV Live must be manually enabled as DeltaV Live workstations. You can configure certain online behaviors for a DeltaV Live workstation, such as which layout, display sets (if any), or themes (if any) are available for use on that workstation/session. DeltaV Live workstations are configured in DeltaV Live Administration (Workstation Management dialog). Updates to DeltaV Live workstation configuration must be published before they can be deployed to the running system. If you remove a DeltaV Live workstation, the affected workstation remains active until all DeltaV Live applications running on it are closed. To provide a more secure operating environment, a DeltaV workstation can be configured as a dedicated DeltaV Live workstation, limiting operators to the DeltaV Live application and to those applications available to the user through DeltaV Live. When the user logs on to a dedicated DeltaV Live workstation, it automatically switches to the DeltaV Desktop and launches directly into DeltaV Live. To configure a dedicated DeltaV Live workstation, the following conditions must be true: The DeltaV Live workstation is configured to start in Full Desktop mode These FlexLock settings are selected: Autoswitch Desktop Autorun DeltaV Live The online applications you select to use determine where the FlexLock settings are configured. If the workstation is configured to use… FlexLock settings are configured in… DeltaV Live only DeltaV Live Administration Both DeltaV Operate and DeltaV Live FlexLock Application Note: DeltaV Live applications are not supported on Application Stations, Remote Operator Stations, Remote Application Stations, or Inter-Zone Servers.

title: DeltaV Series 2 I/O
body_text: DeltaV Series 2 I/O DeltaV Series 2 I/O cards have a wider operating temperature range than pre-Series 2 cards and some Series 2 cards support redundancy. The following DeltaV I/O cards are available as Series 2: AI, 8-Channel, 4-20 mA (Series 2 simplex) AI, 4-20 mA, HART (Series 2 simplex and redundant; 2 and 4 wire) AI, 16, Channel, 4-20 mA, HART (Series 2 simplex) AO, 8-channel, 4-20 mA, HART (Series 2 simplex and redundant) AS-Interface (Series 2 simplex) DeviceNet (Series 2 simplex) DI, 8-Channel, 24 VDC, Dry Contact (Series 2 simplex and redundant) DI, 8-Channel, 24 VDC, Isolated (Series 2 simplex) DI, 8-Channel, 120 VAC, Dry Contact (Series 2 simplex) DI, 8-Channel, 120 VAC, Isolated (Series 2 simplex) DI, 32-Channel, 24 VDC, Dry Contact (Series 2 simplex) DO, 8-Channel, 24 VDC, High-Side (Series 2 simplex and redundant) DO, 8-Channel, 24 VDC, Isolated (Series 2 simplex) DO, 8-Channel, 120 VAC/230 VAC, High-Side (Series 2 simplex) DO, 8-Channel, 120 VAC/230 VAC, Isolated (Series 2 simplex) DO, 32-Channel, 24 VDC, High-Side (Series 2 simplex) Series 2 H1 (Series 2 simplex and redundant) Isolated Input (Series 2 simplex) Multifunction (Series 2 simplex) RTD, ohms (Series 2 simplex) Thermocouple (Series 2 simplex) Series 2 Profibus DP (Series 2 simplex) Series 2 Plus Profibus DP (Series 2 simplex and redundant) Sequence of Events (Series 2 simplex) Series 2 Serial (Series 2 simplex and redundant) Series 2 redundant capable cards are configured, autosensed, upgraded, and operated just like pre-Series 2 cards. Series 2 cards in Simplex mode can function as drop-in replacements for pre-Series 2 cards of the same type. With the exception of the Simplex mode Series 2 H1 card, which requires the Series 2 H1 terminal block, no wiring change is required to replace a pre-Series 2 card. Series 2 cards report their operating mode (simplex or redundant) to the DeltaV controller based on the type of terminal block on which they are installed. Redundant terminal blocks provide wiring terminations for the redundant cards. If a card is installed on a redundant terminal block, it reports itself as operating in Redundant mode; otherwise, it reports itself as operating in Simplex mode. Other than redundant terminal blocks, no additional software or hardware is required to support redundancy. A redundant terminal block spans two adjacent slots on the carrier. A redundant I/O card consists of two Series 2 cards installed in a redundant terminal block. Note: For redundant I/O, the lower slot number (in the carrier) in a redundant pair must be odd and the upper slot number must be the next higher even number. For example, redundant pairs can be installed in slots 1 and 2, 3 and 4, 9 and 10. Redundant pairs cannot be installed in slots 6 and 7, 24 and 25. Configuration tools such as the DeltaV Explorer enforce this requirement. The double-wide redundant terminal blocks require only a single set of wires for each redundant channel or fieldbus segment. (The exception is the Redundant Interface terminal block which uses two sets of wires for the Series 2 Serial card. One set of wires is used for each interface such as a computer.) The redundant terminal blocks contain screw terminals appropriate for the card type and signals from the screw terminals are connected to both cards in a redundant pair. If all cards are redundant, the controller can support up to 32 redundant pairs. Refer to DeltaV Books Online for more information on using Series 2 cards in a DeltaV system. Related information Environmental Specifications

title: DeltaV Series 2 I/O
body_text: DeltaV Series 2 I/O DeltaV Series 2 I/O cards have a wider operating temperature range than pre-Series 2 cards and some Series 2 cards support redundancy. The following DeltaV I/O cards are available as Series 2: AI, 8-Channel, 4-20 mA (Series 2 simplex) AI, 4-20 mA, HART (Series 2 simplex and redundant; 2 and 4 wire) AI, 16, Channel, 4-20 mA, HART (Series 2 simplex) AO, 8-channel, 4-20 mA, HART (Series 2 simplex and redundant) AS-Interface (Series 2 simplex) DeviceNet (Series 2 simplex) DI, 8-Channel, 24 VDC, Dry Contact (Series 2 simplex and redundant) DI, 8-Channel, 24 VDC, Isolated (Series 2 simplex) DI, 8-Channel, 120 VAC, Dry Contact (Series 2 simplex) DI, 8-Channel, 120 VAC, Isolated (Series 2 simplex) DI, 32-Channel, 24 VDC, Dry Contact (Series 2 simplex) DO, 8-Channel, 24 VDC, High-Side (Series 2 simplex and redundant) DO, 8-Channel, 24 VDC, Isolated (Series 2 simplex) DO, 8-Channel, 120 VAC/230 VAC, High-Side (Series 2 simplex) DO, 8-Channel, 120 VAC/230 VAC, Isolated (Series 2 simplex) DO, 32-Channel, 24 VDC, High-Side (Series 2 simplex) Series 2 H1 (Series 2 simplex and redundant) Isolated Input (Series 2 simplex) Multifunction (Series 2 simplex) RTD, ohms (Series 2 simplex) Thermocouple (Series 2 simplex) Series 2 Profibus DP (Series 2 simplex) Series 2 Plus Profibus DP (Series 2 simplex and redundant) Sequence of Events (Series 2 simplex) Series 2 Serial (Series 2 simplex and redundant) Series 2 redundant capable cards are configured, autosensed, upgraded, and operated just like pre-Series 2 cards. Series 2 cards in Simplex mode can function as drop-in replacements for pre-Series 2 cards of the same type. With the exception of the Simplex mode Series 2 H1 card, which requires the Series 2 H1 terminal block, no wiring change is required to replace a pre-Series 2 card. Series 2 cards report their operating mode (simplex or redundant) to the DeltaV controller based on the type of terminal block on which they are installed. Redundant terminal blocks provide wiring terminations for the redundant cards. If a card is installed on a redundant terminal block, it reports itself as operating in Redundant mode; otherwise, it reports itself as operating in Simplex mode. Other than redundant terminal blocks, no additional software or hardware is required to support redundancy. A redundant terminal block spans two adjacent slots on the carrier. A redundant I/O card consists of two Series 2 cards installed in a redundant terminal block. Note: For redundant I/O, the lower slot number (in the carrier) in a redundant pair must be odd and the upper slot number must be the next higher even number. For example, redundant pairs can be installed in slots 1 and 2, 3 and 4, 9 and 10. Redundant pairs cannot be installed in slots 6 and 7, 24 and 25. Configuration tools such as the DeltaV Explorer enforce this requirement. The double-wide redundant terminal blocks require only a single set of wires for each redundant channel or fieldbus segment. (The exception is the Redundant Interface terminal block which uses two sets of wires for the Series 2 Serial card. One set of wires is used for each interface such as a computer.) The redundant terminal blocks contain screw terminals appropriate for the card type and signals from the screw terminals are connected to both cards in a redundant pair. If all cards are redundant, the controller can support up to 32 redundant pairs. Refer to DeltaV Books Online for more information on using Series 2 cards in a DeltaV system. Related information Environmental Specifications

title: DVUpdateInterval
body_text: DVUpdateInterval The update interval determines how often the workbook is refreshed with data from the process, if it has changed. It does not execute write functions. The update interval is stored in the cell you specify as a named range. The name of the range is DVUpdateInterval. The Configure Update Interval dialog allows you to specify the cell location of DVUpdateInterval and the interval in seconds. You can also define the named range yourself using MS Excel. title: DVWrite Function
body_text: DVWrite Function Writes the value specified to the parameter property in the real-time database. The function also returns the status of the call to indicate if any problem occurred between the function call and the DeltaV Excel server, the OPC server, or other DeltaV data handling software. Important: This function affects the process. It is recommended that you only write to user-defined DeltaV parameters that your control strategy can ignore. title: DVWrite Notes
body_text: DVWrite Notes In order to execute a write function, you must specifically choose to execute and confirm the write. A Write function will only execute when you select Execute Write Function from Add-Ins > DeltaV . This makes write functions unlike the read functions in two ways: the update interval does not provide automated execution of write functions when you create or edit a write function, the function will not execute. The software returns the message, "DVWrite Disabled". When the active cell in the spreadsheet is empty, selecting Execute Write Function causes all of the DVWrite functions on the active worksheet to execute. DVWrite functions in other worksheets do not execute. When one or more functions are selected, clicking Execute Write Function executes only those functions. The selected cells must be contiguous. Only functions on the active worksheet can be executed. If MS Excel's calculation mode is manual when DVWrites are executed, the DVWrite functions will show "0" or "success" if they succeeded and the error code or corresponding string if they did not. If MS Excel's calculation mode is automatic when you select Execute Write Function , the software temporarily changes the mode to manual in order to execute the function and send the value. If any function fails to write successfully, the software displays the number of errors and asks you if you want to restore the calculation mode to automatic. You must select No if you want to examine the error values. If you select Yes , the software changes the mode back to automatic which fills the write function cells with a value of "DVWrite disabled". If all write functions succeed, the software changes the node back to automatic which replaces "success" or "0" in the write function cells with "DVWrite disabled". If you use the Configure Write Function dialogs to specify the parameter property, the parameter reference is in uppercase. If you enter the function manually, you must enter the parameter reference in uppercase. Related information DVWrite Function DVWrite Syntax

title: DeltaV SIS documentation
body_text: DeltaV SIS documentation The DeltaV SIS documentation includes this book and the DeltaV SIS Safety Manual and online help for SIS components. The information in this book documents only the features and tasks in DeltaV SIS systems that are unique or different than that in standard DeltaV systems. To configure and operate a safety instrumented system with DeltaV SIS software you use the same tools used by a DeltaV process control system. Features and tasks that are common to both DeltaV SIS systems and basic DeltaV systems are covered in the standard DeltaV documentation. If you are not already familiar with DeltaV systems, please read the DeltaV Getting Started manual to learn how to use the DeltaV engineering tools. Although DeltaV SIS software uses DeltaV engineering tools, and the features and tasks required to design, implement, and operate a safety instrumented system with DeltaV SIS software are similar to the tasks required to implement a process control system with basic DeltaV systems, there are differences between the two. These differences are explained throughout this book in two different ways: Features that are similar for both basic DeltaV systems and DeltaV SIS system are explained by exception. That is, this document explains only the differences and refers to the DeltaV documentation for general information. The User Manager is one example of a feature in this category. Features that are unique to DeltaV SIS systems or that differ greatly between a basic DeltaV system and DeltaV SIS system are explained in full. The DeltaV SIS function blocks are an example of a feature in this category. There are two types of SIS systems, SLS 1508 Logic Solver systems and CHARMs Smart Logic Solver systems. The major differences in the two systems are in the hardware and the configuration of a system within DeltaV Explorer. The two different systems has caused the SIS documentation to be subdivided into three parts: SLS 1508 SIS system information — This part documents features that are unique for SLS 1508 systems. An example of this type of information is SISNet Domains. CHARMs Smart Logic Solver SIS system information — This part documents features that are unique for SIS Controllers and CSLSs. Common information — Both systems use the same function blocks, module types, and secure parameters, the only differences being configuration limits. Minor differences due to the two SIS system types are noted when necessary. When a topic contains information specific to a particular SIS system type, that system type is included in the topic title or topic text. Topics that contain information that is the same in both system types use generic terms like logic solver and SIS and do not specify an SIS system type. The DeltaV SIS documentation (except the DeltaV SIS Safety Manual) is included as a book within the standard DeltaV Books Online. The DeltaV Safety Instrumented Systems book contains the information you need to implement and operate a safety instrumented system. If you need information on basic DeltaV configuration or operation, refer to the DeltaV Books Online. The DeltaV SIS Safety Manual contains additional information on DeltaV SIS systems. The DeltaV SIS Safety Manual is distributed on the DeltaV Documentation Library disk.

body_text: SLS 1508 example SIS Network physical layout The example physical SIS Network layout consisting of three fiber optic rings and three SIS Network domains is shown in the following figure. Example SIS Network Physical Layout The example consists of three physical rings, three SIS Network domains, and two SIS Network bridge connections. This layout is used in most of this section to show how different physical ring and domain definitions appear in DeltaV Explorer and in DeltaV Diagnostics. References to secure parameters requires that the parameters be defined correctly (local, domain, or system) and a physical connection between the publisher of the secure parameter and the logic solver referencing the secure parameter. Therefore the following is a partial list of the communication abilities of the example layout: CTRLR1 and CTRLR2 are in the same domain and on the same physical ring so they can communicate with Domain Global parameters. Even though CTRLR1 and CTRLR4 are on the same physical ring, they are in different domains so they can communicate only with System Global parameters. CTRLR4 and CTRLR6, even though they are in different domains and different physical rings, can communicate with System Global parameters over the SIS Network bridge between CTRLR3 and CTRLR5. CTRLR5 and CTRLR8 are in the same domain but different physical rings. They can communicate only with System Global parameters over the SIS Network bridge between CTRLR6 and CTRLR8. CTRLR7 and CTRLR8 cannot communicate with any controller in DOMAIN_1 or DOMAIN_2 as this would require communication through two bridge connections.

title: Safety Instrumented Systems introduction
body_text: Safety Instrumented Systems introduction A Safety Instrumented System (SIS) is a set of components including sensors, logic solvers, and final control elements whose purpose is to take a process to a safe state when predetermined hazardous conditions arise. A safety instrumented system includes hardware, software, and all field equipment necessary to perform the desired shutdown functions. Safety instrumented systems are applied to a process to substantially reduce the risk from costly or dangerous failures in industrial processes. The magnitude of risk reduction needed is determined from an analysis of the severity of hazardous process events and their probability of occurrence. Safety instrumented systems are typically made up of multiple safety instrumented functions (SIFs). Each SIF can be considered a control loop, defining: The measurements (sensors) to use The actions to take (control elements to drive) When to apply the actions (logic linking the measurements to the actions) How fast to measure and react Every SIF has a Safety Integrity Level (SIL) assigned to it. SIL is a measure of the risk reduction provided by a SIF based on four discrete levels, each representing an order of magnitude of risk reduction. The factors considered in determining a SIL include: Device integrity Diagnostics Failures Testing Operation Maintenance For more information on safety instrumented systems and safety integrity levels, refer to the DeltaV SIS Safety Manual .

title: DeltaV SIS Process Safety Systems overview
main_heading: DeltaV SIS Process Safety Systems overview
body_text: DeltaV SIS Process Safety Systems overview DeltaV SIS hardware and software is used to install, configure, and operate a system to implement a safety instrumented system in conjunction with sensors and final elements to take a process to a configured safe state when hazardous conditions occur. There are two types of DeltaV safety instrumented systems: CHARMs Smart Logic Solver (CSLS) systems SLS 1508 Logic Solver systems The two hardware types are different, and their physical installation and configuration in DeltaV Explorer is different, but both provide similar functionality to implement safety instrumented systems. The differences are explained in other sections of this document. The term logic solver applies to both systems and is used when information being discussed applies to both systems. DeltaV SIS components are physically separate from, but integrated with, the DeltaV distributed control system (also known as a basic process control system or BPCS). The logic solvers execute SIS modules that perform the safety instrumented function. Safety instrumented functions are configured in one or more SIS modules using the DeltaV engineering tools—DeltaV Explorer and Control Studio. Configuration and use of SIS modules is similar in both systems. The main difference is in the system capacities of the two systems. Any differences are explained in this document when necessary. In some cases data needs to be shared between SIS modules as the SIF cannot be completely implemented in a single module. This data is shared between SIS modules through the use of Secure Parameters and Secure Parameter References. Secure Parameters are Boolean with status values that the SIS module can write to and can be referenced by other SIS modules. The number of secure parameters and the scope in which they can be referenced depend on the safety instrumented system implementation. Subtopics: DeltaV SIS documentation DeltaV SLS 1508 hardware CHARMs Smart Logic Solver (CSLS) SIS system example DeltaV SIS software DeltaV SIS configuration DeltaV SIS operator graphics

title: SLS 1508 SIS Simulate task overview
body_text: SLS 1508 SIS Simulate task overview This section includes information on creating an SIS Simulation system from configuration through download and system checkout. The suggested steps to create an SIS Simulation configuration are: Install DeltaV software on the Professional PLUS and Application workstations. In DeltaV Explorer, create the Application Stations you need to simulate other controllers in your system. Install the appropriate multi-node simulation licenses on all workstations. Set the Controller alias name on each workstation's Simulated Logic Solver subsystem properties dialog. Create simulated logic solver cards under the Simulated Logic Solvers subsystem in each workstation. Configure Logic Solvers under the SIS Network subsystem. Define Logic Solver channels. Assign Logic Solvers to the simulated Logic Solver cards. Create your SIS configuration (modules, links, displays, and so on). Download the workstations. Commission and download the logic solvers. Note: You can download an SIS Simulation system only if your workstation has the appropriate license. Perform the system functional test. If you have a DeltaV SIS Simulate Professional license you can also read and write process data to and from SIS modules in the simulation using OPC.

title: DeltaV SIS software
body_text: DeltaV SIS software The DeltaV SIS software components are integrated with the DeltaV software. There are two DeltaV SIS system preferences available: Enable CHARMs Smart Logic Solvers Enable SLS 1508 Logic Solvers Enabling either or both of these from System Preferences adds SIS objects to DeltaV Explorer and Control Studio so you can configure DeltaV SIS Logic Solvers and SIS modules. The objects added depend on the selection. The two SIS systems are similar but there are hardware and software differences between them. If your system has both SLS1508 Logic Solvers and CHARMs Smart Logic Solvers and you have enabled both in the DeltaV software, you must be careful not to inadvertently create SIS modules that will not run on the intended logic solver. DeltaV Operate includes an SIS module faceplate, SIS function block faceplates, an SIS Data Entry Expert, and several SIS dynamos you can use to create or augment operator displays. The faceplates and dynamos provide information on the state of the DeltaV SIS system and allow operators with sufficient privilege to perform tasks such as bypassing a sensor for maintenance. Any online changes to DeltaV SIS parameters use a secure write mechanism that ensures that the messages get to the intended destination without corruption. The mechanism also requires that the operator confirm the change. SIS modules are always function block diagrams. SIS module palettes provide TUV-certified SIS function blocks and other objects.

title: Dynamic References
body_text: Dynamic References A dynamic reference parameter is a variation of the external reference parameter that lets you define a path to a value that is selected at run-time during execution of the algorithm. The selection is based on information not available at configuration (for example, an operator entry, a recipe parameter passed from batch control, or a run-time value of a control variable). The best way to configure dynamic references is by using the parameter browser available in all of the expression dialogs. By selecting a parameter from the browser, you can avoid the potential of typographical errors and case sensitivity when referencing block parameters. Dynamic references are established by assigning a parameter reference path string to the .$REF field of a dynamic reference parameter. For example, if a tank has two input valves, INLETA and INLETB, the value for the dynamic reference parameter, INLET.$REF, can be assigned the setpoint of INLET_A using a statement such as: 'INLET.$REF' := "//INLETA/SP" Following is an example using a parameter of type string to store the parameter reference path: 'STRINGVAR.CV' := "//INLETA/SP" 'INLET.$REF' := 'STRINGVAR.CV' Related information Dynamic Reference Parameter

title: Dynamic alarming
body_text: Dynamic alarming Dynamic alarming describes various techniques for eliminating alarm floods through automatic suppression of redundant and consequential alarms resulting from a significant equipment failure or process disturbance. Alarm flood suppression and first-out alarming are the two most common techniques used in dynamic alarming. Alarm flood suppression logic monitors process conditions to detect a significant equipment failure or process disturbance. When detected, a single common alarm is presented to the operator and all of the expected consequential alarms associated with the event are suppressed. First-out alarming permits the first occurring alarm in a related group of alarms (a single process event) to annunciate while suppressing the remaining alarms in the group. For example, an equipment shutdown causes a cascade of alarms that overload the operator and make it difficult for him to determine the initiating cause and therefore take appropriate corrective action. With first-out alarming implemented, the operator sees only the first occurring alarm while the other related alarms are suppressed. Now the operator can quickly take the appropriate and corrective action. DeltaV includes three dynamic alarming module templates, along with corresponding faceplates and detail displays, that can be used to implement these techniques. ALM_FLOOD_SUP (Alarm flood suppression) ALM_FLOOD_SUP_32 (Alarm flood suppression) FO_ALM_SUP (First-out alarming) Related information AlarmManagement module templates

title: Dynamic unit allocation
body_text: Dynamic unit allocation Dynamic unit allocation is the selection of units based on the configuration database's representation of the physical connectivity of units (by way of the equipment train and downstream units list) and, when programmatic allocation is enacted, the selection criteria defined in the unit selection policy. Equipment trains are required for dynamic unit allocation. Dynamic unit allocation Allows the connectivity of units to be configured so that physical constraints are known to the DeltaV system and can be used to facilitate equipment allocations. Allows logical dependencies between the units to be configured so that recipe constraints are known by the DeltaV system and can be used to facilitate equipment allocations. Allows automated unit allocations that require no operator intervention. Allows soft constraints to be configured so that information (such as, least recently used and clean status) can be used for automated equipment allocations. Simplifies the operator's task in selecting the equipment to be used for running a batch by offering only feasible (connected) sets of equipment. Note: Batches that are running stand-alone unit procedures (or operations) on a single unit do not make use of dynamic unit allocation. Recipes that are not using equipment trains do not make use of dynamic unit allocation. In DeltaV the unit module is the representation of the process unit. A unit module is the instantiation of of a unit class. Subtopics: How dynamic unit allocation works Setup equipment for dynamic unit allocation Writing the unit selection policy Dynamic unit allocation at run time

title: Dynamos overview
body_text: Dynamos overview As you develop a system of operator pictures, you may need to use an object (such as a pipe, pump, or valve) in more than one picture. You can save such custom-built objects as reusable graphics called dynamos . If you assign dynamic properties to an object, those properties are retained when you save it as a dynamo. In configure mode, DeltaV Operate provides prebuilt dynamo sets containing common process control objects, such as pumps, that you can paste into your pictures rather than drawing them yourself. You can modify an existing dynamo and save it in the original set or in a new set. You will likely want to save your most used dynamos in your own dynamo sets. To complete the TANK101 process picture, you will use several different dynamos and modify their dynamic properties. Following is a brief summary of what you will do in the next few procedures. Add a pump dynamo and animate the color. It will change from red to green to signal the pump going from off to on. Add a tank dynamo with dynamic properties. The tank level will change to show the gradual discharge of its contents. Add a block valve and regulatory valve. The valves will change color to show their state (closed or open). Add pipes to connect the other objects. These could also be made to change color, but you will not assign dynamic properties in the example. The picture will look something like the following figure. Use this as a guideline for placing objects on your picture. If DeltaV Operate is not open, open it in configure mode, expand the Pictures folder in the system tree, and then double-click the tank picture file, TANK101. Subtopics: Create a pump using a dynamo Create a tank using a dynamo

title: Easy configuration for fieldbus function blocks
main_heading: Easy configuration for fieldbus function blocks
body_text: Easy configuration for fieldbus function blocks In order to eliminate the guesswork commonly associated with configuring fieldbus function blocks, the DeltaV system provides enhanced selections for configuring all fieldbus function blocks' CHANNEL and XD_SCALE parameters. The fieldbus function blocks must be assigned to fieldbus devices that support these enhanced selections. The enhanced selections for configuring the CHANNEL and XD_SCALE parameters are available in Control Studio and DeltaV Explorer. CHANNEL Parameter For the CHANNEL parameter, the DeltaV system displays the channel numbers and channel descriptions from the device's Device Definition (DD) file in the form channel number - description. Only the channel numbers and descriptions that are relevant to the device are displayed. The following image shows the CHANNEL value selections for a Rosemount Inc. 3051 fieldbus Pressure Transmitter, revision 23. If a value needed for your configuration does not appear in the list, click the Allow user entered value option and enter another value for this device. This feature also allows for backward compatibility. XD_SCALE Parameter For the XD_SCALE parameter, the DeltaV system displays the relevant engineering units from the device's DD file. Only the engineering units that are relevant to the device are displayed. The following image shows the XD_SCALE value selections for a Rosemount Inc. 3051 fieldbus Pressure Transmitter, revision 23. If an XD_SCALE value needed for your configuration does not appear in the list, click the Show all engineering units option to see a complete list of engineering units in the system. To use the enhanced CHANNEL and XD_SCALE parameter values you must: Assign the fieldbus function block to a device that supports this feature. Save the module in Control Studio or DeltaV Explorer.

title: Event Chronicle automated backup utility
body_text: Event Chronicle automated backup utility The Backup Status column in the Event Chronicle Administration application displays the current backup status of a data set. The following values can appear in this column: Value Description Modified Either the data set has changed since the last time it was backed up or the data set has never been backed up. Backed Up The data set has been backed up and no data has changed since the last time it was backed up. Note: During manually-initiated backup operations, screen updates to the value in the Backup Status column are suspended. The Event Chronicle automated backup utility enables you to perform backups of current event data sets using the Windows Task Scheduler or a third party application. You can also run the utility manually from a DOS command prompt. The Event Chronicle automated backup utility supports: Backing up all current event data sets to local/networked storage Backing up only current event data sets that have not been backed up Deleting backed up event data sets in the target directory according to their age Note: If you have configured the Event Chronicle to copy events from the active data set to current data sets, the system performs this copy function at the top of the appropriate hour. Schedule automated backups such that they do not conflict with the copy function. Subtopics: Syntax Examples Creating a batch file for Windows Task Scheduler Error codes

title: Enhanced Device Control module template (VLV_DCC_EDC_)
body_text: Enhanced Device Control module template (VLV_DCC_EDC_) The DeltaV software includes the VLV_DCC_EDC module template. The template is for controlling multi-state discrete devices that require interlocks, permissives, or force setpoints. VLV_DCC_EDC module template This module template is set up for input and output Device Signal Tags. The module template includes configuration tips when viewed in Control Studio. Use the EDC_PMP_ and EDC_VLV_ dynamos to monitor and control discrete devices that use this module template. The dynamo opens the EDC_fp module faceplate. From the faceplate you can open the EDC_dt detail display for the module and the module's DCC function block faceplate (DCC_fp). Implementation example This example uses the Discrete Control Condition function block to configure interlock, permissive, and force setpoint conditions that connect to an EDC function block. The condition outputs of the DCC function block are wired directly to the EDC function block. The following are configuration tips for a simple implementation: Modify the Quick Config parameters presented as needed. Configure the Device Signal Tag for IO_IN_1, the Close status of the valve (1=CLOSED). Configure the Device Signal Tag for IO_IN_2, the Open status of the valve (1=OPEN). Configure the Device Signal Tag for IO_OUT_1, the latching output to the valve (1=OPEN). To configure to drive to Open when interlocks clear, de-select SP Track in DEVICE_OPTS. Note: Change STATE_MASKS if it is necessary to invert the inputs or output, or to add or remove states. (Optional) Configure IO_OUT_DURATION1 to a value different from 0 to pulse the output for this duration). Configure the PASSIVE_STATE as needed. Open the properties of the DCC1 function block. Add and remove the interlock conditions as needed. Double click on the condition to configure. Configure the interlock expression. The expression should evaluate True to cause an interlock. Configure a text description for the condition to appear in the DCC block faceplate. (Optional) Set Higher Managed to prevent the condition from being online disabled. (Optional) Select Reset Required to latch the output of the interlock condition when it evaluates to True. This requires that the function block be reset to unlatch the interlock condition. (Optional) Configure the Delay Off to set the time to elapse before the output of an interlock condition is set to False after the condition clears. (Optional) Configure the Delay On to set the time to elapse before the output of an interlock condition to set to True after the condition is detected. Add or remove the permissive conditions as needed. Double click on the condition to configure. Configuration of permissive conditions is similar to that of interlock conditions. Configure ALGO_OPTS as needed. When Permit is set, configure the permissive expression such that a True evaluation means permit. When Permit is not set, configure the permissive expression such that a True evaluation means prevent . Add and remove the force setpoint conditions as needed. Double click on the condition to configure. Configuration of force setpoints is similar to that of permissive conditions. Modify the priority of FAIL_ALM from Alarms view if desired. Set module properties if desired. Modify the History Collection parameters as desired. Related information EDC valve dynamo (EDC_VLV_) EDC pump dynamo (EDC_PMP_) Enhanced Device Control module faceplate (EDC_fp) EDC module detail display (EDC_dt) Discrete Control Condition function block faceplate (DCC_fp)
