title: Has the H1 card failed?
body_text: Has the H1 card failed? If the H1 card fails, the system loses visibility on the attached fieldbus segments. On a segment that does not support the backup Link Active Scheduler (LAS), if the H1 card failure causes the PCMCIA within the H1 card to go down, all communication on the attached fieldbus segment stops. To recover from an H1 card failure, replace the card. The H1 card is automatically downloaded and resumes functioning as the LAS. Startup of the loop depends on how the loop is configured.

title: History data points in class-based modules
main_heading: History data points in class-based modules
body_text: History data points in class-based modules From DeltaV Explorer you can create history data points in module classes that propagate to module instances. However, from bulk edit, you can only create history data points at the module level. The ability to modify history data points in class-based modules is determined by values in two fields in the exported history point data, hdp_type and use_default. Note: The hdp_type and use_default fields are relevant only for history data points defined in a module class. For all other history data points (including those defined in instances of class-based modules) these fields can be ignored. The following table summarizes the values that can appear for hdp_type and use_default based on settings in the Add History Collection dialog in the class and in the instance. For HDP defined in module... Allow instance history data point to be configured field (in class) Use default value from module class field (in instance) Type field in History Collection dialog hdp_type in Bulk Edit add-in use_default in Bulk Edit add-in Class Checked Checked Configurable Configurable T Class Checked Not Checked Override Override F Class Not Checked NA Definition Definition <NULL> Instance NA NA Instance Instance <NULL> Do not modify the hdp_type values. Depending on the hdp_type value for an HDP you can do the following from Bulk Edit: Configurable — You can change the use_default value from T to F and modify other fields. You cannot create new Configurable history data points. Override — You can modify field values. You cannot create new Override history data points. Definition — You cannot make any changes. Instance — You can create new instances or modify field values of existing instances.

title: Paths in the value_recorded field
body_text: Paths in the value_recorded field The valid values for the value_recorded (path) field depend on the type of data being recorded: Function block parameter value paths look like module/block/parameter.field , for example, MOD1/CALC1/IN1.CV. I/O channel parameter value paths look like controller /IO1/ card / channel/parameter.field , for example, CTLR1/IO1/CO3/CH01/FILTER.CV. There are other variations not shown. To be sure you are using correct path values, export at least one history data point of each type you want to bulk edit.

title: Administer batches advanced options
body_text: Administer batches advanced options This dialog permits the forced shutdown of a batch and allows you to take a snapshot of all the pertinent runtime information for a batch. Taking a Snapshot Log Select the batch. Click the Snapshot Logs button. The batch's runner directory, EVT file and the standard batch log files are copied into a folder under the DeltaV\DVData\Batch\Logs folder Forcing a Batch Shutdown Important: Forcing a shutdown of a batch causes the batch to go into the LOST state, preventing any communication between this batch and its currently active phases. Select the batch to shut down. Click the Force Shutdown button. Click YES to acknowledge the warning message and proceed with the shutdown. Click NO to acknowledge the warning message and cancel the shutdown (no shutdown takes place). Once the batch is in the LOST state, open the Batch Operator Interface (or the Batch Operate controls) and either remove it from the batch list or restart it. If restarting the batch, you will have the option of restarting that batch as a Warm Restart or a Cold Restart.

title: The Batch OI Configuration Tool
body_text: The Batch OI Configuration Tool The Batch OI Configuration tool sets which commands are enabled on this workstation when a client (such as the Batch Operator Interface or DeltaV Operate’s Unacknowledged Prompts control) runs. The settings configured here are set for this workstation. Note: The option, Allow settings to be configured at the local client , must be enabled on the Batch Executive that you are connected to. If not selected, the local client cannot override the Batch Executive server’s selected options. To set this option (Allow settings to be configured at the local client), run DeltaV Explorer, expand the workstation that is the Batch Executive. Select Batch Executive . Right-click and select Client Configuration ). Default Batch Executive Node This sets the default Batch Executive for all DeltaV Batch controls that run on this workstation. Select the Batch Executive from the list of all currently configured Batch Executives. Note: This selection does not apply to the Batch Operator Interface. DeltaV Batch Access Server Settings Click the Advanced button to set the DeltaV Batch Access Server’s advanced options. Important: Changing these options can change the frequency with which the DeltaV Batch Access Server connects to the Batch Executive, affecting the performance of the DeltaV Batch clients (Batch Operator Interface, DeltaV Batch controls, and so on). Actions Select the check boxes in the Enable column for the functions you want to enable in the Batch Executive client. When enabled, a function is available in the client. For example, when the Start command is enabled and the Batch Operator Interface application is the client, the Start button on the button bar is available (provided the logged in user has the appropriate security access level as defined in DeltaV User Manager). If an action is not enabled, the corresponding button is not displayed on the button bar and the function is grayed out on the related context menu, if applicable.

title: System Preferences
body_text: System Preferences DeltaV System Preferences improve system use by allowing you to hide any non-required Engineering Tool functions. Disabling a function conceals the applicable menus and choices but does not remove the application. Any configuration that exists for a disabled function becomes inaccessible, but the data is retained in the database. If needed at a later date, you can re-enable the function. If you uninstall DeltaV software and then install DeltaV software on the same computer, the system preference settings for your previous DeltaV installation are retained. Enabling or disabling a feature is independent of licensing. Options on the System Preferences dialog are arranged in the following groups. General Production System Warnings Simulation Download Signature Policies DeltaV SIS CHARMs Smart Logic Solvers LSN Gateways SLS1508 Logic Solvers Batch Control Batch Advanced Unit Management Networking Zones Smart Network Devices Asset Optimization Alarms Ethernet I/P Integration with Tags I/O AS-Interface DeviceNet Fieldbus Profibus DP PROVOX I/O RS3 I/O I/O Network Wireless I/O Subtopics: Enable or disable a system preference Production System Warnings preference Simulation Download preference Signature Policies preference CHARMs Logic Solvers preference LSN Gateways preference SLS 1508 Logic Solvers preference Batch preference Advanced Unit Management preference Zones preference Smart Network Devices preference Asset Optimization Alarms preference Ethernet I/P Integration with Tags preference AS-Interface preference DeviceNet preference Fieldbus preference Profibus DP preference PROVOX I/O preference RS3 I/O preference I/O Network preference Wireless I/O preference

title: Hiding intellectual property
body_text: Hiding intellectual property Use the Hide Internal Structure command to conceal intellectual property contained in your DeltaV system's Composite Templates, Control Module Classes, Equipment Module Classes, and Phase Classes and in any instance of these templates and classes. Types of items whose internal structure can be hidden The Hide Internal Structure command hides function blocks but module level parameters remain visible. This image shows a composite template whose internal structure is fully visible. Instances of this composite template, such as a module, can be opened in DeltaV Control Studio in online, edit, and debug modes. A fully visible composite template The following image shows the same composite template with a hidden internal structure. Because the internal structure is hidden, this composite template cannot be opened in Control Studio in edit mode. However instances of this template, such as a module, can be opened in online and debug modes but users are not allowed to drill into the composite instance to see the internal structure. Composite template with hidden internal structure A hidden item cannot be: Opened in Edit mode in Control Studio (instances of the item can be opened in Control Studio in online and debug modes). Copied Converted to another type that would reveal the internal structure. For example, a linked composite cannot be converted to an embedded composite. Drilled into (if linked composite) Modified in any way A hidden item's properties and history collection cannot be changed. However, a hidden item can be deleted. An instance of a hidden item can be modified from the Properties , History Collection , and Configure dialogs. Parameter shortcut values can be changed on an instance. After an item's internal structure has been hidden, it can be accessed only with the password used to hide the structure. In most cases the owner of the intellectual property has the password. When a configuration that contains hidden items is exported, the hidden items and password are encrypted. The password persists even if the hidden item is exported, then deleted, and imported or re-imported into a different database. An item from an unencrypted configuration cannot be imported into the DeltaV system if that item already exists in the database and its structure is hidden. It is important to provide information about the owner of a hidden item. For example, suppose a problem arises with a control module with a hidden internal structure and users need to contact the module's owner for help. It is recommended that you use one or more string parameters to hold information about the owner and/or the item's revision. Before hiding an item's internal structure, use Control Studio to add the string parameters. Be sure to add the parameters at the item's top level to ensure that the parameters remain visible after the item is hidden. Refer to the Control Studio online help for information on adding parameters. If DeltaV Version Control (VCAT) is enabled, do not check in an item that is unhidden. If an unhidden item is checked in, the internal structure of that version of the item can be viewed in VCAT history. You must have DeltaV System Admin and Can Configure keys to access the Hide Internal Structure feature. Refer to the Parameter and Function Security topic for more information on locks and keys. Note: The Hide Internal Structure command cannot be applied to an item in a protected category. To hide an item in a protected category, first hide the item and then protect the category to which the item belongs. For information on protecting items refer to Protecting Your Engineering Standards. Subtopics: Hide an item's internal structure Rename module class parameters to avoid revealing parameter paths Related information Parameter, field, and function security Protecting your engineering standards

title: Input parameter
body_text: Input parameter To create an input connector for a specific parameter, drag and drop this icon onto the diagram. The parameter is automatically visible outside of this block or module as an input connector in a function block diagram. That is, if you use this module or composite that you are currently creating inside of another module, the input parameter appears as a connector, and you will be able to connect a wire to this input if it is on a function block diagram.

title: Internal Read parameter
body_text: Internal Read parameter To create a parameter that you can read data from, drag and drop this icon onto the diagram. You can wire from this parameter to a function block, if you are working on a function block diagram. An internal read parameter is NOT automatically visible outside of this object as an input connector. The Show Parameters function can be used to make an Internal Read parameter appear as a connector.

title: Internal Write parameter
body_text: Internal Write parameter To create a parameter on a function block diagram to which you can wire, drag and drop this icon onto the diagram. An internal write parameter is NOT automatically visible outside of this object as an output connector. Use the Show Parameters function to make an Internal Write parameter appear as a connector.

title: Output parameter
body_text: Output parameter To create an output connector to a specific parameter, drag and drop this icon onto the drawing. The parameter you identify will automatically be visible outside of this block or module as an output connector. That is, if you use this module or composite inside of another module, the output parameter appears as a connector. You can connect a wire to this output if it is on a function block diagram.

title: Historian installation
body_text: Historian installation You can install, enable, and run the DeltaV Continuous Historian, the default historian for DeltaV, on the following local (inside the DeltaV ACN) or remote workstations: Local: Professional PLUS workstation , Application Station, or Operator Station Remote: Application Station or Operator Station You can install, enable, and run the Advanced Continuous Historian on the following local (inside the DeltaV ACN) or remote workstations: Local: Application Station Remote: Application Station You can install, enable, and run OSIsoft PI Server on the following local (inside the DeltaV ACN) or remote workstations: Local: Application Station Remote: Application Station or non-DeltaV workstation Install and enable the DeltaV Continuous Historian To install and enable the DeltaV Continuous Historian to run on an Application Station: While installing DeltaV, select the DeltaV Continuous Historian option in the Select Historian dialog. After installing DeltaV, start DeltaV Explorer, and then navigate to the Application Station node under System Configuration > Physical Network > Control Network > node_name > Continuous Historian in the DeltaV_System pane. Right-click Continuous Historian , and then select Properties to open the General tab of the Continuous Historian Properties dialog. Select the Enabled option and the Use DeltaV Continuous Historian option in the Continuous Historian Selection box. When you install DeltaV on a Professional PLUS or Operator Station, the DeltaV Continuous Historian is automatically installed by default. To enable the DeltaV Continuous Historian after installing DeltaV: Start DeltaV Explorer, and then navigate to the Professional PLUS or Operator Station node under System Configuration > Physical Network > Control Network > node_name > Continuous Historian in the DeltaV_System pane. Right-click Continuous Historian , and then select Properties to open the General tab of the Continuous Historian Properties dialog. Select the Enabled option. Install and enable the Advanced Continuous Historian To install and enable the Advanced Continuous Historian to run on an Application Station: While installing DeltaV, select the Advanced Continuous Historian option in the Select Historian dialog. After installing DeltaV, start DeltaV Explorer, and then navigate to the Application Station node under System Configuration > Physical Network > Control Network > node_name > Continuous Historian in the DeltaV_System pane. Right-click Continuous Historian , and then select Properties to open the General tab of the Continuous Historian Properties dialog. Select the Enabled option and the Use Advanced Continuous Historian option in the Continuous Historian Selection box. Install and enable PI Server To install and enable PI Server to run on an Application Station: While installing DeltaV, select the Enterprise Historian option in the Select Historian dialog. After installing Deltav, install PI Server on the Application Station according to the documentation from OSIsoft. Start DeltaV Explorer, and then navigate to the Application Station node under System Configuration > Physical Network > Control Network > node_name > Continuous Historian in the DeltaV_System pane. Right-click Continuous Historian , and then select Properties to open the General tab of the Continuous Historian Properties dialog. Select the Enabled option and the Use Enterprise Historian option in the Continuous Historian Selection box. Configure PI Server to run on the Application Station according to the documentation from OSIsoft. To install and configure PI Server to run on a non-DeltaV workstation: Refer to the documentation from OSIsoft. Related information The Continuous Historian subsystem Uninstall the Advanced Continuous Historian

title: Historian run-time processes
body_text: Historian run-time processes The run-time history service processes are started automatically when DeltaV services are started, and the Continuous Historian subsystem has been configured to be active on that workstation. History collection and historical data services for client applications are not available until these processes are started. These run-time processes terminate when DeltaV services terminate. Real-time data collection When history tags are configured for collection, the DeltaV workstation hosting the active historian periodically samples the parameter field and Ff status field for storage in the active historical data set. The time stamp of the data sample is attached by the workstation during the sampling/storage process. Heavy ACN communications loading and/or historian workstation loading can decrease the accuracy of the time stamp. System clock adjustments Users who are especially concerned with having accurately time-stamped historical data can purchase an NTP server to ensure accurate time bases in all nodes in the DeltaV system and very small system time adjustment amounts. If an NTP server is not used, a system clock adjustment, either forward or backward in time, could occur on a node hosting a historian. If the system time on a historian node is set forward (time increased), the history clients will see historical data as if it had not changed for the time span the clock was set forward. There will be flat lines or gaps between samples plotted. No unusual status values will be inserted indicating the time shift. If the system time is set backward (time decreased), the new data from the same time period is added to the historical database. If you plot this in Process History View, you will see that the line jumps back in time on the chart. No unusual status values will be inserted indicating the time shift. Related information System time

title: Historian terminology
body_text: Historian terminology The following list provides terms and definitions specific to historian terminology: active historical data set Holds the most recent historical data captured for all configured history tags. The data set holds the contiguous historical data record from the time it was created until the present. archives Files used to store historical data. Each archive file contains events for a time period specified by the archive start time and end time. current historical data set Data set created by rollover of the active historical data set. A current historical data set is a former active historical data set that has been completed by hitting the time or size limit rules or by direct creation of a new active data set. A current historical data set holds historical data for a collection of history tags within the time span of the data set. One or more current historical data sets may exist in Primary storage. extended historical data set A historical data set that has been placed back online through the use of the Continuous Historian Administration application. Such data sets may be for any history tags for any period of time, without continuity with the active and current historical data sets. Primary storage A storage area on each workstation with a historical data server installed. This area holds a collection of historical data sets, including one active historical data set, zero or more current data sets, and zero or more extended historical data sets.

title: Historical data files
body_text: Historical data files Historical data files hold offline historical data for long term storage or bulk transfer, including DeltaV Continuous Historian version migration.

title: Historical data retrieval
body_text: Historical data retrieval Client applications can request that data be retrieved from the historical data server in several ways, including: Read raw samples – This provides access to the individual history samples stored in the historical data sets. If data compression is enabled, the number of samples stored per unit of time could vary a great deal. The number of raw samples available online for a history tag that has a frequently changing value and with little or no compression could be quite large. Read processed data – This tells the server to return information for a history tag, derived by processing the raw history samples; it usually involves a substantial reduction in the volume of data returned, but the data is still useful for a specific purpose: drawing charts, performing analysis, looking for missing data, etc. Processing involves: Subdividing the time span bounded by the start and end time into one or more, evenly sized subintervals; for example, 24-hour subintervals for the last month. Computing one or more aggregate functions for each subinterval. In either type of request, a time span, ultimately resolved as a start time and an end time, is specified in the request to establish the time boundaries for the request. Time stamps that exactly match the start time are considered within the time span. Time stamps that exactly match the end time are not within the time span. Start and end times from a client application will often not exactly hit the time stamps for raw samples stored in the historical data server, so the following options exist for specifying how the server should handle the boundary sample situations: No boundary sample – specifies that no samples should be returned/used outside of the start and end times. The first sample to be used would be the first raw sample stored after the start time, and the last one used would be the last raw sample stored before the end time Outside of span – specifies that the time span should be increased to include the first raw sample beyond the specified start and/or end time Interpolate – specifies that a sample should be derived for the start and/or end time by interpolation, as appropriate for the data type, from the raw samples that are immediately before and after the boundary time specified. A complicating factor for historical data retrieval is that there may be discontinuities ( holes ) in the historical data record. Reading raw samples should return hole start samples that indicate the starting time and the reason for the hole; for example, the parameter cannot be read, the historian shut down, the tag was not configured to collect at that time, etc. Reading processed data should return sufficient information to let the client know if the requested aggregate was adversely affected by any holes in the historical data record within each subinterval. Another kind of discontinuity in the historical data record involves requesting historical data for time spans up to and including the present. It is usually convenient for clients if the historical data server would, in this case, return a raw history sample representing what the historical data server currently considers now . It is expected that a client repeating the same request for a now sample some time later would see different, more current, results. Subtopics: Data compression Composite Ff status values Composite historian status values Aggregate functions supported

title: Historical data sets
body_text: Historical data sets Historical data sets are collections of online history tag sets that are currently accessible to history client applications. There are three classifications of historical data sets: Active Current Extended Active historical data sets An active historical data set holds the most recent historical data captured for all history tags configured for this historian. It holds the contiguous historical data record from the time it was started until the present. The content of an active historical data set grows as it accumulates history tags and history samples from the real-time data stream from the data capture system. To assist in data management, the DeltaV Continuous Historian can be configured to automatically roll over the active historical data set. The active historical data set is closed and becomes a current historical data set. A new, empty active historical data set is started. The configuration rules for performing a rollover can be based on: The approximate historical data file size limit, so that the current historical data sets will usually fit on long-term storage media Calendar/time targets, so that current historical data sets will represent convenient time spans; for example, days starting at midnight, weeks starting on Sundays at midnight, etc. A new active historical data set can also be created directly using the Create New Active Data Set tool in the Continuous Historian Administration application. Current historical data sets Current historical data sets are created by active historical data set rollover operations. They hold historical data for a collection of history tags within the time span of the data set. They provide a means to manipulate historical data captured in manageable chunks , while keeping as much of the recently captured data accessible to history client applications as possible. For the current historical data sets, you can configure the following on the Advanced tab of the Continuous Historian Properties dialog: A data set size A time span An export destination directory If automatic export has been configured, once the Primary storage size limit has been reached, the DeltaV Continuous Historian will perform an export of the oldest data set and remove it from Primary storage. You can manually export data from and/or discard current historical data sets using the Continuous Historian Administration application. Extended historical data sets Extended historical data sets provide a means to bring back online historical data that has been exported and no longer online; that is, made re-accessible to history client applications. The Continuous Historian Administration application allows you to create extended historical data sets from historical data files. Once created, historical data in the extended historical data set is accessible in the same way as the data in the active and current historical data sets. There are no assumptions about continuity of the data in an extended historical data set with any of the other data online. The history tags in the extended historical data set need not match, nor are they constrained by, the other history tags available online. The DeltaV Continuous Historian performs no automatic data management for extended historical data sets. They remain online and occupy storage until you manually remove them. Subtopics: History samples Historical data files Related information The Continuous Historian Administration application

title: Historical data set security
body_text: Historical data set security Historical data set security is part of the overall DeltaV security scheme. Access to individual Continuous Historian Administration options, such as exporting or deleting historical data sets, is restricted to those users who have been granted an access key individually or who belong to a group that has been granted a key. In addition, user-defined locks can be created, and Continuous Historian Administration options can be assigned to the new locks. All Continuous Historian Administration options function on a site-wide level, requiring that <Sitewide> be assigned to the System Admin key in DeltaV User Manager when assigning keys to a user or user group. However, the specific options, such as creating a new active data set, still require the appropriate key be granted to the correct areas. Note: For more information about locks and keys, refer to the online help for the User Manager application. Security keys by function Function name Controls whether the current DeltaV user can: HDS_ACTIVE Create a new active data set HDS_EXPORT Export historical data sets HDS_DELETE Delete historical data sets HDS_EXTENDED Create extended historical data sets HDS_BACKUP Back up all current historical data sets to an offline directory HDS_RESTORE Restore current historical data sets from an offline directory to Primary storage HISTORICAL_DATA_ENTRY Write data to a DeltaV Continuous Historian database using DeltaV Reporter HISTORICAL_REMOTE_ACCESS Read DeltaV Continuous Historian data from a non-DeltaV workstation or from a DeltaV workstation in a different DeltaV system using DeltaV Reporter Related information Parameter, field, and function security DeltaV Reporter

title: Collecting history data
body_text: Collecting history data The history collection function defines the module or node parameters that are monitored and stored in the DeltaV Continuous Historian. History collection is an integral part of a module. If you copy a module that has history collection, the new module includes the history collection. This enables you to set up history collection for key parameters and copy the module for similar applications. Library modules include history collection so that you do not have to set up history collection when you copy a library module to an area. You can add additional history collection to a library module. In earlier exercises, you set up history collection in Control Studio for the module that you created from scratch (LI-101) and acquired history collection for the other modules that you copied from the Library. Related information Add history collection to the PV parameter

title: History for class-based modules and linked composites
main_heading: History for class-based modules and linked composites
body_text: History for class-based modules and linked composites The values in class-based modules and linked composite modules are derived from objects in the DeltaV Explorer library. After creating these module types from the library objects, users typically modify them to suit a specific control need. Such modifications are tracked in version control history. Class-based modules and linked composite modules also enable users to reset parameter values to the original values of the library objects. The Use default value from library object check box resets a value to the value of the associated library object. This check box is available for the editable parameters in the class-based module instance or linked composite. Note how version control history indicates changes resulting from the Use default value from library object check box: resetting a parameter value in this way simply removes the information about the parameter from the history view of the associated version of the object. For example, L_TYPE is a configurable parameter in the instance of a module class. If you change the L_TYPE of the AI block in the module instance by manually editing the properties of the parameter, version control history adds this change to the history because the value is no longer derived from the class. The differences viewed from history would look similar to the following: L_TYPE now has an override value because it is not derived from the class. A subsequent change to the override value of L_TYPE would look similar to the following: If the value of L_TYPE is reset using the Use default value from library object check box, the history for L_TYPE is deleted for the instance. The L_TYPE parameter itself has not been deleted from the instance, but the value is now derived from the library default rather than from an override in the instance. When a parameter is actually deleted from a class or composite block, VCAT history indicates this in the same way. To determine if the deleted information is the result of reverting to a library value or a deletion of a parameter in the class or linked composite, you must look at the history for the class or linked composite rather than the instance.

title: History for library function blocks
body_text: History for library function blocks Modules in the Version Control database remain linked to the library function block definitions but also contain any values that have been overridden. Understanding this relationship is helpful when viewing the Version Control history for a module. For example, if you change the value of the GAIN parameter in a particular module's PID block, the change is made to that module. When you check this change in and view history for the module, it appears that the GAIN parameter has been added to the module. This is because the history is documenting the override of a value in the library definition for the PID block. The following graphic shows how the change is displayed. When you make additional changes to GAIN, these values appear as side-by-side changes since the parameter already exists in the previous checked in version. When a parameter value is reset to its default value the parameter appears to have been deleted from the module since the parameter once again obtains its value from the library definition. This occurs when you import the module or perform a Version Control rollback or recovery and the value matches the value in the library.

title: History Report
body_text: History Report Use the History Report to create a list of objects filtered by criteria you select. To create a history report, select an object, then select Tools > Version Control > History Report . The History Options dialog opens. The History Report command opens the following dialog from which you query the configuration database. The query lets you specify the time interval during which the changes were made as well as the user who made the changes. The options in the Filter drop-down list are: All History (with Labels) — Shows the history of the selected item, including labels assigned to the selected object. General Activity — The report shows user check ins and check outs, rollbacks, labels, and so on. It does not include upgrade check ins or check outs. Upgrade Check In Only — Lists only the item check ins due to a DeltaV upgrade. You can also specify a recursive query. A recursive query searches the selected item as well as its subordinate items. After you specify options and click the OK button, the report appears, similar to the following. The buttons on the dialog are: Rollback - Replaces the current version of the item in the configuration database with the selected version. Note that Rollback does not affect downloaded modules or physical devices in the field. Rollback only modifies the configuration database. For example, when you roll back to an earlier version of a module, the module does not change the module in its assigned controller. You must download the controller in order for the changes to take effect in the controller. Another example is a situation in which you have commissioned fieldbus device and you roll back to a previous, decommissioned version of the device. The device is not decommissioned by the rollback. Differences - Compares the selected version of an item to any other version, or with a version you are currently working on in a DeltaV application. To compare two different versions of an item, hold down the CTRL key while selecting the two versions of interest. Then click the Differences button. Details - Displays user and system comments associated with the object. View - Opens the item in the VCAT viewer. Print History - Prints the history list. Print Latest Changes - For every unique selected item (for example, AREA_A and version 4) a difference report is created for that item comparing that version with its previous version (in this case, AREA_A version 3 to version 4 differences). Sorting the list You can sort the information in the list by clicking a column header. The sorting behavior for the headers is: Name – First click sorts alphabetically. Additional clicking toggles the sort order. If there are multiple instances of the same name, the instances are sorted by Date. The Date sort is always newest to oldest. Version – First click sorts by decreasing number (latest version at top). Additional clicking toggles the sort order. If there are multiple instances of the same version number, the instances of each version are sorted by date. The date sort order is the same as the version sort (increasing if version increases and vice-versa). User – First click sorts alphabetically. Additional clicking toggles the sort order. If there are multiple instances of the same user, the instances of each user are sorted by by date (most recent first). Date – First click sorts from newest to oldest date and time. Additional clicking toggles the sort order. If there are multiple instances of the same date and time, the instances are sorted by Version. The Version sort will be the same sort as the Date (increasing if Date increases, and vise-versa). Action – First click sorts alphabetically. Additional clicking toggles the sort order. The label prefix is not used to determine sort order. If there are multiple instances of the same action, the instances are sorted by Date. The Date sort is always newest to oldest. Archive Status – First click sorts alphabetically. Additional clicking toggles the sort order. Multiple instances of the same status are not sorted. Related information Item differences Print latest changes

title: History samples
body_text: History samples When data is collected for a history tag, a history sample is produced. A history sample is the basic unit of historical data for a history tag, composed of: A value – one of the DeltaV data types A time stamp – the date and time when the history tag had this value A parameter status value – an Ff style (.ST field) status value A history status value – with information such as whether the historical data stream was broken and the type of break DeltaV supports the following data types for history sample values: 32-bit float 32-bit signed integer; smaller, DeltaV signed integer parameter fields are converted to this type 32-bit unsigned integer; smaller, DeltaV unsigned integer parameter fields are converted to this type UNICODE string, up to 512 characters Byte-enum, holding both number and state name for a DeltaV named set parameter

title: Hold batches on switchover option
body_text: Hold batches on switchover option Active batches can be held on switchover by configuring the Batch Executive's option, Hold any running batches on switchover, in the Batch Application Manager's Advanced Configuration Settings. The default value is No. When set to Yes, you can investigate the cause of the switchover before allowing the batches to proceed. Changing this option does not require a download. Each constituent batch executes a HOLD as soon as successfully recovered on the new active, subsequent to the switchover, provided the batch was in one of the following states: RUNNING, STARTING, RESTARTING. The batch is held from the top level, regardless of the mode. Additionally, the mode of each level is preserved. The option, Hold any running batches on switchover, applies to the Redundant Batch system and is not available for a simplex Batch system. Note: Batches can go to Held after switchover even if the option, Hold any running batches on switchover, is not enabled. This can be due to latency of synchronization data (persisted information not being transferred due to issues of data transfer across the network) or due to a download to the controller making the phase be idle or unloaded.

title: Holding a batch
body_text: Holding a batch Holding a batch temporarily stops operation of the batch and transitions the batch to the Held state. Generally, the Held state is a safe state that is determined by the plant engineering and operations group. A batch can also automatically go into the Held state if a device failure is detected by the DeltaV system. You can hold batches when they are in the: Running state Restarting state The following figure shows a batch that received a Hold command while in the Running state. Holding a Batch For example, in the paint recipe there is a scheduled prompt sent to the operator. This prompt requests a value that the operator obtains from taking a test during the QA_TEST phase and evaluating the pH level of the batch. Typically, the operator enters that value and batch production continues. A supervisor can then place the batch into the Hold state to verify the results of the operator's test. Once the supervisor has verified the results, the batch is placed in the Restarting state.

title: Hold logic
body_text: Hold logic The hold logic is the logic that is used to get the process into a safe state when a failure is detected. The phase transitions from the RUNNING or RESTARTING state to the HOLDING state and starts executing the hold logic when a HOLD is received, or if the FAIL_INDEX parameter is set. The phase checks to see if a request was being performed by the run logic and, if so, stores the request and sends an ABORT_REQUEST code to the Batch Executive. If the state was RUNNING, the run logic is suspended until the phase goes back into the RUNNING state. If the state was RESTARTING, then the restart logic is stopped. When the hold logic completes, the state changes to HELD and remains HELD until some user action is taken. CAUTION: It is not recommended to send requests in the Hold logic. However, if a request must be used, always check to see if the Watchdog parameter has tripped first. Write the logic to not sent the request if the Watchdog is tripped. Failing to do this can cause the phase to be unable to resume.

title: Housing
body_text: Housing Only technicians authorized by Emerson are permitted to open the housing. The lower covering panel of the MD20/MD30 and MD20-ES/MD34-ES housing is grounded by the DIN rail and, as an option, by the separate ground screw. The FP20 and FP20-ES is grounded through a separate ground screw located on the left under the front panel. The switch basic module forms an inseparable unity. By removing the display and connecting parts, you risk damage to the switch basic module. Make sure that the electrical installation meets local or nationally applicable safety regulations. The ventilation slits must not be covered to ensure free air circulation. The distance to the ventilation slots of the housing has to be a minimum of 10 cm. Never insert pointed objects (thin screwdrivers, wires, etc.) into the inside of the subrack. This especially applies to the area behind the socket connectors. Failure to observe this point may result in injuries caused by electric shocks. The device has to be mounted in an upright position. If installed in a living area or office environment, the device must be operated exclusively in switch cabinets with fire protection characteristics according to EN 60950-1.

title: Housing (DeltaV RM100/RM104 switches)
body_text: Housing (DeltaV RM100/RM104 switches) Only technicians authorized by Emerson are permitted to open the housing. The device is grounded via the voltage supply socket. Make sure that the electrical installation meets local or nationally applicable safety regulations. The ventilation slits must not be covered to ensure free air circulation. The distance to the ventilation slots of the housing has to be a minimum of 10 cm. Never insert pointed objects (thin screwdrivers, wires, etc.) into the inside of the subrack. Failure to observe this point may result in injuries caused by electrical shocks. Close all empty slots with a covering panel. The device must be installed in the horizontal or upright position, either as a table unit in the switch cabinet or on the wall. When installing the device, make sure there is at least one free rack space (approx. 5 cm) above the device, because heat is discharged via the housing of the device. If you are operating the device in a 19-inch switch cabinet: install sliding/mounting rails for holding the device.

title: How can you detect a problem with the backup Link Active Scheduler (LAS)?
main_heading: How can you detect a problem with the backup Link Active Scheduler (LAS)?

title: How DeltaV SIS systems annunciate faults
main_heading: How DeltaV SIS systems annunciate faults
body_text: How DeltaV SIS systems annunciate faults DeltaV SIS systems provide standard alarms to annunciate, in DeltaV Operate, faults detected by the CSLS. No special configuration is needed. At runtime the alarms are part of a container with the CSLS name. When a CSLS alarm appears on the alarm banner in DeltaV Operate and is clicked by the operator, the CSLS faceplate opens. The faceplate shows the active alarm(s): FAILED_ALM, MAINT_ALM, ADVISE_ALM, or COMM_ALM. It also shows the text for the active condition or the words Multiple conditions if more than one alert condition is active for the particular alarm. A button on the faceplate toolbar opens Diagnostics Explorer in the context of the CSLS. The CSLS container has a number of diagnostic parameters accessible at runtime by the CSLS path similar to those of controllers. For example, the following are examples of the paths supported: CSLS_name / param_name , CSLS_name /COMM/ param_name , CSLS_name /CHARMS/CHM x-xx / param_name , CSLS_name /REDU/ param_name , CSLS_name /REDU/STBY/ param_name , A redundant CSLS has diagnostic parameters for each CSLS unit. Additional diagnostics parameters are provided under active CSLS unit to report the state of the redundant pair. The following figure is an example of Diagnostics Explorer showing the diagnostic parameters for the highlighted CSLS. There is an alerts bitstring parameter associated with the Failed, Maint, and Advise alarms. The alarm is active if any bit is set in the corresponding alerts parameter. The Comm alarm is active if the DeltaV SIS controller cannot communicate with the CSLS (with both units, if redundant). Please note that CSLS Comm alarm is not necessarily an indication of the CSLS failure since it could be merely a wire disconnect. Diagnostics Explorer Showing Contents of the CSLS The following figure is an example of the Diagnostics Explorer showing the diagnostic parameters of the standby CSLS unit of a redundant pair. There is a bitstring parameter for the status of each subsystem. The bits in these subsystem status parameters map into bits of the alerts parameters in the CSLS. A simplex CSLS has direct mapping, but a redundant CSLS combines most of the subsystem status conditions from both partners into the alerts parameters. If the subsystem status condition is active in either CSLS unit, the mapped alert condition is active. Diagnostics Explorer Showing Contents of the standby CSLS unit Refer to the SLS Diagnostic Parameters topic in the DeltaV SIS book in DeltaV Books Online for details on the subsystem status and alert bitstring parameters. The topic describes: The text and meaning of each condition How subsystem status bits map into alert bits What action to take when an alert condition becomes active Which conditions annunciate and impact device integrity Which conditions are event-only and do not impact device integrity You can change the priority of the Failed, Maint, Advise, and Comm alarms. Because certain error conditions can exist momentarily, avoid alarm priorities that are auto-acknowledging.

title: Independent DeltaV Domain Controller
body_text: Independent DeltaV Domain Controller The Independent DeltaV Domain Controller (IDDC) decouples the Windows Domain Controller role in a DeltaV domain from the DeltaV ProfessionalPLUS (as the first promoted domain controller) and DeltaV Application Station (as an additional domain controller). The Independent DeltaV Domain Controller improves performance on the ProfessionalPLUS (or Application Station) and adds additional security to the DeltaV system. Subtopics: Considerations for the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller IP addressing for the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller Firewalls and the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller Network time and the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller Maintaining the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller The setup application for the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller

title: Network time and the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller
main_heading: Network time and the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller
body_text: Network time and the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller It is critical that the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller (IDDC) and all the DeltaV nodes remain time synchronized. DeltaV uses Network Time Protocol (NTP) to maintain time synchronization between the DeltaV workstations and the DeltaV controllers. The Independent DeltaV Domain Controller setup application disables the Windows Time Service and installs/configures the NTP service such that it listens to the DeltaV master time server (the ProfessionalPLUS by default). This ensures that the IDDC remains time synchronized with all other DeltaV nodes. Important: If the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller is also connected to a network level other than the DeltaV ACN, you must block any NTP/Time communications from that non-ACN network using a firewall (physical or Windows).

title: Considerations for the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller
main_heading: Considerations for the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller
body_text: Considerations for the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller The following must be considered when using the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller. The Independent DeltaV Domain Controller: must be configured using the setup application provided with the DeltaV media. The Independent DeltaV Domain Controller setup application will not proceed on a computer previously configured as a domain controller by some means other than with the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller setup application. cannot be used in conjunction with DeltaV systems where any DeltaV node is also configured as a domain controller. can only be used as a domain controller and cannot be used as a multi-purpose computer. must use a firewall (physical or Windows) for all network connections. must evaluate any non-domain trust/authentication activity on the external (non-ACN) network card and block (with a firewall) any non-essential communications (for example, NTP communication must be blocked). can be a virtual machine using the appropriate DeltaV Virtual Studio blank operating system template for the supported operating system. For a complete specification of the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller (along with Emerson part numbers for ordering), refer to the DeltaV Workstation and Server Hardware product data sheet. It is strongly recommended to use the DeltaV Firewall IPD between the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller and the rest of the workstations on the DeltaV domain. The DeltaV Firewall IPD is documented in DeltaV Books Online as well as in the Emerson KBA NK-1600-0290. Important: Other than the configuration changes outlined in KBA NK-1600-0290, do not change the firewall IPD configuration unless you are specifically instructed to do so by Emerson. Changing the configuration may adversely affect communications on the network. Related information DeltaV Firewall IPD Firewalls and the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller Network time and the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller The setup application for the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller

title: Maintaining the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller
main_heading: Maintaining the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller
body_text: Maintaining the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller The Independent DeltaV Domain Controller must be maintained the same as any DeltaV node. For example, the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller should be backed up regularly. should be protected by antivirus software. should have all approved Windows updates applied (refer to Emerson KBAs for a list of approved updates). should be inspected for general health (including, but not limited to: available hard drive space, any power supply noises, verifying it is still functioning as a domain controller).

title: The setup application for the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller
main_heading:
The setup application for the Independent DeltaV Domain
	 Controller
body_text: The setup application for the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller The Independent DeltaV Domain Controller (IDDC) setup application configures the computer as a domain controller for the DeltaV network (ACN). The application performs the following configuration tasks. Enables the Domain Controller role. Creates the first domain controller in the domain. Creates additional domain controllers. Sets the IP address for the DeltaV networks (including the subnet mask, default gateway, and DNS server entries). Configures Network Time Protocol (NTP) services on the computer to work with the DeltaV master time server. Hardens the computer based on the Center for Internet Security (CIS) benchmarks and other DeltaV hardening features (such as disabling Windows services and features not required for DeltaV systems). To create the domain controller, certain information is required. The setup application prompts you for the following information. A fully qualified domain name. This names the domain. The format is DeltaV system name.System.company name.local (Where DeltaV system name , System , and company name are names you provide). The Directory Services Restore Mode (DSRM) password. This password does not exist until you enter it in the setup application. Network redundancy. This is when the DeltaV ACN has redundant (Primary and Secondary) networks. Domain administrator credentials. This user must exist as a local administrator prior to starting the setup application You can find the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller setup application in the DeltaV Installation Autorun menu ( Set Up Independent DeltaV Domain Controller ). You can also browse to the DVExtras\IDDC folder on the DeltaV installation media. Subtopics: Create the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller This procedure creates the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller (either primary or additional domain controller) for use with a DeltaV domain-based system. Create a DeltaV workstation in an Independent DeltaV Domain Controller environment This procedure highlights the steps required when creating a DeltaV workstation in an Independent DeltaV Domain Controller environment.

title: Firewalls and the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller
main_heading: Firewalls and the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller
body_text: Firewalls and the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller Windows Firewalls On all DeltaV nodes, the Windows Firewall is disabled on the DeltaV ACN NICs (Network Interface Cards). This must occur on the Independent Domain Controller as well. For non-DeltaV networks, (such as the 3rd NIC on the IDDC), configure the Windows Firewall to allow only the domain authentication traffic through. Physical Firewalls To protect the DeltaV ACN, an optional, physical Firewall-IPD is available with rules to allow only the domain authentication and time synchronization traffic through. The Emerson Firewall-IPD is used on the DeltaV ACNs (primary and secondary, where exists). It is connected between the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller (IDDC) and the rest of the DeltaV workstations. Firewall Rules for all Firewalls The following table outlines the rules to configure on your firewall. These rules ALLOW communication through the firewall on the ports specified in the direction specified (where the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller is the point of reference). The Emerson Firewall-IPD comes with the rules configured. Other firewalls (including the Windows firewall) might also need the rules to be created. Firewall rules Function Ports Direction (where the starting point is the DeltaV Independent Domain Controller) Configure on the following network: Comment DeltaV ACNs Non-ACN network Domain controller to domain controller (RPC) Client to domain controller (RPC) UDP 135 TCP 135 Incoming Outgoing Yes Yes High Range (RCP) Ports (Ephemeral Ports) TCP 1024 to 65535 Incoming Outgoing Yes No Client queries to the domain controller (LDAP) UDP 389 TCP 389 Incoming Outgoing Yes Yes Kerberos Password Change TCP 464 UDP 464 Incoming Outgoing Yes Yes DNS client-to-Domain Controller TCP 53 UDP 53 Incoming Outgoing Yes Yes Kerberos TCP 88 UDP 88 Incoming Outgoing Yes Yes Kerberos V5 TCP 464 UDP 464 Incoming Outgoing Yes Yes User and Computer Authentication TCP 139 UDP 137 Incoming Outgoing Yes Yes File Replications Service Sysvol Share (SMB) TCP 445 UDP 445 Incoming Outgoing Yes No Necessary for group policy distribution between the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller and the DeltaV workstations. Important: This should not be opened on the non-DeltaV NICs (connecting the Independent DeltaV Domain Controller and a non-ACN network). title: Identifying common resources
body_text: Identifying common resources There can be equipment in your plant that is not partitioned as part of a group, that is, a piece of equipment that operates entirely without other equipment to perform a task. In the DeltaV system, you still define these common resources as a unit. A unit can be a single piece of equipment or multiple pieces that work together as one unit. When configuring your control or equipment module classes, you designate the common resource's ownership type as a shared. A typical example of a common resource unit is a three-way valve. As illustrated in the following figure, the Base and Additive units share a three-way valve to transfer material into the Reactor unit. Once the valve is defined as its own unit in the DeltaV system, you can assign it as 'needed equipment' to the XFER_OUT phase. Using this configuration, the XFER_OUT phase will not start executing until it acquires the valve. If the valve is already acquired, the phase waits until the valve is available. Three-way Valve as a Common Resource

title: Identifying the process flow
body_text: Identifying the process flow Identifying your application's process flow is the first step in designing the DeltaV batch control strategy. A process flow diagram provides a high-level view of your process while grouping related process functions.

title: Identifying and troubleshooting Series 2 redundant cards
main_heading: Identifying and troubleshooting Series 2 redundant cards
body_text: Identifying and troubleshooting Series 2 redundant cards The redundant card icon, , makes it easy to identify redundant Series 2 cards in DeltaV Explorer, and the card's LEDs and DeltaV Diagnostics program provide troubleshooting and diagnostic information. DeltaV Explorer The redundant card icon, , appears on the odd slot number in DeltaV Explorer. The odd slot is the first slot on which the terminal block is installed. In this example from DeltaV Explorer, the redundant pair, C01, occupies slots 1 and 2. The procedure for enabling and disabling ports or channels on redundant Series 2 cards is the same as that for pre-Series 2 cards: rght-click the channel or port, select Properties , and then select Enabled . To enable multiple channels or ports, right-click the I/O subsystem, and then select Configure I/O . LEDs The LEDs on the Series 2 cards show basic operating data. The correct operating conditions for the green Power/Active LED is solid for the active card and flashing for the standby card. The red LED (continuous on or flashing) indicates fault conditions. topic for complete information on each Series 2 card. Use DeltaV Diagnostics to diagnose problems. Diagnostics The left pane in DeltaV Diagnostics shows a redundant pair of cards slotwise. In the following image, a redundant DI, 8-Channel, 24 VDC Dry Contact card is installed in slots 1 and 2 (C01 and C02). The active card is depicted with two darkened icons (C01), and the standby card is depicted with one darkened icon and one grey icon (C02). Diagnostic Parameters The right pane in DeltaV Diagnostics shows diagnostic parameters for the selected card in the redundant pair. The following image shows the diagnostic parameters for a redundant DI card. The online help for the Diagnostics program provides descriptions of all the parameters. Following are descriptions of the SwitchAvail, Pstatus, POInteg, and State parameters: SwitchAvail (Switchover Available) - Indicates if the redundant pair is available for switchover. Possible values include: Unavailable - Missing Cards Available Disabled Available - common faults (resolve problem and clear saved fault information) Unavailable - missing standby Unavailable - standby faulty Unavailable - switchback disabled Unavailable - both cards faulty (resolve problem and clear saved fault information) PStatus (Pair Status) - Shows the status of the redundant pair. Possible values are: No Card Good Integrity Error Termination Block Incorrectly Installed No Communication Between Cards No Communication With Partner Active Card Problem Standby Card Problem Standby Card Not Present Both Cards Report Problem Switchover Occurred, Possible Field Problem Possible Loss of Field Power Not Operational POInteg (Pair Integrity) - Overall integrity (good or bad) of the redundant pair State (Redundant cards) - Indicates whether or not the selected card is active. A state of Standby means not active; it does not mean that the card is necessarily available to take over as active. To view parameter values for channels or ports, select the active card. The values are shown for the active card only; Diagnostics displays "Not Available on Standby" if the standby card is selected. If the channels or ports are disabled, Diagnostics shows "@@@@@" for the channel or port's Value parameter and "No installed configuration" for the Status parameter. Clearing Saved Fault Information on Redundant Cards Use the Clear Saved Fault Information command in DeltaV Diagnostics after any problems reported by the redundant card pair are identified and resolved. Redundant cards hold back previous error information to prevent switching back and forth. Users must acknowledge the problem and then clear the saved fault information. The Clear Saved Fault Information command re-enables switchovers if the same problems are detected again. One way to determine if you need to use this command is to look at the card's SwitchAvail parameter. If the value for the SwitchAvail parameter reads "Available – common fault" or "Unavailable - both cards faulty," send the Clear Saved Fault Information command. For example, suppose a wire becomes loose on an Analog Input termination block. As soon as the active card detects the open loop, the controller records the fault, and the redundant pair switches over. Then, the new active card detects the open loop, and the controller records the fault again. In such a situation, detection of the same open loop will not cause a switchover. Once you find and secure the loose wire, use the Clear Saved Fault Information command to enable switchover if the condition is detected again. Note: If switchovers are not occurring as expected, be sure that the ENABLE_AUTO_SWBK parameter is enabled. To access the Clear Saved Fault Information command : Right-click the redundant I/O card that is reporting either of the above values in the SwitchAvail parameter. Select Clear Saved Fault Information . Related information The enable auto switchback parameter Step 3. Checking the LED Indicators on Each Device

title: Important Information about Hazardous Live Voltages
main_heading: Important Information about Hazardous Live Voltages
body_text: Important Information about Hazardous Live Voltages Warning: The AC input and output I/O cards and carriers may have hazardous live voltages present on the input or output terminals. These devices switch or sense the presence of 120 VAC or 250 VAC field power. Ensure that proper safety precautions, such as de-energizing field power, are observed during installation, maintenance, or any time wiring changes are made to any of the following devices: KJ4001X1-BE1: 8-Wide I/O Interface Carrier KJ4002X1-BA1 and BB1: Left and Right 8-Wide Legacy Vertical Carriers KJ4003X1- BA1 and BB1: Left and Right VerticalPLUS Carriers KJ3207X1: Series 2 AC input Cards KJ3209X1 and KJ3210X1: Series 2 AC output cards KJ4001X1-CA1: I/O Terminal Block KJ4001X1-CB1: Fused I/O Terminal block

title: Implementing a named set
body_text: Implementing a named set Once named sets are configured, recipe formulators can implement them as follows: During recipe development, formulators can select from a named set to assign phase parameter values to a recipe. During batch execution, operators can select from a named set in response to an operator message. The following figure illustrates how named sets can be configured and implemented in a sample paint application. In this example, the recipe author takes advantage of the flexibility built into the XFER_IN phase. The XFER_IN phase uses an Ingredient named set, which enables the recipe formulator to build one recipe that can produce several colors of paint. Named sets are used to select the appropriate color additive depending on the color of paint being made. For example, if the operator selects RED DYE as the ingredient, the DeltaV Batch system sends a value of 0 to the phase logic. This action instructs the controller to open the valve for the tank containing the RED DYE. Example Implementation of a Named Set

title: Implementing class-based units
body_text: Implementing class-based units Implementing class-based units allows recipe authors to build class-based recipes. Class-based recipes are recipes that can execute on any unit within a class of units. The specific unit is determined when the batch is added to the Batch Operator Interface. For more information on class-based recipes, refer to the Class-Based Recipes topic. Use a class-based design when a process cell contains several identical units, such as mixers or storage tanks. As illustrated in the following figure, the process cell contains five storage tanks and three mixers. Rather than defining ten unique units, two classes are defined. Five instances of the raw class and three instances of the mixer class are created and can be used in a class-based recipe. The operator (or the system) chooses the specific unit at runtime. Note: Units are assigned to process cells which are, in turn, assigned to areas. Areas are assigned to a Batch Executive. The recipe is also assigned to a Batch Executive. In order for a class-based recipe to run using class-based equipment, all units required by the recipe must be assigned to the same Batch Executive (by way of process cell and area) as the recipe. The recipe will not run if all required units are not found on the same Batch Executive. Unit Classes and Instances

title: Implementing external phases
body_text: Implementing external phases An external phase is equivalent to a DeltaV phase, except that the logic is from a source external to the DeltaV controllers. External phases are DeltaV Soft Phases (logic written in Visual C++ or Visual Basic), PROVOX phases, or Syncade phases. Related information DeltaV Soft Phases

title: Implementing DeltaV Zones
body_text: Implementing DeltaV Zones The following figure shows a portion of the DeltaV Explorer hierarchy of a DeltaV system whose zone name is ZONE_A. IZS_A is the Inter-Zone Server in ZONE_A. The following list contains general procedures to implement DeltaV Zones to connect existing DeltaV systems. The following assumes the DeltaV systems are offline, not running a process. Install, configure, and set binding order for network interface connections (NIC) in the Inter-Zone Servers. Connect Inter-Zone Servers to DeltaV Networks and each other through switches. Upgrade DeltaV software on all workstations within each DeltaV system Install DeltaV software on Inter-Zone Servers. On the Select Your Workstation Type dialog, select Inter-Zone Server . From the ProfessionalPLUS workstation in each DeltaV system: Select the Enable Zones check box in the System Preferences dialog. Name the zone from the Properties dialog of top-level node (DeltaV_System) in DeltaV Explorer. This name is how other DeltaV systems specify this system. Create an Inter-Zone Server under the Control Network. This Inter-Zone Server represents the IZS hardware installed in the DeltaV system. If you are installing redundant Inter-Zone Servers, select the Inter-Zone Server is redundant check box on the server's Properties dialog. Create a Remote Zone container under the IZS for every other DeltaV system this system is connected to. You create the Remote Zone containers manually by selecting the Inter-Zone Server and then selecting New Zone from the context menu. Note: The Remote Zone container names must be the zone names given to the other systems in their configurations. Each Remote Zone container has two subfolders: Local Shared Areas and Remote Zone Areas. You manually populate the Local Shared Areas folder. The Remote Zone Areas folder is populated either by exporting and importing zone topologies or by auto-sensing remote zones. In Local Shared Areas under each Remote Zone container, specify the areas in this DeltaV system whose parameter data you want to be visible in the system represented by the Remote Zone container. You also specify whether the other system has read or read and write access to each area. Select File > Export > Workstation Configuration to create a cfg file. You will use this configuration file to set up the Inter-Zone Server in this DeltaV system. From the Inter-Zone Server in each DeltaV system: Run Workstation Configuration. Select Inter-Zone Server in the Select Workstation Type area of the dialog. Browse to and select the .cfg file you created earlier. Determine if you are installing redundant Inter-Zone Servers. Set the Primary and Secondary DeltaV and Primary and Secondary IZCN network NICs. If you want users to be able to write to areas you shared as read and write from other zones, populate Remote Zone Areas. There are two ways to populate Remote Zone Areas. After you create all Remote Zone containers and populate all Local Shared Areas in the Remote Zone containers from every ProfessionalPLUS workstation: Auto-sensing Zone topologies Importing Zone topologies Assign the Remote Zone Areas to the Alarms and Events subsystem of a local Operator Station (not an Application Station) to have alarms appear in the alarm banner and displays (if the areas are shared as read and write) and alarms and events to be recorded in the Event Chronicle. The Remote Zone Areas are also available in the DeltaV User Manager when you assign members to groups or keys to users. From the ProfessionalPLUS workstation in each DeltaV system: After Workstation Configuration completes on the IZS, download the Inter-Zone Server from the ProfessionalPLUS workstation. Create new modules or modify existing modules to read data from other DeltaV systems as required for your situation. Create new operator pictures or modify existing pictures to incorporate data from other DeltaV systems as required for your situation. You can use the DeltaV Upgrade Picture Expert to use existing pictures to create pictures that access data from other DeltaV systems. The following sections expand on installation procedures that are unique for DeltaV Zones. Related information Auto-sensing Remote Zone Areas Exporting and importing Zone topologies Hardware alarm messages Inter-Zone alarms and events Redundant Inter-Zone Servers Remote Zone Areas

title: Implementing security for a DeltaV OPC UA client
main_heading: Implementing security for a DeltaV OPC UA client
body_text: Implementing security for a DeltaV OPC UA client When you implement security on the client, you perform these steps: Assign a certificate to the client in one of these ways: Generate a self-signed certificate Import a CA-signed certificate Export the client certificate Import server certificates If you want to assign a CA signed certificate, you must send a certificate signing request to a third-party certificate authority, and then import the signed certificate to assign it to the server. Additionally, you can set up user authentication for the communications between clients and servers. User authentication requires that client/server communications use a DeltaV user account with OPC UA authority. Note: In order for Username/Password logon authentication to work on a DeltaV workstation client, you must trust the OPC UA server certificate. Subtopics: Assigning a certificate to an OPC UA client Generate a self-signed client certificate and assign it to the client Import a CA-signed certificate and assign it to the client Export an OPC UA client certificate Import an OPC UA server certificate to the client’s list of issuers Import a self-signed server certificate to the client physical device Related information OPC UA user authentication

title: Implementing SLS 1508 DeltaV SIS systems
body_text: Implementing SLS 1508 DeltaV SIS systems The following list is a suggested order to perform the tasks required to install, setup, and configure an SLS 1508 DeltaV SIS system: Install the DeltaV hardware and connect it to support your domain strategy. Install the DeltaV software and set it up for your needs. Enable SLS 1508 Logic Solvers. Create user accounts if needed. Assign DeltaV SIS keys and locks as needed. Configure the logic solvers . Configure logic solver channels . Configure logic solvers into the SIS domains you need. Configure physical logic solver cards . Commission logic solvers . Assign logic solvers to logic solver cards . Create SIS modules to execute the logic your safety strategy requires. Create operator graphics for your SIS system. Download the configuration . title: Important equipment configuration notes for dynamic unit allocation
main_heading: Important equipment configuration notes for dynamic unit allocation
body_text: Important equipment configuration notes for dynamic unit allocation Multiple batches can auto-select the same unit if the maximum owners property of the unit (on the Arbitration tab in the Unit Properties dialog) is set to greater than one. Convergent paths, in which there is no intersection of possible units, are not supported with equipment trains. When divergent paths converge, the operator or unit selection policy can only select units that are in common with all possible upstream paths. Parallel paths that do not have common downstream units (either because the downstream unit aliases or downstream units are different) will display all units possible to the operator. That is, the system will display all units that are in the intersection of the unit classes (in the case of downstream units aliases being different) or all unit modules in the downstream lists of all upstream units in all parallel paths. Security is not checked when unit selection policies are used. The selections are performed by the system and not by the operator therefore there is no security to check. Changes to unit selection (when prompted) and selection modes do require the appropriate keys. Example Circular Equipment Configuration When a recipe is circular (one step is used both before and after another step), the downstream units must be configured accordingly. Unit1 -> Unit2 -> Unit3 -> Unit2 -> Unit4 Where the Unit Class Configuration is UnitClass1 contains Unit1 UnitClass2 contains Unit2 UnitClass3 contains Unit3 UnitClass4 contains Unit4 And the Unit Aliases Are Assigned as UnitAlias1 is assigned to UnitClass1 UnitAlias2 is assigned to UnitClass2 UnitAlias3 is assigned to UnitClass3 UnitAlias4 is assigned to UnitClass4 Requires Circular Equipment Train Unit Alias Configuration UnitAlias1 has UnitAlias2 as a downstream unit alias UnitAlias2 has UnitAlias3 AND UnitAlias4 as downstream unit aliases UnitAlias3 has UnitAlias2 as a downstream unit alias UnitAlias4 does not have any downstream unit aliases And Requires Circular Downstream Unit Configuration Unit1 has Unit2 as a downstream unit Unit2 has Unit3 AND Unit4 as downstream units Unit3 has Unit2 as a downstream unit Unit4 does not have any downstream units.

body_text: Important information about installation Warning: The installation procedure contains steps that are to be performed in non-hazardous or safe locations only.
