title: Archive sizing guidelines
body_text: Archive sizing guidelines This topic describes an approach to sizing the Advanced Continuous Historian archive files to meet the data recording needs of a specific implementation. Archives are the files that the Advanced Continuous Historian uses to store historical data. Each archive file contains events for a time period specified by the archive start time and end time. Since the Advanced Continuous Historian uses compression algorithms to reduce the amount of data storage, the information presented here will not provide exact results. However, information to estimate initial archive sizing and a methodology to view the actual data storage rate and adjust accordingly are provided. The Advanced Continuous Historian system stores data into archive files. You can have multiple archive files of various sizes. The archive files range in size from 2 MB to 2 TB. The default installation configures one file of 256 MB. It is recommended that you create no fewer than three archive files. The maximum number of archives is limited by the operating system and the maximum file handles available, as well as by the available memory in the computer. The theoretical limit is tens of thousands of archive files, although the actual number is typically between 30 to 100 archive files on medium to large systems. Consider the following when determining archive file size and count: The total archive volume, the size of a single archive file times the number of archive files, affects the length of time that files store data before being overwritten. The individual archive volume, the size of a single archive file, affects how often an archive shift occurs. The Advanced Continuous Historian performs an archive shift to switch archiving from the active file to the file that contains the oldest data. The individual archive volume also affects how much available data is discarded when an archive shift occurs. For example, if each archive stored approximately one month of data and there were three archives, there would be a maximum of three months data online just prior to the shift and a maximum of two months data online after the archive shift. Take the following items into consideration before setting the archive files: Consider future expansion. Estimate the point count for the next year or two and size archive files accordingly. Data storage rate increases with an increase in scan rate and decreases with an increase in compression deviation. The default compression values are Compression=ON with a Compression Deviation of 0. If this is left unchanged, every change in data values will be stored to disk, possibly consuming the archives much faster than expected. Each point stored requires a minimum of 2 KB of storage for the archive system to work correctly. However, archive storage is more efficient if 5 KB per point are used. An archive file can be any size, as long as it meets the minimum storage requirements, but it is recommended that all archives be the same size to facilitate system administration. Once created, the size of a fixed archive cannot be changed. It must be deleted and then recreated at the larger size. Therefore, it is much easier to add archives than to change archive sizes. Be generous in archive file sizing to meet the point count estimates and use the archive count to adjust for total archive duration. General guidelines Follow the general guidelines below to decide how to provision and size the archive files for the Advanced Continuous Historian. For specific questions or requirements, contact Emerson Technical Support. Archive creation Turn on Automatic Archive Creation . This feature is enabled by default for new installations of the Advanced Continuous Historian. The Advanced Continuous Historian will create new archive files as needed, which means that you will only need to monitor available disk space. For more information, refer to How PI 3.4 Automatic Archive Creation Feature Works (OSIsoft KB 3122OSI8). Alternatively, you can create enough archive files to cover a given time range. Once all files are used and contain data, the Advanced Continuous Historian automatically overrides the archive file containing the oldest data. You can take this archive offline, turn its shift flag off, or mark it read-only if you don’t want data to be overwritten. Archive type Always use fixed-size archive files for the Primary storage area and all other archives receiving online data. The Advanced Continuous Historian automatically grows fixed-size archives if they become full. Such archives will be identified with the “auto-dynamic” type. Dynamic archives can be used for older systems or for offline operations such as combining two or more small archives. For details about fixed size versus dynamic archives, refer to Advantages of using Fixed archives vs. Dynamic archives (OSIsoft KB 2998OSI8 ) and PI Server Reference Guide . Recommended size The default archive size is 256 MB. It is recommended that you use the default size. Otherwise, archive file size should be kept between five and 10 times the expected point count, expressed in kilobytes (KB). For instance, a system with 30,000 points should function well with archive files between 150 MB and 300 MB. The minimum archive size is 2,048 times the point count in bytes, which yields approximately 2 MB with 1,000 points. Maximum size The recommended maximum size of an archive is one-third of installed random access memory (RAM) on Windows Server. If point count and archive sizing needs exceed recommended maximum size, you should consider installing more memory. Additional considerations Consider the items below when deciding on archive size: Data rates Archive size should provide a balance between data rates, storage consumed per unit of time, and shift frequency, number of files per unit of time. Increasing shift frequency is usually better than increasing archive size beyond the recommended range. You can find data rate information for your archives by using the Archives plugin in the PI System Management Tools (PI SMT), or by running the piartool -al command. Each registered archive shows the Add Rate/Hour which is the average rate of records in kilobytes used per hour to the archive, showing how quickly the archive files are filling up. Compression settings Although disk space is usually inexpensive, disk access – in bytes and/or I/O per second – remains expensive. Be sure to apply the appropriate compression settings for tags on large systems as this will reduce disk space used and increase disk access performance. For more information about recommended exception and compression settings, refer to What are recommended Exception and Compression settings (OSIsoft KB 3226OSI8). Windows file system cache Archive throughput will improve when the archive size is significantly smaller than the Windows File System Cache (FSC) so that the most commonly requested data resides in memory. For more information, refer to File Cache Performance and Tuning at the Microsoft TechNet web site. No limit for maximum FSC size exists for Windows Server operating systems. You can monitor cache and disk performance by looking at the Windows Performance Counters: Cache\Copy Read Hits % and Physical Disk(<Volume>)\% Idle Time. Values significantly above 90% for both of these counters usually indicate a healthy system. System backups Since the most recent archive files are usually backed up in every system backup, do not create archives that exceed the limits of your physical backup media. Smaller files will also speed up the verification phase of the Advanced Continuous Historical backups. For specific details about the Advanced Continuous Historian archive sizing and storage space utilization, refer to the Hardware System Sizing Recommendations spreadsheet accompanying the Advanced Continuous Historian documentation. title: Sizing modules
body_text: Sizing modules Typically, you want a module to perform one main function. This way, you know which modules to work on and what impact changing them has when you are troubleshooting or maintaining your system. Modules can be downloaded and modified independently from other modules. A module's execution can be stopped or debugged without affecting other modules. Because of this modularity, it makes sense to define your modules so that they contain one functional piece of your system. This enables you to operate, debug, download, and take out of service a single module without affecting other modules. Generally define control modules for one or more field devices and their related control logic. If modules are very large and have multiple functions, it is difficult to troubleshoot and maintain the system and isolate problems and areas for modification. Also, the diagrams for the algorithm get very large and harder to maintain. Conversely, using several small modules to perform a single control task makes it harder to troubleshoot (one module at a time). Smaller modules require that the operators know several module tags to operate a single control device. You must also read and write many external parameters in order to define the module-to-module communications and transfer the information to other modules. Ultimately, you must determine how your system and its functions should be logically divided into modules. However, if you find that a module is getting large and complex, you might want to look for ways to divide it up logically; conversely, if you are defining a large number of external parameters to transfer data between modules, consider containing smaller modules within a larger control module or equipment module. The following figure shows a simple tank-level example and how it might be logically segmented into three control modules. The control modules are circled. If these three modules require coordination, the three control modules shown could be contained within a single equipment module. Example of modular tank-level control

title: Secure parameters in SLS 1508 SIS systems
main_heading: Secure parameters in SLS 1508 SIS systems
body_text: Secure parameters in SLS 1508 SIS systems A checkbox in each SLS 1508 Logic Solver's properties dialog sets whether it has eight secure parameters or 16 high-density secure parameters. Secure parameters can be read by other modules in Logic Solvers on the same controller. Additionally, you can configure a logic solver to publish its secure parameters globally to the SIS Network domain it is in or to publish globally to the entire SIS Network. Publishing as domain global makes the secure parameter data available to all other logic solvers in the SIS Network domain on the same fiber optic ring. A total of 32 logic solvers in each SIS Network domain (no more than 16 on any controller) can publish globally to the domain. In addition as many as 16 logic solvers in the SIS Network can be configured as system global publishers. System global data can move around the entire SIS Network, depending on Ethernet connections between fiber optic rings.

title: SLS 1508 SIS systems in DeltaV Explorer
main_heading: SLS 1508 SIS systems in DeltaV Explorer
body_text: SLS 1508 SIS systems in DeltaV Explorer The DeltaV SIS software components are integrated with the DeltaV software. Enabling DeltaV SIS software from System Preferences adds SIS objects to the DeltaV Explorer and Control Studio so you can configure DeltaV logic solvers and SIS modules. For example, the following figure shows DeltaV Explorer after the SLS 1508 logic solvers preference has been enabled and some configuration has been completed. Explorer hierarchy with SLS 1508 logic solvers enabled The most obvious difference when SLS 1508 logic solvers are enabled is the appearance of the SIS Network. The SIS Network contains the SLS 1508 logic solvers (SLS1, SLS2, SLS3, and SLS4 in the figure). Each Logic Solver contains the configuration information (assigned SIS modules, I/O configuration, alarms, and secure parameters) that will ultimately be downloaded to a physical Logic Solver card. The other noticeable differences (in this figure) are the icons for Logic Solver cards (C01) and SIS module (SIFEXMPL). Enabling DeltaV SIS software also adds SIS items to Library and Setup.

title: SLS 1508 system configuration overview
body_text: SLS 1508 system configuration overview SLS 1508 hardware and DeltaV SIS software is used to install, configure, and operate a system to implement a safety instrumented system in conjunction with sensors and final elements to take a process to a safe state when hazardous conditions occur. Safety instrumented functions are implemented in DeltaV SIS software using SLS 1508 logic solver cards that are installed on DeltaV I/O interface carriers. Each Logic Solver card (that appears in the I/O configuration in DeltaV Explorer) is associated with a Logic Solver (that appears in the SIS Network configuration in DeltaV Explorer). Throughout the SLS 1508 documentation logic solver refers to either of these depending on the context. Logic solver card always refers to the physical card. Logic solvers are where the safety configuration is created. Logic solver cards are where the configuration is downloaded and run. DeltaV SIS components are physically separate from, but integrated with, the DeltaV distributed control system (also known as a basic process control system or BPCS). The SLS 1508 logic solver cards mount on standard DeltaV I/O interface carriers but they are powered separately from the BPCS power supplies. Each logic solver executes up to four SIS modules that perform the safety instrumented function. Safety instrumented functions are configured in one or more SIS modules using the DeltaV engineering tools—DeltaV Explorer and Control Studio. SIS modules are downloaded to run in Logic Solvers. In some cases data needs to be shared between SIS modules as the SIF cannot be completely implemented in a single module. This data is shared between SIS modules through the use of Secure Parameters and Secure Parameter References. Each logic solver can publish up to 16 Secure Parameters. These are Boolean with status values that the SIS module can write to and can be referenced by any other SIS modules in the same logic solver or in a different logic solver on the same node. For larger SIS applications, SIS modules running in logic solvers on different nodes may also need to access these secure parameters. This is accomplished using SIS Network domains. The simplest SLS 1508 system consists of the Logic Solvers on a single node. In DeltaV Explorer these would be configured in the default SIS Network domain folder. For SIS applications that require communication between nodes, larger SIS networks become necessary. The larger networks are configured as one or more fiber optic rings containing multiple SIS Network domains. To allow their Secure Parameters to be seen by Logic Solvers on other controllers these Logic Solvers must be configured as Global Publishers. Logic Solvers can be configured as either Domain or System Global Publishers which define their scope. For information on the capacities of secure parameters in a DeltaV SIS Network refer to the System Capacities topic. title: Emerson Smart Firewall
body_text: Emerson Smart Firewall The Smart Firewall was developed in response to the increased frequency and sophistication of cyber security risks to industrial networks. It is used to protect the DeltaV network from potential security issues and to help ensure reliable and resilient industrial operations. The firewall controls traffic going into the DeltaV network, in particular HTTP, OPC, and remote desktop traffic. It also controls traffic coming out of the DeltaV network such as HTTP and OPC. Web UI The firewall has a built-in web based user interface (web UI) that can be accessed from any workstation on the DeltaV network. The web UI is used to configure the firewall, create the communications protection rules, and control user access. The web UI logs information about network traffic allowing you to monitor the traffic passing through the firewall. The web UI has extensive online help that will guide you through all configuration and troubleshooting procedures. Easy configuration of communication rules A main feature of the firewall is a predefined drop-down list of DeltaV applications that can be used to easily configure the communication rules. Simply select the description of the communications you wish to establish between the DeltaV workstation and the computer on the external network, provide the computer names, and the firewall automatically creates the communications rule to permit the communications through the firewall. All other communication attempts, except those explicitly permitted, are blocked by the firewall. Intrusion Prevention/Detection System The firewall contains an Intrusion Prevention/Detection System (IPS/IDS) that filters traffic based on inspecting the payload of the packets. The IPS/IDS can be loaded with intrusion signatures that are used to compare the packet content with known security threats. The intrusion protection signatures isolate particular types of traffic and stop it from passing through the firewall. New intrusion signatures are issued regularly to keep ahead of the latest security vulnerabilities, ensuring that the DeltaV network is continuously protected. Maintaining the intrusion protection and preventing attacks at the system perimeter can substantially reduce the frequency and cost of vulnerability patching activities on the network devices. Adding a firewall to the Network Device Command Center (NDCC) When you add a firewall using the NDCC, the firewall is given a network address and creates a corresponding control module so that firewall hardware conditions can be interpreted as DeltaV alarms. Adding the firewall to the NDCC also provides access to firewall diagnostics. Smart Firewall features include: The DeltaV-integrated NDCC application that is the user interface for adding a firewall and viewing diagnostic information. Control function block module classes that hold the DeltaV configuration for Emerson Smart Firewalls. Firewall modules (one for each firewall) are instantiated from these classes and run in ProfessionalPLUS or Application Stations. The modules detect active Hardware Alarm Conditions (HAC) based on real-time information read from Smart Firewalls and potentially cause hardware alarms. Support for PlantWeb-style hardware alarms driven by alert conditions detected in Emerson Smart Firewalls. title: Safety instructions for the Emerson Smart Firewall
main_heading: Safety instructions for the Emerson Smart Firewall
body_text: Safety instructions for the Emerson Smart Firewall Product safety The Emerson Smart Firewall complies with product safety requirements for the United States, Canada, the European Union and Russia. General safety instructions The Emerson Smart Firewall is electrically operated. Connect only to AC power supplied according to appropriate national requirements. This product is intended for installation and operation only by personnel who have received appropriate training for its use. Use only undamaged parts. Use the Emerson Smart Firewall only in the manner indicated. To ensure safety, pay attention to all warnings and information relating to safety. Only qualified service personnel should install or service the Emerson Smart Firewall. All power cords must be disconnected before opening the chassis or servicing the unit. This product contains Light Emitting Diode (LED) or Laser components that comply with the IEC 60825-1 (2001) requirements: Class1 Laser Product. Light Emitting Diode - Class 1 LED Product. National and international safety regulations Ensure the electrical installation meets all local or nationally applicable safety regulations. Electro-Static Discharge (ESD) guidelines The Emerson Smart Firewall contains components that are electrostatically sensitive. Inappropriate handling can destroy these components, cause latent, intermittent failures, or reduce the product lifecycle. Adhere to the following protection measures for ESD sensitive assemblies before servicing or touching any components inside the Emerson Smart Firewall: Use properly sealed, conductive bags to transport ESD sensitive components. Use an appropriate method of ESD protection (such as an ESD wristband connected to ground, ESD straps or ESD footwear on an ESD floor) to create electrical equipotential bonding between yourself and your working environment. Once you are properly protected from ESD hazards, you can begin to service ESD sensitive components. CE marking The Emerson Smart Firewall complies with all applicable directives and regulations required for CE marking and import into the European Union, including the following: European (EU) directives: 2004/108/EC - Electro-Magnetic Compatibility Directive 2006/95/EC - Low Voltage Directive 2011/65/EU - RoHS recast Directive REACH Regulation In accordance with the preceding EU directives, an EU Declaration of Conformity has been issued and is available for the Emerson Smart Firewall. The Emerson Smart Firewall complies with the following European standards: Safety: EN60950-1:2006 +A1: 2010 + A11:2009 + A12:2011 Immunity: EN 55024:2010 Emissions: EN55022:2010 Electro-Magnetic Compatibility This is a Class A device. This device can be used in living areas, places of business, and in industrial areas. This device can cause interference in living areas, and in this case the operator may be required to take appropriate measures. The assembly guidelines must be strictly adhered to in order to observe the EMC value limits. The Emerson Smart Firewall complies with EMC requirements for Australia and New Zealand necessary for C-Tick marking. FCC note The Emerson Smart Firewall has been appropriately tested to ensure compliance with Part 15 of the FCC Rules. Operation is subject to the following two conditions: (1) this device may not cause harmful interference, and (2) this device must accept any interference received, including interference that may cause undesired operation. Marine Certification The Emerson Smart Firewall complies with the requirements of DNV 2.4 - Marine Certification for shipboard installations. GOST-R certification The Emerson Smart Firewall is in compliance with Russian quality standards (GOST-R) that are intended to exclude potentially hazardous or unsafe products from entering Russia's commercial space. Recycling note Properly dispose of the Emerson Smart Firewall as electronic waste in accordance with the current disposal regulations of your country, state, or county.

title: SmartPlant Excel Interface
body_text: SmartPlant Excel Interface The DeltaV software includes Excel add-ins that are the interface you use to exchange instrumentation configuration data between the Intergraph SmartPlant Instrumentation (SPI) application and the DeltaV configuration database. The add-ins create the following menus under DeltaV in Excel: SPI Interface — Supports the exchange of data between the SPI application and the Excel worksheet. The interface supports SPI 2013 and SPI 2016 I/O Support — Supports creation and manipulation of configuration data in the Excel worksheet and the exchange of data between the worksheet and the DeltaV configuration database. The add-ins are included on the DeltaV installation media and they do not require any additional licensing or DeltaV software. They also do not require any of the other DeltaV Excel add-ins (DeltaV Reporter, for example) to function. Note: The Excel DeltaV > I/O Support menu is not intended for general purpose bulk editing. Some features in this add-in may be removed or altered to support the SmartPlant Instrumentation interface as it evolves. There are two additional components from Intergraph that work with SPI that support moving data from the DeltaV software to the SmartPlant Instrumentation software: Intergraph SmartPlant Instrumentation Schema Component Intergraph SmartPlant Instrumentation Client. These components are also included with the DeltaV software. This release of the add-ins supports the following functionality in the listed versions of SmartPlant Instrumentation (SPI) software: SPI Version Excel Version Move Data from SPI to DeltaV Move Data from DeltaV to SPI SPI 2013 or latest version 2013 32-bit Yes Yes Note: Excel 2013 supports all of the SPI features that DeltaV software requires. If you use other features of SPI software, refer to its documentation for versions of Excel that it supports. title: DeltaV Smart Switches overview
body_text: DeltaV Smart Switches overview DeltaV Smart Switches are used to construct DeltaV Control Networks according to the IEEE 802.3 Local and Metropolitan Area Networks standards. The DeltaV Smart switches are DeltaV MD base Smart Switches and media modules DeltaV RM100 base Smart Switches and media modules DeltaV RM104 Smart Switches DeltaV RM1040 Smart Switches DeltaV FP20 8-port Smart Switches DeltaV Smart Switches are intended for plug-and-play use with a DeltaV system as unmanaged switches. No configuration is necessary unless you want to use the Network Device Command Center (NDCC) to manage the switches (commission and decommission, lock switches and ports, and so on). If you do not use the NDCC, or you need to perform some initial switch setup such as configuring an IP address before the NDCC is available, you can use the switch’s command line interface by connecting a terminal or a Management station running a terminal emulator to the switch's serial port. A serial interface cable is required to connect the switch’s serial port to the Management station. The serial interface cable can be purchased separately from Emerson Automation Solutions or you can build the cable assembly. Once the switch has an IP address you can access it from a Telnet session or monitor it from the web browser interface. Note, however, that after configuring an IP address using the switch's command line interface instead of the NDCC, you must then decommission the smart switch before it is available for configuration using the NDCC. Refer to the topics on DeltaV Smart Switches in Books Online for information on the Network Device Command Center, for information on configuring, monitoring, and accessing the switches with Telnet, and for information on downloading Java software. Before installing and using DeltaV Smart Switches and media modules, read all safety instructions for DeltaV Smart Switches and media modules. title: Smart cards
body_text: Smart cards The DeltaV system supports the use of smart cards for logging on to DeltaV workstations. The use of smart cards in the DeltaV system requires the following: A Domain-based environment using Active Directory. A smart card reader that supports the Microsoft CryptoAPI. A smart card for each DeltaV user who requires access to the workstation. A smart card reader installed on the workstation and the smart card reader's service is running. A Certificate Authority installed (that is, Active Directory Certificate Services enabled with the Certification Authority role installed) on the DeltaV control network. Note: When using Smart Cards to log into DeltaV, do not enable the policy: Interactive logon: Require smart card , as this will prevent the system from functioning as expected. The DeltaV system administrator has the option of requiring the use of smart card, or making it optional on a per DeltaV workstation basis. The system administrator is responsible for the following on each workstation where the smart card is used Installing the smart card software and hardware. Setting up certificates for each card on the server machine where certification authority is deployed. Note: After enrolling the certificate for a smart card, you typically must pull the card and reinsert it before you can use it to log on. To make sure a smart card is working correctly, use it first to log on to Windows before logging on to the DeltaV system. The card must be able to log a user on to Windows in order to ensure that it can be used to log a user on to the DeltaV system. Leave the card in the reader when using applications that interface with the DeltaV database (for example, Control Studio, DeltaV Explorer and Recipe Studio). If you remove the card from the reader you lose user privileges for certain functions on these applications. Tip: If an error occurs stating the Smart Card logon is not supported for your user account, contact your system administrator. The issue could be with how the certificate is configured on the DeltaV domain controller. For example, the following steps might be needed On the domain controller, run Microsoft Management Console (mmc.exe). Go to File > Add/Remove Snap-ins . Select Certificates , click Add and when prompted, select Computer account . Click Next , Finish , and OK . In the hierarchy, expand Certificates (Local Computer) , right-click Personal , click All Tasks , then click Request New Certificate . Click Next (accepting defaults) until you are on the Request Certificates page. There, select Domain Controller Authentication and click Next until the final page and then click Finish .

title: Smart Commissioning for HART devices
body_text: Smart Commissioning for HART devices Smart Commissioning enables you to configure control strategies and safety logic using only the Device Signal Tags (DSTs), eliminating the need to define the physical location of the I/O. Each I/O function block is linked to a DST that is not assigned to any particular I/O channel. In a traditional configuration approach, I/O references within control strategies are bound to specific channels, creating unnecessary dependencies in the project schedule. With Smart Commissioning, you can configure HART devices and CHARM properties without defining specific CHARM locations. Smart Commissioning consists of the following four components: Auto-sensing devices: Devices are identified by the device tag. The wiring or channel position is no longer relevant for device identification purposes. It does not matter if the device was pre-tagged by the vendor or tagged on site before mechanical completion. Automatic Device Identification, or auto-sensing, is performed using DeltaV Device Commissioner. Automatic binding to control or safety logic: Once the device has been identified, it is automatically bound to the right control strategy based on the device tag. Binding is performed using DeltaV Device Commissioner. Automatic device configuration: Either late configuration changes or the whole device configuration can be applied on site in just a few minutes. Automatic device configuration is performed using I/O Studio. Automatic loop test. Devices are tested using HART commands to set the device output and the response verified all the way to the control or safety logic. Automatic loop testing is performed using DST Simulate. Smart Commissioning consists of the following DeltaV applications: I/O Studio: Create device placeholders and manage the I/O Studio Library. DeltaV Device Commissioner: Commission field devices, CHARMs, and other DeltaV hardware. Auto-sense connected field devices without first having to configure and download CHARMs. Device Signal Simulator: Test the control logic and displays without having to configure I/O or have I/O hardware present. Subtopics: Glossary Terms

title: DeltaV Smart Connector for OSIsoft PI Server
main_heading: DeltaV Smart Connector for OSIsoft PI Server
body_text: DeltaV Smart Connector for OSIsoft PI Server The DeltaV Smart Connector is used to collect configuration and process data from the DeltaV system and populate this data in the OSIsoft PI Server. The DeltaV Asset Connector is a component of the DeltaV Smart Connector and is used specifically for transferring DeltaV parameter configuration data to PI Server. The DeltaV Asset Connector automatically creates and configures attributes on the configured parameters based on the data contained in the PI Server configuration file. The following table lists the DeltaV parameter attributes and the source of their property values from the historian configuration file. PI Point Attributes Source of Values Tag Name <PATH>Tag name </PATH> Scan <ENAB> Enabled </ENAB> (Value of 1 or 0) The Scan attribute of a parameter may also be set to 0 if a tag that was previously in the historian configuration file is removed from history collection. CompDev/Compressing <CDEV> Compression Deviation </CDEV> If CDEV is set to –1, the Compressing parameter attribute is set to 0. If CDEV is not set to –1, the Compressing attribute is set to 1 and the CompDev attribute will be set to the value of CDEV. Step <STEP> Step </STEP> If the DeltaV STEP value is 0, the Step attribute is set to 1. If the DeltaV STEP value is 1, the Step attribute is set to 0. If the DeltaV STEP value is 2 and the parameter type is Integer, the Step attribute is set to 1. If the DeltaV STEP value is 2 and the parameter type is Float, the Step attribute is set to 0. InstrumentTag <PATH> Tag name </PATH> Pointtype <PTYPE> Point type </PTYPE> Source DeltaV Parameter Type XML File PTYPE Value Destination DeltaV Parameter Type INT32 1 Int32 UINT32 2 Float64 FLOAT32 3 Float32 NAMED SET 4 Digital/String UNICODE STRING 5 String Note: If the DeltaV Asset Connector receives an invalid point type value in the historian configuration file, it log an error and do the following: If the corresponding point does not already exist, an error will be logged and the historical parameter will not be created. If the corresponding point already exists, the DeltaV Asset Connector does not edit its configuration and only outputs an error message to the log file. Additionally, all attributes of a point with an invalid point type listed in the historian configuration file will be written to an Error Tag.csv file so that the one or more parameter configurations can be reviewed and/or corrected at a later time. CompMax <MAX> Compression Max </MAX> Zero <EU0> EngUnits 0 </EU0> Location4 (Scan Class) <RATE> Scan Rate in seconds </RATE> Span <EU100> EngUnits 100 </EU100> EU100 is the maximum value, so the Span point attribute is set to EU100–EU0. Descriptor <DESC> Module description </DESC> EngUnits <UNITS> Engineering units </UNITS> DigitalSet <NAMEDSET> Digital State set </NAMEDSET> Related information Configure security options for OSIsoft PI Server Set up OSIsoft PI Server with a new DeltaV system

title: Adding Hosts file entries
body_text: Adding Hosts file entries You will need the IP addresses and full computer names of the computers on the external network to create the Hosts file entries. Full computer names are in the form: Name.company.org or name.company.com. The full computer name can be found on the Control Panel's System page or on the System Properties dialog. As an example, if the full computer name is batch_manager_server.pharma_co.com and the IP address is 192.168.1.24, the entry in the Hosts file would be: 192.168.1.24 batch_manager_server.pharma_co.com as shown in the following example Hosts file. For example: # # 102.54.94.97 rhino.acme.com # source server # 38.25.63.10 x.acme.com # x client host # localhost name resolution is handled within DNS itself. # 127.0.0.1 localhost # ::1 localhost 192.168.1.24 batch_manager_server.pharma_co.com Be sure to save the modified Hosts file after adding new entries.

title: Gathering information to configure the Smart Firewall
main_heading: Gathering information to configure the Smart Firewall
body_text: Gathering information to configure the Smart Firewall The following topics help you to gather the information that is required to configure the firewall and provide suggestions on how to select from the firewall's setup options to ensure that the firewall works correctly within the existing or proposed network architecture after you configure the firewall. After gathering all of the necessary information, follow the procedures in Setting up and configuring the Emerson Smart Firewall to configure the firewall. In order to install the Emerson Smart Firewall and get it up and running properly in your network we suggest that you: Gather the information needed to setup the firewall and to setup communications. Configure the firewall parameters to enable the firewall to work within the existing or proposed networks. Establish communications between the computers on either side of the firewall. Create the communication rules to ensure only authorized communications are allowed through the firewall. Creating communication rules comprises the protection phase of firewall configuration. Firewall configuration can be done on the bench or after the firewall is installed in the network. If the firewall is to be installed in an existing network to replace a router, switch, or existing firewall, it is best to do the configuration on the bench prior to installing the firewall in the existing network. If the firewall is to be installed in a new network, the configuration can be done either on the bench or with the firewall installed in the network. It will be necessary to work with your IT department to obtain the information needed to configure the firewall. Corporate or site-wide IT network and security policies must be followed to ensure the setup conforms (as much as possible) with the policies. You will also need IT support to establish communications between the computers on either side of the firewall. It is always a good idea to include your IT department anytime you connect to their networks or use their networks to move data or to give users external access to the DeltaV system. Note: The Emerson Smart Firewall creates a secure environment in which the addition of new connections or new computers to the system requires deliberate action by the system administrator. This prevents unauthorized users from easily gaining access to the system without the knowledge of the administrator. We recommend using firewall settings that encourage or enforce a more secure environment rather than settings that might create a more automatic, plug and play environment. It is up to the individual user to decide if and how a more secure environment is enforced. Note: In this document DeltaV workstation means any computer connected to the DeltaV 2.5 LAN whether or not DeltaV is installed on the computer. title: Information needed to enable communications through the Smart Firewall
main_heading:
Information needed to enable communications through the Smart
	 Firewall
body_text: Information needed to enable communications through the Smart Firewall The firewall requires that routing is configured on the external workstations since the external workstations are on different subnets from the DeltaV workstations. Routing provides the communications path from the external workstations to the internal workstations. If routing is not configured, the external workstations cannot find the internal workstations. The network administrators can add routing information to the devices that route network traffic such as routers or use the route add command on each external workstation to allow external workstations to locate internal workstations. In a network architecture where the external workstations are two or more network hops away from the firewall (workstations communicating through two or more routers or firewalls) the IT department will need to add routing information to the routing devices to allow the external workstations to communicate with the internal workstations. Consult with your IT department and obtain the following information required to enable communications through the firewall. We recommend that you record this information on the worksheets. Are any of the external workstations across subnets (multiple routing devices)? If yes, assistance from the IT department is required. Will routing be added to network devices? Will each external workstation be configured with a route add statement? Subtopics: Add a static route to a workstation Resolving workstation names Modifying the Hosts file Adding Hosts file entries Testing modifications to the Hosts file Related information Configure the external network

title: Information needed to configure the external network
main_heading: Information needed to configure the external network
body_text: Information needed to configure the external network The address of the firewall's external network (business, plant LAN, DMZ) port can act as a DHCP client and can be assigned by the site's DHCP server or it can be set to a static address by the firewall administrator. This address will be the gateway address to the firewall's routing function. It is used when providing network routing information to configure external routes or to manually update the computer routing table using the route add command. Emerson recommends that you give the firewall a static IP address without DNS information. When a firewall with static IP addressing is rebooted, its IP address persists; the DHCP server does not give it a different IP address. This ensures that the routing information configured for the external workstations remains correct. Correct routing information is required for the external workstations to communicate with internal workstations across the firewall. Consult with your IT department and obtain the following information required to configure the firewall's external network for static IP addressing. We recommend that you record this information on the Worksheet for Smart Firewall Configuration and record the external workstation names and IP addresses on the Worksheet for external workstation names and IP addresses . Does the firewall have a dedicated IP address assigned by the administrator (recommended)? What is the external network address? What is the external network subnet mask? If DNS servers are used, what are their IP addresses (2 max)? Note: Emerson strongly recommends that DNS addresses are not used. This prevents users from entering a URL address in an internet browser on a DeltaV workstation and accessing the internet. What is the gateway's IP address? Note: For the Smart Firewall this is the same address as the external network address. This is also the address used as the gateway parameter in the route add command. Can users on the external network log into the firewall with read-only privileges? When you have gathered all the necessary information and completed the worksheet, you are ready to configure the external network.
