title: Terminators
body_text: Terminators A fieldbus segment acts as a transmission line for data communications between the various devices. A terminator balances the impedance at each end of a transmission line to ensure reliable communications. The H1 card requires an external terminator for each segment as well as a second terminator at the device end of the segment. Some fieldbus power supplies and device connection blocks may provide a fixed or switchable terminator for one end of the segment. The H1 with Integrated Power card contains an integrated terminator for each segment. A second terminator is required at the field end of each segment. Ensure that each segment is terminated in two places.

title: DeltaV system terminology
body_text: DeltaV system terminology Control strategies in the DeltaV system are configured in modules . A module, which is the smallest logical control entity in the system, contains algorithms, conditions, alarms, displays, historical information, and other characteristics that define the process equipment. Algorithms are the logical steps that define how a module behaves. The DeltaV system provides control, equipment, and unit modules. Generally, a control module contains one uniquely tagged control entity, such as a control loop or motor, with its associated logic. Defining a module around a single field device and its related control logic makes it easy to create, download, operate, debug, and take a single module out of service without affecting other modules. Equipment modules coordinate the operation of control modules and other equipment modules that work together to control related equipment. The algorithm for the containing equipment module manages the operation of the contained modules. Unit modules can be used in non-batch applications to group control modules and equipment modules for alarm management purposes. For example, alarms for a specific unit, such as a boiler, can be combined. All control and equipment modules associated with the unit will be contained within the unit module. Function blocks are building blocks for creating the continuous and discrete algorithms that perform the control or monitoring for the process. The DeltaV Library contains function block templates for analog control (bias/gain, lead/lag, PID, etc.), Logical, I/O (analog and discrete input/output), and other basic functions. Each function block contains parameters that can be modified to customize the algorithm. Algorithms range from simple input conversions to complex control strategies. Function blocks can be combined into composite function blocks to build complex algorithms. In addition to Function Block algorithms, the DeltaV system supports Sequential Function Charts (SFCs) as well as Command-driven and State-driven algorithms for control tasks requiring sequencing strategies. Parameters are the user-defined data used within a module's algorithm to perform its calculations and logic. Parameters can be described by the type of information they provide, such as input or output. Tables listing the parameters and their properties are included in Books Online . The DeltaV system includes a library of pre-engineered module templates with basic characteristics. You can customize these library modules or create your own modules from scratch. You can then add your customized modules to the library, making them available for reuse in the development of your control strategy. Modules that work closely together to perform a specific process control function are typically grouped in an area . An area is a logical division of a plant. Areas typically represent plant locations or main processing functions. The configuration engineer determines how to logically divide the plant into areas. Nodes are physical pieces of equipment on the control network, such as a controller or a workstation. You control your process by downloading modules to the controller nodes. The configuration tells the node how to act and what information to receive or save from the process. Device Tags represent the instruments, valves, and other field devices. A Device Signal Tag consists of a specific signal from a device. Alarms alert the operator that an event has occurred. (Alarms are assigned to modules.) Typically, you want the operator to perform some action and respond to the alarm. Alarms can be both visible and audible. The database contains configuration information and lets you make off-line changes without affecting the process. Online control algorithm monitoring and modification are also available. The following diagram shows an example of a DeltaV system hierarchical structure.

title: Terminology
body_text: Terminology Following is a list of terms and their definitions. DeltaV Remote Client - the DeltaV application that allows access to a DeltaV server through a Microsoft Remote Desktop connection. Remote Client server - the DeltaV ProfessionalPLUS or Operator Station that is set up to function as a host machine (server) for clients accessing a DeltaV system through the DeltaV Remote Client application. Remote Client node - a computer, such as a desktop PC, laptop computer, or any DeltaV workstation that can be used to access a DeltaV system through the DeltaV Remote Client application. Remote Client session - an object configured in the DeltaV Explorer that represents the availability of a remote session. It contains an assigned license, assigned areas (from the DeltaV application's control strategy), and optional reserved lists of users/nodes. Remote Session - an actual session in which a Remote Client server is accessed by a Remote Client node. Remote Desktop Services (formerly Terminal Server) - a Microsoft application and role that includes the basic functions necessary for administrators to set up server and client nodes, manage connections, send messages, view sessions, and so forth. Remote Desktop Connection - a Microsoft communications tool that allows a remote PC to connect to a host computer's desktop and run applications as if the user were sitting at the host machine. It is available by clicking Start > Programs > Accessories > Communications . Note: You can use the DeltaV screen saver to set up the auto-logoff feature on a remote terminal. Related information Recommended maintenance practices

title: Testing communications between the internal and external network
main_heading:
Testing communications between the internal and external
	 network
body_text: Testing communications between the internal and external network Once the networks have been configured, the next step is to ensure the computers and devices on either side of the firewall can communicate with each other. It is assumed that you have worked with your IT department to complete the firewall configuration worksheets and that you have set up the necessary routing information on the external workstations and routers. Further, it is assumed that the DeltaV workstations' NICs have the default gateway defined as the firewall's IP address. We will use the standard network ping command to verify that the workstations on either side of the firewall can communicate with each other. Before testing, you will put the firewall in Allow all mode so you can easily ping between the computers or devices. The firewall's Allow all mode allows any computer on either side of the firewall to communicate through the firewall. The firewall essentially acts as a simple router and does not block any communications. During operation the Allow all mode is used only if there are problems with critical applications that must remain working. The firewall is set to Allow all mode temporarily as the problem is resolved. We will use Allow all mode during setup so that we can test communications between the computers on either side of the firewall so there is no chance of the firewall configuration impacting the communications. Note: In Allow all mode, there is no logging and no connections are listed unless you create protection rules to allow pinging between computers. As rules are not necessary to verify communications we will not build rules now. Subtopics: Test communications between the internal and external network

title: Testing graphics configurations online prior to publishing
main_heading: Testing graphics configurations online prior to publishing
body_text: Testing graphics configurations online prior to publishing In addition to verifying configurations before you publish, you can also see how your graphics configurations appear and behave online using the Quick Online View feature. Displays, display sets, and layouts are tested online by adding them to the Quick Online View using the ribbon's Quick Online View command. The displays and layouts in Quick Online View also reflect and test any standards and functions referenced by these displays and layouts as well as any GEMs contained by the displays. Active languages and themes can also be tested in conjunction with displays by switching the theme or language in Graphics Studio to see how they look. Languages and themes must also be assigned to the workstation on which they are being tested, and the workstation settings must be published. You can test multiple displays simultaneously to see how they work together, such as when you want to test opening a contextual display from a button on a different display. The Manage Quick Online View pop-up lists all configurations that have been added to Quick Online View for all instances of Graphics Studio; all items on the list are available to be tested in Quick Online View. The first item you add to the Manage Quick Online View list opens the DeltaV Live Quick Online View instance. From that point, each time you add a new item to the list, the Quick Online View instance receives the new content. Configurations remain in the list until you click Remove All in the pop-up or close all instances of Graphics Studio, along with the Quick Online View instance. You can test any layout or display set regardless of which layout or display set is assigned to that workstation; testing configurations that are not assigned to that workstation does not change the workstation's assignments. Only one layout and one display set at a time can be tested, however, because only one of each can be available online. The Manage Quick Online View list reflects the layout and display set most recently added to the list. Configurations can still be edited after they have been added to Quick Online View, but you must re-add them to Quick Online View to make the changes available for testing. Configurations that are locked for editing can still be added to Quick Online View.

title: Testing target to actual integer values in expressions
main_heading: Testing target to actual integer values in expressions
body_text: Testing target to actual integer values in expressions When writing expressions to read modes the .ACTUAL integer value is sometimes different from the .TARGET integer value even if the word (CAS, RCAS, etc.) is the same. This is a result of the way fieldbus has defined modes. The following expression provides a way to test for equality between TARGET and ACTUAL even when the integer values could be different. ('MODE.ACTUAL' & 239) = ('MODE.TARGET' & 239)

title: Testing the revised DRAIN phase
body_text: Testing the revised DRAIN phase To test the operator prompt, you will need to open the Batch Operator Interface. You might also want to open DeltaV Operate to see if all the valves are closed and that the process is otherwise in a state of readiness. With both operator interfaces open, you can switch back and forth to run the batch recipes and watch the batch progress on the Process picture. You can resize the operator interface screens so you can see the important parts of both at one time. You might even want to open the unit module UM_BLEND_500 in Control Studio. Select the DRAIN running logic and put it in online mode so you can see the phase progress through the steps of the Sequential Function Chart. (This is useful if you encounter any errors that you need to fix.) Note: In the following procedure, the Batch Executive is stopped before downloading. Subtopics: Test the revised DRAIN phase Related information Effects of configuration changes

title: Testing UM_COLOR_100 using the Batch graphic
main_heading: Testing UM_COLOR_100 using the Batch graphic
body_text: Testing UM_COLOR_100 using the Batch graphic Now you are ready to test the FILL unit phase for UM_COLOR_100. You will start by launching DeltaV Operate in run mode and opening the graphic named Batch, which shows the unit modules you will create for this tutorial. This is not a graphic that you would normally create for an application. We have provided it as a testing tool. Each box on this graphic represents a unit module with its list of assigned phases. Each box also has data links for request and batch input parameters. For example, the box representing the UM_COLOR_100 unit module looks like this: One reason for having the Batch graphic is that it has been set up with data links that allow us to open unit module faceplates and directly manipulate the phases. To open the faceplate for a unit module, click the unit module name. A phase faceplate can then be opened from the unit module faceplate by loading the phase and clicking the Faceplate button beside the phase name. At this point in our configuration effort, the Batch graphic provides this direct access to the unit modules and unit phases and is therefore a useful tool for testing and troubleshooting. After you open the Batch graphic, you will open the faceplate for the UM_COLOR_100 unit module, load the FILL phase, open its faceplate, and then go to the Process graphic to watch what happens when you manipulate the phase states. When you start the FILL phase, the valve state changes to OPEN, and the tank begins to fill, as shown by the fill level. (A Total Flow value appears above the tank.) Then, you will change the FILL_AMOUNT parameter. When the tank fill level is reached, the phase goes to COMPLETE. At that point, you will reset the phase and unload it. title: The Batch Executive properties
body_text: The Batch Executive properties To support loading and handling of large batch systems, every DeltaV system supports multiple Batch Executive subsystems. Each Batch Executive subsystem is configured in the DeltaV Explorer and consists of the Batch Executive, Assigned Areas, and Assigned Recipes components. A maximum of four Batch Executives can be enabled on a single DeltaV Network. A Batch Executive Subsystem Configuring a Batch Executive's properties entails enabling the Batch Executive, which designates a machine as a location for the Batch Executive server to run, and defining the behavior of the Batch Executive server. Below each Batch Executive is the Assigned Areas object. This container provides a way to quickly see the equipment that has been assigned to this Batch Executive. Batch control is organized through process cells that contain the batch equipment (units) and areas that contain the process cells. Therefore, when you assign an area to a Batch Executive subsystem, you also assign the equipment contained in that area to that Batch Executive. An area can be assigned to only one Batch subsystem at a time. Each Batch Executive also contains an Assigned Recipes object. When you assign recipes and recipe folders to the Batch Executive, you release the recipe to production, making it available to the operator to create and run the recipe. Individual recipes and recipe folders can be assigned to run on multiple Batch Executives; however, all the units needed for a particular recipe must reside on one Batch Executive. All of the batch components can still be configured without enabling the Batch Executive but they cannot be tested. Note: Each Batch Executive sends its events to one Batch Historian. Subtopics: Enabling the Batch Executive Batch Executive Server configuration Batch Executive action confirmation Batch Executive Server's client configuration Failure handling for the Batch Executive Related information Input configuration Assigning a plant area to a Batch Executive subsystem Assigning recipes and recipe folders to a Batch Executive subsystem

title: The Batch Historian properties
body_text: The Batch Historian properties You use the Batch Historian properties to identify the machines and subsystems that will be the data sources for the Batch Historian and to specify the storage locations for the Batch Historian database. Note: When you make a change to a Batch Historian that is not on the ProfessionalPLUS workstation, you must download the ProfessionalPLUS workstation in order for all the workstations in the system receive the change. title: The Batch Historian software
body_text: The Batch Historian software The Batch Historian software includes the Batch History View application, the Batch Historian Server, and the Batch Historian Administration Tool. The Batch Historian Server and the Batch Historian Administration Tool applications are installed separately from the standard DeltaV software to protect the Batch Historian from inadvertently being installed and run on a non-supported workstation. (Emerson supports the Batch Historian only when it is installed on an Application Station .) The Batch History View application is installed with the DeltaV software. The Historian Administration Tool is installed with the Batch Historian server. Note: Emerson strongly recommends that the Batch Executive and Batch Historian not be installed on the same workstation. Up to four Batch Historians can be enabled on a DeltaV system. The Batch Historian requires Microsoft SQL Server Standard to be installed. If not already installed on the Batch Historian computer (can be accomplished as part of the DeltaV installation process), the Batch Historian Server installation will install it. This is the screen that opens by default when the Batch Operator Interface is launched. Batch List Screen The following tasks are performed only through the Batch List screen: Adding a batch Removing a batch In addition, all other commands can be issued from the Batch List screen. The summary column in the Batch List screen uses the following abbreviations to represent all the statuses found in that recipe. A number listed next to the abbreviation represents the number of phases in that state. title: The Batch Operator Interface screens
body_text: The Batch Operator Interface screens The Batch Operator Interface is a graphical environment used by the operator to monitor and control all automated batch operations. It is the application provided by the DeltaV system that is immediately available to issue batch commands. The Batch Operator Interface provides the operator many different views into the batch production process by providing the following Batch Operator Interface screens: Batch List Procedure as PFC Procedure as Table Event Journal Unacknowledged Prompts Phase Control Arbitration Active Phase Summary Alarm Summary System Configuration and Defaults The Batch Operator Interface Operators can easily switch between the screens by selecting the appropriate button on the toolbar at the top of the Batch Operator Interface. Each screen provides a high level of information. It is necessary for operators to have a good understanding of each screen's primary function so that they can choose the best screen for their specific monitoring and control needs. To refresh any screen, the operator can press the F5 key. Refreshing the screen forces the application to request updated information and repopulates the screen. The Batch Operator Interface normally refreshes the data on its own; however, you can force this by pressing the F5 key. For a detailed explanation of each of the Batch Operator Interface screens, refer to the appropriate sections. title: The batch redundancy server
body_text: The batch redundancy server The Batch Redundancy Server facilitates interactions between any redundancy aware batch applications and the redundancy subsystem. The Batch Redundancy Server is also responsible for the synchronization activities required to accomplish redundant batch functionality. Therefore, the Batch Redundancy Server on the active attempts to be in communication with the Batch Redundancy Server on the standby at all times. The Batch Redundancy Server is launched under the DeltaVAdmin account credentials. The Batch Redundancy Server has the following responsibilities: Interface to the redundancy subsystem Monitor relevant batch processes Handle batch data synchronization Manage Direct Link and ACN connections Manage batch redundancy licensing Generate redundancy related events and alerts On-line upgrade support for batch components

title: The Campaign Manager's client configuration
body_text: The Campaign Manager's client configuration The Campaign Manager client configuration is an option on the context menu of the Campaign Manager sub-system. This option sets the configuration of the default options that all Campaign Manager Operator Interfaces (CMOI) attaching to this Campaign Manager server node will use. If selected in the Client Configuration dialog, the individual CMOI clients can override the default settings. This allows you to set the defaults for all CMOI clients to start with and allows for individual changes to be made on each CMOI client as needed. In the client configuration dialogs, you can Configure the General Defaults Set the Column Order Define the Display Colors Refer to DeltaV Explorer help for more information about the Client Configuration dialog.

title: The Campaign Manager components
body_text: The Campaign Manager components The DeltaV Campaign Manager is composed of several software modules that work together to form a classic client/server-based, distributed application. Note: All nodes have to be part of the same domain or workgroup. The major components are as follows: DeltaV Batch Campaign Manager Operator Interface This client application supplied with the DeltaV Campaign Manager product allows end-users to define and manipulate campaigns along with the individual batches within a given campaign. This includes selecting recipes, formulas, unit binding, and parameter information for each batch within a campaign (as well as the campaign itself) as well as releasing, starting, and removing batches to the Batch Executive. The client application can be installed and used on any Windows workstation or Windows server operating system that is currently supported for DeltaV, even if the computer is not a DeltaV computer. DeltaV Batch Campaign Manager Client Control The Campaign Manager client control is a standard ActiveX control that provides all client applications (including the one provided with the DeltaV Campaign Manager product) with a programmable API (Application Programming Interface) to the Campaign Manager server. This API can be programmed against from a variety of environments, including C\C++, and VB. Like the client application, the client control can be run on any Windows workstation or Windows server operating system that is currently supported for DeltaV, even if the computer is not a DeltaV computer. DeltaV Batch Campaign Manager Server The Campaign Manager server provides all Campaign Manager clients with a single point of entry for all campaign-related information. It is responsible for both maintaining and monitoring all of the campaigns defined throughout the system along with all of the batches within the campaigns. The Campaign Manager server communicates with the Batch Executive to allow limited control of batches (release, start, and remove) and to keep track of various batch states, for example, RUNNING, STOPPING, HELD, and so on. Running Controls on an Non-DeltaV Node To run the Campaign Manager Operator Interface or Campaign Manager client control on a non-DeltaV node, you must perform the following steps: Register the files, dvbcampaignmgrps.dll and dvbctrlcampaignmgr.dll (regsvr32 dvbcampaignmgrps.dll and regsvr32 dvbctrlcampaignmgr.dll). Note: When registering the DLL(s) on a 64-bit operating system, you must use the 64-bit version of regsvr32.exe. This can be found at C:\Windows\SysWOW64\regsvr32.exe . Create the DeltaVAdmin account on a the non-DeltaV node with the same password as the DeltaVAdmin account on the Campaign Manager Server node. It is recommended that any accounts that jointly exist on DeltaV systems and non-DeltaV systems (such as the DeltaVAdmin account) be set as non-interactive users. That is, the user account cannot be used to log onto Windows. This can be set using GPOs or local policies (in a workgroup). Set the DCOM option to permit unauthenticated users. Log in to the non-DeltaV node as a user that matches a DeltaV user (same user name and password as on a DeltaV node). This user must have the appropriate DeltaV keys for the Campaign Manager actions to be performed (start/stop campaign or batch and so on).

title: The Campaign Manager Operator Interface
body_text: The Campaign Manager Operator Interface The Campaign Manager Operator Interface is similar in appearance to the DeltaV Explorer. However, the commands and buttons are quite different. To start the Campaign Manager Operator Interface, click Start > DeltaV Operator > Campaign Manager Operator Interface . The left pane shows the information in your campaigns. To explore the hierarchy, you can click the plus sign next to an object. Continue to click the plus signs to drill down into the campaign hierarchy. Click an object in the left pane to display details about the object in the right pane. Select and right-click an object in the left pane. The resulting context menu allows you to do things with the object such as edit, delete, and add a new object. The options available depend on the type of object you select. The right pane displays the information associated with the item selected in the left pane. Select an object in the right pane, and then right-click. The resulting context menu allows you to do things with the object, such as edit, delete, and add a new object. The options available depend on the type of object you select. Subtopics: Campaign Manager toolbar icons Install and uninstall the Campaign Manager Operator Interface

title: The Campaign Manager server
body_text: The Campaign Manager server The Campaign Manager Server controls the execution of a campaign, maintains all the runtime information about each campaign, and forwards the data to the DeltaV Batch Historian. The Campaign Manager Server is configured in DeltaV Explorer by selecting the node on which the Campaign Manager server will run. You can also define the client properties for Campaign Manager Operator Interface clients that connect to this server under the Campaign Manager Server node in DeltaV Explorer. The Campaign Manager Server is started and stopped using DeltaV Application Manager ( Start > DeltaV Batch > Application Manager ). To start the Campaign Manager Server, start the Application Manager, select the Executive tab and start the Batch Executive. Then select the Campaign Manager tab and click the Start button. Refer to the DeltaV Application Manager help topics for more information on setting up the Batch Executive and starting the servers. The help system also contains specifics about configuring the Campaign Manager Server, including such actions as setting and clearing campaign locks and clearing the purge persistence. Clearing the purge persistence clears the campaign journal files and the Campaign Manager's current state. This is equivalent to a cold restart of the Campaign Manager server since the last known state of the server is cleared.

body_text: The Campaign Manager Server properties The Campaign Manager server properties enables and configures the Campaign Manager server on the node. You configure the Campaign Manager server through DeltaV Explorer. Select and right-click the node that is the Campaign Manager Server, and then select Properties . The Properties dialog opens with three tabs; General , Server , and Action Confirmation . The Campaign Manager server must be enabled, a Batch Executive node must be selected, and the Campaign Manager must be downloaded before the Campaign Manager client can run. title: The DVBCMBatchEdit/Info objects
body_text: The DVBCMBatchEdit/Info objects The DVBCMBatchEdit and DVBCMBatchInfo objects are used to edit or read information about a specific batch within a given campaign. These objects cannot be instantiated unto themselves. Instead, both must be retrieved using the appropriate DVBCMCampaignEdit or DVBCMCampaignInfo method (get_BatchEdit or get_BatchInfo). The DVBCMBatchEdit object encapsulates all data of a specific batch of the campaign edit object from which it was derived. It has read and write capabilities and is used to configure, change, or manipulate all properties of a batch. The object has two lock methods: DVBCMBatchEdit.LockControl and DVBCMBatchEdit.LockEdit. All properties of the batch edit object are read only except Index. The batch edit object can be used to view the batch's state, ID, and so on. The object can be used to view or set lockout info. The object can also be used to determine if the batch is a setup or cleanup batch (refer to the Order of Execution section for more information). When only reading (not writing) a batch's data, always use an info object rather than edit object to save system resources and avoid lockout problems. The DVBCMBatchinfo object encapsulates all data of a specific batch of the campaign info object from which it was derived. It has read-only capabilities and is only used to view the properties of a batch. The object does not have a lockout property since it is read only. The object can be used to view a batch's state, index, ID, and so on; to retrieve the batch's recipe info object; to view recipe properties of the batch; or to view lockout info. When only reading (not writing) a batch's data, always use an info object rather than an edit object to save system resources and avoid lockout problems. Subtopics: IDVBCMBatchEdit/Info interface methods IDVBCMBatchEdit/Info::interface properties

title: The DVBCMCampaignEdit/Info objects
body_text: The DVBCMCampaignEdit/Info objects The DVBCMCampaignEdit and DVBCMCampaignInfo objects are used to edit or read information about a specific campaign within the Campaign Manager's campaign list. These objects cannot be instantiated unto themselves. Instead, both must be retrieved using the appropriate DVBCMClient object method, either get_CampaignEdit or get_CampaignInfo. The DVBCMCampaignEdit object encapsulates all data of a specific campaign on the Campaign Manager server. It has read and write capabilities and is used to configure, change, and manipulate the campaign and its properties. This object has a lock method, DVBCMCampaignEdit.LockEdit, so only one user at a time is able to edit the campaign's data. The object can be used to edit a campaign's prefix, suffix, description, or maximum active batches; to add batches; to retrieve a batch edit object or base recipe edit object; to view the campaign's batch list; to lock or unlock the campaign for edit; or to view the campaign's name, batch count, state, and so on. Only use the edit object when editing a campaign's data. To view a campaign's data, an info object should be used to save resources and avoid lockout problems. The DVBCMCampaignInfo object encapsulates all data of a specific campaign on the Campaign Manager server. It has read-only capabilities and is used to view all properties of a campaign. The object does not have a lock method since it is read only. The object can be used to view a campaign's name, prefix, suffix, description, maximum active batches, batch count, or state; to retrieve a batch edit info or base recipe info object; or to view a campaign batch list. When only reading (not writing) a campaign's data, always use an info object rather than an edit object to save system resources and avoid lockout problems. Subtopics: IDVBCMCampaignEdit/Info interface methods IDVBCMCampaignEdit/Info interface properties

title: The DVBCMClient object
body_text: The DVBCMClient object The DVBCMClient is the main object exposed by the DVBCtrlCampaignMgr control. All other API exposed objects must be obtained from this main object. Also, update event notifications are fired from the main API object. The DVBCMClient object can be connected to one, and only one, Campaign Manager server. After connecting, the DVBCMClient object is used to retrieve data from and write data to all campaigns and batches on the connected Campaign Manager server. The object can retrieve a campaign object, retrieve the campaign list, show the current DeltaV user, and be used to create a new campaign. Finally, it can be used to obtain Batch Executive information to view recipes, unit, and parameter lists, or to gather recipe parameter information. This is the only interface that can be retrieved from the DVBCtrlCampaignMgr control through the COM API (for example, CoGetClassObject, CoCreateInstatnce, CreateObject, and so on). This interface provides the highest level methods to the Campaign Manager Server and also provides methods to retrieve the other exported interfaces. Subtopics: IDVBCMClient interface methods IDVBCMClient interface properties

title: The DVBCM enumerated sets
body_text: The DVBCM enumerated sets The following topics list the DVBCM Enumerated Sets and their enumerations. Subtopics: DVBCMBATCHSTATE DVBCMCAMPAIGNSTATE DVBCMRECIPEPARAMTYPE DVBCMERRORCODE DVBCMCONFIGUREDACTION

title: The DVBCMExecInfo object
body_text: The DVBCMExecInfo object The DVBCMExecInfo object allows a client application to retrieve recipe and equipment information from a given executive. Use DVBCMExecInfo to view enumerated sets and recipe lists for the Batch Executive configured for the connected Campaign Manager server. Also use this object to obtain a Batch Executive recipe info object (DVBCMExecRecipeInfo) to view recipe information. All of the information visible from this object (as well as any of its subordinate objects) is read only and cannot be changed. This object has no lockout properties. This object cannot be instantiated unto itself. Instead, it must be retrieved using the IDVBCMClient::get_ExecutiveInfo method. All Batch Executive Access objects in the Campaign Manager get their information from the DeltaV Batch Access Server (which gets it information directly from the Batch Executive). All Batch Executive information is downloaded from the DeltaV system and is not created or managed by the Campaign Manager server. Subtopics: IDVBCMExecInfo interface methods IDVBCMExecInfo interface properties

title: The DVBCMExecRecipeInfo object
body_text: The DVBCMExecRecipeInfo object The DVBCMExecRecipeInfo object allows a client application to retrieve read-only information about a specific recipe from a given Batch Executive on the connected Campaign Manager server. This information is used when creating a new campaign or changing the recipe of a campaign or batch. The object can be used to view all the recipe steps and the unit classes on which they are based. The object can also be used to view formula information, including parameter names and values, for the selected recipe. The object can be used to retrieve a Batch Executive parameter info object (DVBCMExecParamInfo) to view the properties of an individual parameter. The DVBCMExecRecipeInfo is a read-only object; therefore, it has no lockout properties. This object cannot be instantiated unto itself. Instead, it must be retrieved using the DVBCMExecInfo method, get_ExecutiveRecipeInfo. All Batch Executive Access objects in the Campaign Manager get their information from the DeltaV Batch Access Server (which gets its information directly from the Batch Executive). All Batch Executive information is downloaded from the DeltaV system and is not created or managed by the Campaign Manager server. Subtopics: IDVBCMExecRecipeInfo interface methods IDVBCMExecRecipeInfo interface properties

title: The DVBCMRecipeEdit/Info objects
body_text: The DVBCMRecipeEdit/Info objects The DVBCMRecipeEdit and DVBCMRecipeInfo objects are used to edit or read information about a recipe object within a given batch. These objects cannot be instantiated unto themselves. Instead, both must be retrieved using the appropriate DVBCMBatchEdit or DVBCMBatchInfo object, or DVBCMCampaignEdit or DVBCMCampaignInfo object methods (get_RecipeEdit or get_RecipeInfo). The DVBCMRecipeEdit object can represent two types of recipes, depending on where it is called. If the object is called from a campaign's edit object, then it encapsulates all the data for the campaign's base recipe and is used to fill the recipe objects of all future batches added to the campaign. The campaign's recipe edit object can only be retrieved when the campaign is in the defined state. Once any of the campaign's batches have been released to the Batch Executive, the recipe object can no longer be retrieved. If the DVBCMRecipeEdit object is called from a batch's (versus a campaign's) edit object, then the recipe edit object is used to display and edit the recipe information for that specific batch. The batch recipe edit object can only be retrieved while that batch is in the defined state. Once that batch has been released to the Batch Executive, the recipe edit object can no longer be retrieved. The recipe edit object can be used to view or edit the recipe's scale, formula, parameters or bound units. If only reading (not writing) data, an info object should be used to save system resources and avoid lockout problems. The DVBCMRecipeInfo object can represent two types of recipes, depending on where it is called. If the object is called from a campaign's info object, it encapsulates all the data for the campaign's base recipe and provides information for all batches currently based on the campaign's base recipe as well as all batches in the future that will be based on the campaign's base recipe. If it is called from a batch's info object, it is used to display the recipe information for that specific batch. The object can be used to view the name, formula, scale, parameter names and values, and bound units and values of the campaign's base recipe or the batch's recipe. If only reading (not writing) data, an info object should be used to save system resources and avoid lockout problems. Subtopics: IDVBCMRecipeEdit/Info interface methods IDVBCMRecipeEdit/Info interface properties

title: The event journal screen
body_text: The event journal screen The DeltaV Event Journal screen displays a brief history of all batches that have been added to the Batch Operator Interface. It can be used to determine the following: the start and completion time of a batch when and why a batch was placed in a Hold state prompt information, such as: when users were prompted what the prompts were and when the responses to the prompts occurred Subtopics: Components of the event journal screen Journal events Customizing the event journal file

title: The general tab
body_text: The general tab When the Use local client configuration option is checked, the user can: Select how many digits (from 3 to 5) are to be used in the sequence number portion of the Batch ID Select which actions will be enabled for the operator Decide whether or not completed batches will be displayed in the batch list If the Use local client configuration option is not selected, or is not permitted based on the Client Configuration options on the Campaign Manager Server, all changes must be made on the Campaign Manager Server. The Restore General Defaults button restores the General tab to the defaults as configured on the Campaign Manager server's Client Configuration.

title: The HORN parameter
body_text: The HORN parameter The HORN parameter is a parameter associated with the current user that determines when the horn sounds and whether the horn has been enabled. The format for the parameter is THISUSER/HORN. The fields supported are: HENAB (1 is enabled. 0 is disabled.) CV (0 stops the horn from sounding.) The HORN parameter is intended to be used only by the operator's alarm banner. Its use in other displays or by applications other than DeltaV Operate might interfere with the operation of the alarm banner and is not recommended.

title: Themes overview
body_text: Themes overview Themes allow the same graphics configuration to appear differently on different workstations or at different times on the same workstation. Themes can be created for entire displays, including all graphics elements contributing to the display. By applying various themes to the same display, that display can be used for varying situations. When themes have been configured, activated, and published, DeltaV Live users with the appropriate security can select the theme that best meets their needs. For example, you can create a theme that minimizes eye fatigue in low-lighting control room environments, a theme that provides high contrast in brightly lit control room environments; or, an RGS (Reds and Greens Shifted) theme that aids operators who have difficulty distinguishing between certain colors. A theme consists of theme-specific values configured on a standard. A standard can have one theme-specific value (of the same type) for each theme existing in the database. While theme-specific values are assigned to a theme, these values belong to their associated standard rather than the theme to which they are assigned. Figure 1 illustrates this concept. Figure 1 When an active theme is applied in Graphics Studio or DeltaV Live, its theme-specific values replace the standards, system-wide, in all displays. Using themes on a DeltaV Live workstation is optional. If no theme is assigned to that workstation, it uses the published standards. The following themes are provided for you out of the box: Silver (Default Theme) Dark Blue (DB) Dark Blue (DB) Tan (TAN) Light Blue (LB) Creating themes A Themes folder in the Library Explorer pane provides the means for you to access and create themes. When you create a theme, it immediately appears on the Themes tab in the Workstation Management dialog (DeltaV Live Administration), with no publishing required. However, themes must be selected as Active to be used in the system. After adding a new theme, you can add theme-specific values to a standard using either the standard's Graphics Configuration pane or the Theme Guide. Theme-specific values can be configured only for themes that are currently active, but theme-specific values for non-active themes remain in the database as long as their associated standard exist. When you copy or delete a standard, all theme-specific values are copied or deleted with it. Activating themes Themes must be selected as Active to be used in the system. When added manually in Graphics Studio, themes are active by default; when imported, they are non-active by default. Once a theme is active, you can perform the following activities with without publishing: Operation you can perform with an active theme Where Select it as the current theme in Graphics Studio Graphics Studio > Application Preferences selector Configure its theme-specific values Graphics Studio > Theme Guide Assign it to a workstation to be available for theme selection in DeltaV Live online DeltaV Live Administration > Workstation Management dialog > Themes tab When at least one theme is both active and assigned to a workstation, a theme-selection button appears on that workstation's DeltaV Live online toolbar. Users can then click the button and select the theme that most appropriately meets their needs. If a workstation has no active themes assigned to it, that workstation does not have a theme-selection button available in DeltaV Live. When you deactivate a theme, it is removed from the theme-selection list in DeltaV Live once it is published. The related configuration for that theme remains, and thus is easily reversed. Publishing themes Themes must be published when you do any of the following activities: Create or delete a theme Modify a theme's name, title, or description Change the Active status of a theme A new theme, deleted theme, or theme whose Active status has been changed is not added to or removed from the theme-selection list in DeltaV Live online until both the theme and the workstation to which it is assigned are published. Publishing a theme, however, does not publish the theme-specific values associated with it. When you add, modify, or remove a theme-specific value in the Theme Guide, its corresponding standard must be published. Themes are published as a group. When you select a theme or themes to publish, all themes are published. For example, if three themes appear in the Publish dialog and you select the Publish check box for only one of them, all three themes are still published. Managing themes and theme-specific values Theme-specific values are managed through their corresponding standards; therefore, when you import, export, or copy a theme, only its name, title, description, and Active/Inactive status are imported, exported, or copied. When you import, export, copy, or delete a standard, all of its theme-specific values are imported, exported, copied, or deleted with it. Theme-specific values cannot be individually imported or exported. Theme-specific values cannot be individually imported or exported. Deleting themes When you delete a theme in Graphics Studio, that theme is removed from all graphics configurations using that theme. All theme-specific values belonging to the deleted theme are removed from their corresponding standards. (The standards are not deleted.) The deleted theme remains, as an unbound theme, on the theme-selection list for any workstations referencing that theme. You can later replace an unbound theme with another theme having the same name and thereby satisfy the reference. Because the name of the new theme matches the previous theme's name, DeltaV Live workstation configuration does not require any changes. Using themes in DeltaV Live For a theme to appear on a workstation's theme-selection list in DeltaV Live online, the following conditions must be true: The theme is published The theme's corresponding standards are published The theme is active The theme is assigned to the workstation The workstation is published You can designate an initial theme to use when a new instance of DeltaV Live launches. The default theme is used when the following is true: When no DeltaV user is currently logged on When the DeltaV user currently logged on has not previously selected a theme on this workstation When the previously selected theme is no longer available on this workstation Otherwise, when the DeltaV user currently logged on has previously selected a theme and the theme is still available on this workstation, this previously selected theme is used.

title: The phase control and active phase summary screens
main_heading: The phase control and active phase summary screens
body_text: The phase control and active phase summary screens From the Phase Control screen, the operator can focus on a particular phase in a batch and execute it manually. This screen displays the areas, process cells or units, allowing close control of each phase. If the area or process cell is blank, it appears on the display but is grayed out. Phase Control Screen Note: If the unit has an MMI picture defined, the unit is marked with an asterisk on this screen. You can open the picture in DeltaV Operate by clicking the View button. DeltaV Operate (run mode) must have been started first, before Batch Operator Interface is launched. This will not work on a Remote Desktop Services machine. The Batch Operator Interface also includes an Active Phase Summary screen from which the operator can immediately see all active phases. This overview allows operators to quickly identify units and their related phases. Active Phase Summary Screen Related information Controlling phases

title: The physical model
body_text: The physical model The equipment hierarchy used by the DeltaV system is based on the S88 standard physical model. The physical model, illustrated in the following figure, defines a hierarchy consisting of several levels that identifies the equipment within an enterprise. Pieces of equipment are grouped together at a lower level to create a piece of equipment in the next higher level. The S88 Standard Physical Model The objective of this model is to define equipment that: You can group together to perform a specific function Works as independently of each other as possible Performing this task requires you to have clearly understood and defined the purpose for each piece of equipment in your plant. The S88 standard presents the following guidelines to define equipment: Define each piece of equipment to perform a distinct, consistent task regardless of the product. Define each piece of equipment to work independently. Establish a consistent set of rules to prevent confusion. The following subsections describe each level in the physical model and its application in the DeltaV system. Subtopics: Enterprise, site, and area levels Process cell Unit Equipment and control modules

title: The Recipe Studio window panes
body_text: The Recipe Studio window panes The Recipe Studio window is divided into five window panes. These panes are referred to as views: Hierarchy View, Diagram View, Palette View, Parameter View, and Formula View. The Recipe Studio Windows

title: The Soft Phase application
body_text: The Soft Phase application The Soft Phase application is the user-created soft phase executable. The soft phase is created from a template that allows the user to add their code in the same way as code is added to the controller phase class or phase logic module. In DeltaV Explorer, the name of the phase class (from which a soft phase is created) must be the name of the executable soft phase created here. For example, the soft phase FILL_TANKA is created from the phase class FILL. Therefore, the soft phase application must be FILL.EXE, the same name as the phase class. The Soft Phase Broker and Soft Phase Server use the soft phase name to communicate to the soft phase. Hence, when two soft phases are created from the same class and are both active at the same time, there will be two instances of the executable running. Subtopics: Writing soft phases

title: The Soft Phase Broker
body_text: The Soft Phase Broker The Soft Phase Broker creates and monitors soft phases on the workstation and communicates with the Soft Phase Server about those soft phases. When the Soft Phase Server receives a start command it sends a start request to the Soft Phase Broker. The Soft Phase Broker then creates an instance of the soft phase and passes the name of the Soft Phase Server machine to the soft phase. The soft phase then connects to the Soft Phase Server directly and all parameter information is passed between the soft phase and Soft Phase Server. The Soft Phase Broker maintains a list of all active soft phases on the local node. This list is used by the Soft Phase Server when the server is shut down and restarted.

title: The Soft Phase DLL
body_text: The Soft Phase DLL The Soft Phase DLL is responsible for handling all communications with the Soft Phase Server. The Soft Phase DLL implements the same phase state transitions that are used by controller-based phases. The Soft Phase DLL supports soft phases created with either Visual C++ or Visual Basic. Note: It may be necessary to recompile your soft phase with current versions of Visual C++ or Visual Basic compilers to work with updated versions of the Soft Phase DLL. The Soft Phase DLL functions the same for Visual C++ or Visual Basic soft phases, except in one instance. For the Visual C++ soft phase, the DLL suspends the run logic immediately if a Hold, Stop or Abort command is received. The run logic is then resumed following a restart if the Restart Mode is set to continue. In some cases, the run logic may be in the middle of an operation that the user does not want interrupted when the command is received. To prevent this, the user can lock the run thread to prevent it being suspended during these types of operations. For a Visual Basic (version 6 and prior) soft phase, there can only be a single active thread. This means the Soft Phase DLL cannot suspend the run thread and start the hold, stop or abort thread as it would for Visual C++ soft phase. The Soft Phase DLL cannot switch to the other logic until the run thread completes, therefore the user must write their run logic to periodically check the phase state. If the phase state is no longer running then the run logic should terminate allowing the hold, abort or stop logic to run. This is not true for Visual Basic .NET as that is multi-threaded. Related information State transition diagram

title: The Soft Phase Server
body_text: The Soft Phase Server The DeltaV Soft Phase Server controls all communication between the soft phase and the Batch Executive. The Soft Phase Server resides on the Batch Executive machine. The Batch Executive starts the Soft Phase Server if at least one soft phase is configured in the Executive when it starts. When the Batch Executive is shut down, the Soft Phase Server is also shut down. Note: The information associated with the execution of a soft phase is recorded by the Batch Historian. The Soft Phase Server uses the Soft Phase Broker application to create and monitor soft phases on that node.

title: The Soft Phase Tester
body_text: The Soft Phase Tester The Soft Phase Tester is a stand-alone application that tests user-created soft phases without having the Batch Executive and Soft Phase Server running. The Soft Phase Tester is designed to run on a non-DeltaV machine using a soft phase compiled as release mode (not debug mode). Because DeltaV software does not exist on the Soft Phase Tester machine, it does not have an area model and cannot get any recipe information. In order to test soft phases that use download or report parameters, the user must supply these values. However, these configurations can be saved and reused. To run the Soft Phase Tester, you must first install the Soft Phase Environment. To start the Soft Phase Tester, select Start > DeltaV Batch > Soft Phase Tester . Subtopics: Test a soft phase Soft phase test parameters Configure the test parameters Save the configuration Exit the soft phase tester Related information Install the Soft Phase environment

title: The system configuration and defaults screen
main_heading: The system configuration and defaults screen
body_text: The system configuration and defaults screen The System Configuration and Defaults screen is the mechanism for customizing the Batch Operator Interface screens. The screen contains a dialog with 15 labeled tabs. Each of these tabs opens a dialog that allows you to configure the corresponding Batch Operator Interface screen or section of a Batch Operator Interface screen. This is the screen from which the prompts are most readily accessible to the operator, who can then respond to the prompt in the most timely manner possible. Unacknowledged Prompts Screen Related information Acknowledging prompts

title: The AGITATE running logic
body_text: The AGITATE running logic The first step in the SFC for the AGITATE phase running logic includes a number of actions. If we confirmed them all in a single transition statement, it would look like this: ('//#BLENDER_OUT_1#/A_TARGET' = '$outlet_state:Closed' AND '//#COLOR_IN_VLV#/DC1/PV_D' = 'vlvnc-pv:CLOSED' AND '//#BASE_IN_VLV#/DC1/PV_D' = 'vlvnc-pv:CLOSED') To simplify the logic, each action will have a confirm expression. For example, here is the Properties dialog for the first step action, which sets the BLENDER_OUTLET equipment module to a closed state. Note: If you imported the Complete.fhx database, the logic for the AGITATE phase class will not match exactly the figures shown in the next few topics. The phase classes in the database include changes that will be made later in this tutorial to allow us to monitor failure conditions. Before you configure the running logic, you will add the new phase algorithm parameter, AGIT_FLAG, so that you will be able to browse for it when you create the running logic.

title: The Batch Operator Interface
body_text: The Batch Operator Interface The DeltaV Batch system has two main operator interfaces: Batch Operator Interface - used primarily to manage batch recipes DeltaV Operate - used primarily to monitor the process equipment You should already be familiar with DeltaV Operate. In the following topics, you will learn about the Batch Operator Interface and how to use it along with DeltaV Operate to manage the batch production process . The Batch Operator interface provides different views of the batch process through a number of operator displays, which are described in the Batch Reference manual. These displays allow users to perform the following tasks: Create batches from the list of recipes assigned to a Batch Executive Control and monitor recipe-based batches through the use of START, HOLD, RESTART, STOP, and ABORT commands Provide advanced batch control (change the mode of a batch, bind equipment to a recipe, scale a recipe, or run a segment of a recipe ) Acquire and release batch resources and monitor resource arbitration Control and monitor individual phases Respond to prompts for parameter input View event logs of current or past batches Monitor, acknowledge, and clear batch-related alarms The Procedure as PFC display in the Batch Operator Interface allows the operator to view each step of the batch as it progresses. As a recipe executes, each phase transitions according to the state transition diagram. In the simplest case (when there are no failures or operator intervention), a phase goes from Idle to Running to Complete. Using the Batch Operator Interface, an operator can create a batch, start it, watch the progress, interrupt if necessary, and restart or abort the batch. The batch state is displayed on most operator screens because it is important for the operator to be aware of the current state. The commands available for the operator to issue are dependent on the current state . The Batch Executive must be running before you can use the Batch Operator Interface. Subtopics: Using the Batch Operator Interface Adding and starting a batch Related information The Batch Operator Interface screens The DeltaV Batch Executive

title: The CHG_BASE and DRAIN phase classes
main_heading: The CHG_BASE and DRAIN phase classes
body_text: The CHG_BASE and DRAIN phase classes Two additional phase classes (CHG_BASE and DRAIN) were imported as part of the Startup.fhx file. The diagrams for the running logic for these phase classes are included in the following topics. CHG_BASE requires creation of a BASE_HEADER module similar to the COLOR_HEADER module created earlier. When CHG_BASE is assigned to the BLENDER unit class, two aliases, BASE_OUT_FLOW and BASE_OUT_PUMP, are automatically generated. title: The COARSE_VALVE and FINE_VALVE control modules
main_heading: The COARSE_VALVE and FINE_VALVE control modules
body_text: The COARSE_VALVE and FINE_VALVE control modules COARSE_VALVE and FINE_VALVE use the same algorithm. In a real plant application, these control modules are so similar that they could be based on a single control module class. Refer to Module Classes for more information. Because COARSE_VALVE and FINE_VALVE are to be contained in the TOTALIZER equipment module, it is necessary to provide access to key parameters through the use of input parameters. The input parameters are the interface between the equipment module and the contained control modules. In the example, TARGET_STATE is an input parameter wired to SP_D that controls the state of the module. CURRENT_STATE is an output parameter wired to PV_D that monitors the state of the module.

title: The DeltaV Continuous Historian
body_text: The DeltaV Continuous Historian The DeltaV Continuous Historian is a collection of features and applications, well integrated into the DeltaV system, that provide capture of, access to, and management of time-series parameter values from the run-time DeltaV system. The DeltaV Continuous Historian is automatically started by DeltaV services on DeltaV workstations on which the DeltaV Continuous Historian software is installed and its subsystem enabled. On new DeltaV systems, the 250-tag DeltaV Continuous Historian is installed by default on every local DeltaV workstation type. It may be scaled up to 30,250 tags on the Application Station. While running, the DeltaV Continuous Historian supports: Historical data capture and storage as determined by the history collection configuration for that workstation. Any automatic historical data management services that have been configured, such as automatic data discarding, moving to offline storage, and so on. Historical data services, such as (browsing, reading, or writing, for local and remote client applications. Important: When using the DeltaV Continuous Historian in a DeltaV Zones environment, refer to DeltaV Books Online for important considerations regarding system time synchronization in a DeltaV Zones environment. Subtopics: DeltaV Continuous Historian fundamentals Licenses for the DeltaV Continuous Historian DeltaV Reporter Excel Add-in The Continuous Historian Administration application Automated backup utility Legacy Historian data conversion Related information Inter-Zone alarms and events Client application support Historian installation Uninstall a historian

title: The Continuous Historian Administration application
body_text: The Continuous Historian Administration application The Continuous Historian Administration application provides a number of tools to help you manage DeltaV Continuous Historian data captured and available online. When the volume of online data grows too large, decisions need to be made about how to handle it. You can define rules to automatically discard selected data or move selected historical data from online historical data storage to offline data files. You can also interactively choose the historical data to discard or move to offline storage. Additional tools are available to let you temporarily bring online the historical data from offline storage files. You must run the Continuous Historian Administration application on the same workstation where the DeltaV Continuous Historian is installed. To start the Continuous Historian Administration application, click Start > DeltaV Engineering > Continuous Historian Administration . The Primary storage area in the left pane lists active, current, and extended historical data sets in the right pane. The size and time span properties of the Primary storage area, data set size and time span properties, and the automatic actions for data set export are defined on the Continuous Historian Properties dialog in the DeltaV Explorer. The Automatic Exports area in the left pane lists the data sets that have been automatically exported in the right pane. One or more of these data sets can be returned to the Primary storage area as extended data sets using Tools > Create Extended History Data Set(s) . For detailed information about all the tools available in the Continuous Historian Administration application, refer to its online help. Subtopics: Historical data set security Version compatibility of exported and backed up data sets

title: The DeltaV command (serial port interface) for the Smart Switch
main_heading:
The DeltaV command (serial port interface) for the Smart
	 Switch
body_text: The DeltaV command (serial port interface) for the Smart Switch Use the DeltaV command to access advanced configuration for the switch. You must respond to four questions to reach the advanced configuration. Because the switch is already commissioned, you must not make any changes to these settings: Enter DeltaV at the Emerson prompt. The switch responds with: DeltaV: Enter DeltaV IP address for the Switch [Currently nn.nn.nn.nn ]: Enter an IP to continue without changing the IP address. The switch responds with: DeltaV: Enter Name for the Switch [max. 63 chars]: Press Enter to continue. The switch responds with: DeltaV: Enter Location for the Switch [max. 63 chars]: Press Enter to continue. The switch responds with: DeltaV: Disable Network Switch Discovery? (y/n) [Recommended for use with DeltaV v10.x systems] [Default = y]: Press N to enable network switch discovery. If you disable switch discovery you cannot flash switch LEDs from Network Device Command Center (NDCC). The switch responds with: DeltaV: Advanced Configuration? (y/n) To save your changes and continue to advanced configuration, press Y. Any other response saves your changes and returns you to the Emerson prompt. Disconnect the serial cable or continue to the next section.

title: The DeltaV desktop
body_text: The DeltaV desktop The DeltaV system offers dual desktops, the Windows desktop and the DeltaV desktop, to provide both a secure operating environment and open engineering environment. The Windows desktop allows access to DeltaV applications and Windows resources, including other Windows programs that might be on the system. The DeltaV desktop limits the user to the DeltaV Operate or DeltaV Live application and to those applications available to the user through DeltaV Operate or DeltaV Live. Access to the Windows desktop is determined by the current user's privileges, which are based on group membership. A user with Windows administrative, DeltaV administrative, or DeltaV access privileges has access to both the DeltaV desktop and the Windows desktop. A user who is not a member of the Administrators group, the DeltaV Admins Group, or the DeltaV Access group cannot access the Windows desktop. Initial DeltaV configuration defaults to the DeltaV desktop. Users with the proper privileges can switch to the Windows desktop. Unprivileged users are limited to the DeltaV desktop. This default setting can be changed so that all users (regardless of their privileges) go directly to the Windows desktop upon logging on to the system. Note: To secure your operating environment, consider giving operators access only to the DeltaV desktop and other users, such as engineers, access to both the DeltaV desktop and the Windows desktop. Note: Keep the default setting to restrict unauthorized users from accessing the Windows desktop. Related information DeltaV FlexLock

body_text: The DeltaV I/O network The DeltaV I/O Network contains CHARM I/O Cards (CIOC) and CHARMs , Remote I/O Nodes and remote I/O cards and Ethernet I/O Cards (EIOCs) . The I/O Network must be enabled as a DeltaV System Preference before it is available to the DeltaV system. To enable the I/O Network, click Start > DeltaV Engineering > System Preferences . After the I/O Network is enabled, it appears under the Control Network in the DeltaV Explorer. CHARM I/O cards , Remote I/O Nodes, and EIOCs are added to the DeltaV Explorer hierarchy from the I/O Network. CHARMs, which are contained by a CIOC , and remote I/O cards, which are contained by a Remote I/O Node, are then assigned to controllers in the control network. The following image shows a DeltaV Explorer hierarchy with an I/O Network containing a CIOC with assigned CHARMs, a Remote I/O Node and remote I/O card, and EIOCs. The Assigned I/O container holds a CIOC with assigned CHARMs and an assigned Remote I/O Node. body_text: The Recipe Studio application Recipe Studio, the application used to configure recipes, is similar in look and feel to Control Studio, the application used to configure control module and phase class logic diagrams. The steps and transitions in a recipe make up a procedural function chart rather than a sequential function chart. At the operation level, the steps are phases; at the unit procedure level, the steps are operations; and at the procedure level, the steps are unit procedures. title: The sequence for the tank process
main_heading: The sequence for the tank process
body_text: The sequence for the tank process For the tank process, you will create an SFC to control the tank discharge. As a way to start and stop the SFC, you will create an SFC parameter called SP that the operator will be able to change. The SP will be manipulated with a named set called SFCCTRL. A named set defines names and equates them to integer values. For the tank example, you will create the named set with two values: 0 = IDLE and 1 = START. Following is a suggested sequence for the tank discharge application. Step 1: Stop (that is, set the SP to IDLE). Transition: Wait for the user to change the SP to START. Step 2: Put the flow loop in auto mode and set the setpoint to 50 gpm. Transition: Wait for the regulatory valve to be 30% open. Step 3: Open the block valve. Transition: Confirm that the block valve is open. Step 4: Start the pump. Transition: Confirm that the pump has started. First, you will create the named set, SFCCTRL, in DeltaV Explorer. Then you will go to Control Studio to create the module containing the Sequential Function Chart.

title: Three-state motor module templates
body_text: Three-state motor module templates This category includes templates for forward/reversing and fast/slow motors that have two latching discrete outputs or three momentary discrete outputs. There are variations of each type for motors with and without interlock conditions. If you are not familiar with the motor control module templates in the Library, read Two-state motor module templates before proceeding. Quick Config parameters for the Three-State Motors module templates Parameter Description IO_IN_1 An I/O Reference parameter that configures the DST for the Forward or Fast running status from the motor starter. IO_IN_2 An I/O Reference parameter that configures the DST for the Reverse or Slow running status from the motor starter. IO_OUT_1 An I/O Reference parameter that configures the DST for the latching FORWARD or FAST output to the motor starter (or the momentary STOP output when the module has momentary outputs). IO_OUT_2 An I/O Reference parameter that configures the DST for the latching REVERSE or SLOW output to the motor starter (or momentary FORWARD or FAST output when the module has momentary outputs). IO_OUT_3 An I/O Reference parameter that configures the DST for the momentary REVERSE or SLOW output to the motor starter (not applicable when the module has latching outputs). CFM_ACT1_TIME The amount of time in seconds for the motor to confirm that it is running Forward or Fast following a command to the Forward or Fast state. If the motor does not confirm within this time, a fail condition occurs. The default is 5 seconds. CFM_ACT2_TIME The amount of time in seconds for the motor to confirm that it is running Reverse or Slow following a command to the Reverse or Slow state. If the motor does not confirm within this time, a fail condition occurs. The default is 5 seconds. CFM_PASS_TIME The amount of time in seconds for the motor to confirm that it has stopped following a command to Stop. If the motor does not stop within this time, a fail condition occurs. The default is 5 seconds. DEVICE_OPTS Configuration options for the Device Control block. The option that defaults to enabled for modules without interlock conditions is SP Track. The options that default to enabled for modules with interlock conditions are SP Track, Permissive, and Interlock. Passive on Active Timeout is enabled for the modules with latching outputs. Device options that are not enabled as a default, but are applicable to three-state motors, include Trip and Reset Required. RESTART_TIME A Quick Config parameter in the Forward/Reversing motor module templates. When SP_D in the Device Control block is changed from Forward to Reverse or from Reverse to Forward, OUT_D is driven to Stop for this period of time, in seconds. The default is 5 seconds. Related information Two-state motor module templates

title: TIME function
body_text: TIME function Returns the current Local or UTC time as an Epoch time value (the number of seconds since midnight, January 1, 1972). Syntax: 'external reference' := TIME('Named Set:Type'); Where the Named Set is $time_format and the available types are Local and UTC. Note: Assign the output of this value directly to an output parameter to have it update at one second intervals. If you set an OUT value in a Calc block, then wire the output to a parameter, it updates every 64 seconds. Example: '/PARAM2.CV' := time('$time_format:UTC'); The above example defines the current value of PARAM2 as the UTC Epoch time.

title: TIME_TO_STR function
body_text: TIME_TO_STR function Returns the time of day (in ISO 8601 format) based on the specified format and Epoch time (in seconds). Syntax: 'external reference' := TIME_TO_STR("format", Epoch time); The following table explains the available formats. Format Explanation %A Local time in the form YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ss %d Day of month in the form DD %D Date in the form YYYY-MM-DD %h Hour of the day in the form hh %i Minutes past the hour in the form mm %j Day of year (001 - 366) %m Month in the form MM %P Period format as follows: PXXXXXThh:mm:ss %s Seconds past the minute in the form ss %T Time in the form hh:mm:ss %w Day of week (1-7) %W Week of year (01-53) %y Year in the form YYYY Where: P = literal p character indicates this is a time period XXXXX = five-digit number of days (00000 - 99999) T = literal T character indicates beginning of time component YYYY = year MM = month DD = day of month hh = hour mm = minutes ss = seconds Example: (* get the current LOCAL time in ISO-8601 format *) '/CURRENT_TIME' := time('$time_format:Local'); '/TIME_STAMP' := time_to_str("%A", '/CURRENT_TIME'); The above example shows how to get the current time and convert it to an ISO 8061 format for local time. To get the current UTC time as a string, use $time_format:UTC.

title: Tips for using the DeltaV Excel Add-in
main_heading: Tips for using the DeltaV Excel Add-in
body_text: Tips for using the DeltaV Excel Add-in The DeltaV Function Wizard supports the A1 reference style. It does not support the R1C1 reference style. (A1 reference style is the default.) In general, while a workbook is under construction it is a good idea to put Excel into manual calculation mode. While Excel is in manual mode, updates are suspended. Pressing F9 will still allow you to retrieve data in a manual fashion. When the workbook is finished being heavily edited, simply put Excel back into automatic calculation mode to resume DeltaV data updates.

title: Tips for writing expressions
body_text: Tips for writing expressions Here are some tips for writing expressions: Minimize the number of CPU-intensive functions, such as EXPT, LOG2, and **. Minimize the number of CPU-intensive parameter reads and writes by reducing the number of duplicate reads. Use the Named Set command instead of the numerical equivalent to improve readability. The following example shows the original expression and the same expression improved through a reduced number of reads: Original IF OUT1 = 1 AND IN2 = 1 AND 'A_UNIT/B_MODE.CV' = 3 THEN 'A_UNIT/STEP.CV' := 7; ENDIF; IF OUT1 = 1 AND IN2 = 0 AND 'A_UNIT/B_MODE.CV' = 2 THEN 'A_UNIT/STEP.CV' := 5; ENDIF; Improved with Reduced Reads IF OUT1 = 1 THEN IF IN2 = 1 AND 'A_UNIT/B_MODE.CV' = 3 THEN 'A_UNIT/STEP.CV' := 7; ENDIF; IF IN2 = 0 AND 'A_UNIT/B_MODE.CV' = 2 THEN 'A_UNIT/STEP.CV' :=5; ENDIF; ENDIF; The following example shows the original expression and the same expression improved through the use of a temporary variable TEMPMODE: Original IF 'A_UNIT/B_MODE.CV' = 4 THEN 'A_UNIT/STEP.CV' :=9; ENDIF; IF 'A_UNIT/B_MODE.CV' = 5 THEN 'A_UNIT/STEP.CV' := 11; ENDIF; Improved with Temporary Variable TEMPMODE := 'A_UNIT/B_MODE.CV': IF TEMPMODE = 4 THEN 'A_UNIT/STEP.CV' := 9; ENDIF; IF TEMPMODE = 5 THEN 'A_UNIT/STEP.CV' :=11; ENDIF; The following example shows the original expression and a more readable and informative version of the same expression that uses the Named Set Reference: Original IF 'UNIT/B_MODE.CV' = 3 THEN 'A_UNIT/STEP.CV' := 7; ENDIF; Improved with Named Set Reference IF 'A_UNIT/B_MODE.CV' = 'Bch_Mode: Auto' THEN 'A_UNIT/STEP.CV' := 'Step_Cmd: Step7'; ENDIF;

title: The Recipe Studio ribbon and quick access toolbar
main_heading: The Recipe Studio ribbon and quick access toolbar
body_text: The Recipe Studio ribbon and quick access toolbar Recipe Studio uses both menus and toolbars. Each item on a menu and each button on a toolbar is a command that Recipe Studio executes. For example, if you want to save the current recipe (the one you are working on), you can select the File > Save option from the menus, or you can click the button on the toolbar. The same command is given to Recipe Studio, and the same function (saving the recipe) occurs. The menus are fixed in place and cannot be moved. They are always in the same order and always appears across the top of your window. However, the toolbars can be moved around to better suit you and how you use Recipe Studio. For example, you might find that you use the PFC editing toolbar extensively when working with recipes. You can move the toolbar to a convenient spot, such as, across the top of the window or to the Diagram View.

title: Toolbars and the Toolbox - overview
body_text: Toolbars and the Toolbox - overview Toolbars contain buttons that provide shortcuts to menu commands. For example, instead of selecting File > Save , you can click the Save Picture button on the Toolbar. Buttons that perform similar functions are grouped into separate toolbars. For example, the standard toolbar usually contains the Open , Close , Save , and Print buttons. Toolbars are owned by the workspace or by pictures. The owner of a toolbar defines when that toolbar appears. For example, workspace toolbars appear whenever the workspace runs, whereas picture toolbars appear only when one or more pictures are displayed. Note: Picture toolbars are assigned to all pictures. You cannot assign toolbars to specific pictures. Note: You can hide the Toolbox by selecting and right-clicking its title bar, and then selecting Hide . You can move and resize the Toolbox and enable docking. To open the Toolbox after hiding it, click Workspace > Toolbars , and then select Picture in the Owner field. Scroll down, select the DeltaV_Toolbox check box, and then click Close in the Toolbars dialog. Subtopics: Practice using the Toolbars dialog Move and resize the toolbox Practice docking the toolbox
