title: Two-state motor module templates
body_text: Two-state motor module templates This category provides templates with STOP/START motor control capabilities for field devices such as pumps and agitators. Some motors require a single latching discrete output, and others require two outputs, a momentary start, and a latching permit. For each type of motor, there is a template with interlock conditions and one without interlock conditions. Another template is used when the motor has a field HAND/OFF/AUTO (HOA) or LOCAL/REMOTE switch. The motor templates are designed around the Device Control function block. This function block has several named set parameters (SP_D, PV_D, FV_D, DC_STATE, and FAIL) that have default named sets associated with them. In the motor module templates, the default named sets for these parameters have been replaced with appropriate named sets for the application. Therefore, these parameters are not in the Quick Config view and do not need editing. You can, however, edit the named sets or associate different named sets when the text strings that are displayed on the motor faceplate do not fit your particular application. When you edit the named set associated with SP_D, be sure that the state names are 10 characters or shorter. Because the STATE_MASKS parameter in the Device Control function block has been customized for the particular motor module template, it does not need editing. Two-state motor module Quick Config parameters for the Device Control function block Parameter Description IO_IN_1 An I/O Reference parameter that configures the DST for the Stop/Start status from the motor starter. IO_OUT_1 An I/O Reference parameter that configures the DST for the latching output to the motor starter (or the latching permit output if the module has a momentary START output). IO_OUT_2 An I/O Reference parameter that configures the DST for the momentary START output to the motor starter (not applicable when the module has a single latching output). CFM_ACT1_TIME The amount of time in seconds for the motor to confirm that it has started following a command to start. If the motor does not start within this time, a fail condition occurs. The default is 5 seconds. CFM_PASS_TIME The amount of time in seconds for the motor to confirm that it has stopped following a command to Stop. If the motor does not stop within this time, a fail condition occurs. The default is 5 seconds. DEVICE_OPTS Configuration options for the Device Control block. The option that defaults to enabled for modules without interlock conditions is SP Track. The options that default to enabled for modules with interlock conditions are SP Track, Permissive, and Interlock. Passive on Active Timeout is enabled for modules with one latching output. Device options that are not enabled as a default, but are applicable to two-state motors, include Trip and Reset Required. The two-state motor module templates include an alarm parameter, FAIL_ALM. Keep this alarm enabled at all times. The priority of FAIL_ALM, initially Medium, can be changed as necessary. MTR-11_ILOCK and MTR-21_ILOCK include function blocks that configure interlock logic for the motor and perform a first-out trap on the interlock conditions. There are several variations of the Motor and Valve Module detail display (DL_DTx), the difference between them being the number of rows appearing in the Interlocks section of each display. DL_DT0.DET does not have an Interlocks section. DL_DT1.DET through DL_DT8.DET contain a corresponding number of interlock conditions. In the function block diagram for MTR-11_ILOCK interlock conditions are configured using expressions in the Condition function blocks. Write interlock expressions so that the result is True when a shutdown state is required. Typically, interlock conditions should be written in separate Condition function block expressions so that the text description appears on the detail display. It is recommended that you write interlock conditions that are ANDed in a single expression since the logical OR of the Condition block outputs is calculated by the Boolean Fan In (BFI) block. You can access the expression editor by selecting and right-clicking the Condition block in the function block diagram, and then selecting Expression . Each condition block has a DESC parameter to enter the text description for the interlock condition. This text string must be no longer than 20 characters in order to fit on the detail display. Each condition block has a TIME_DURATION parameter that can be configured so the expression must evaluate True for the time period in order to set OUT_D to True. If fewer than eight interlock conditions are used, remove the unused Condition blocks to reduce the load on the controller. Next, open the Module Properties dialog and change the name of the detail display to correspond to the number of interlock conditions used. For example, if you have three interlock conditions, change the detail display name from DL_DT8 to DL_DT3. The motor modules with interlock conditions have a provision for configuring permissive conditions. Generally, conditions that should allow a motor to start (permissive conditions) will shut down the motor in the opposite state. However, there are cases when a condition must be present for a motor to start, but a shutdown (interlock) should not occur when the condition is no longer present. When you have permissive conditions that are not also interlock conditions, add additional logic to the function block diagram. Wire the result of this logic into IN_D1 of the AND1 function block. Next, click Auto Calc Execution Order from the Diagram menu or toolbar icon to insert the new blocks correctly into the execution order. When PERMISSIVE_D of the Device Control (DC1) block is True, a change of SP_D from Stop to Start is allowed. Therefore, permissive conditions should be True to allow the motor to start, and multiple permissive conditions should be ANDed together. Remember that interlock conditions should be True to cause a shutdown of the motor, even though a shutdown occurs when INTERLOCK_D of the Device Control block is False. The logical OR of the interlock conditions is inverted prior to the Device Control block. In summary, permissive conditions should evaluate True for a permit and interlock conditions should evaluate True to shutdown. There are module templates in this category that are intended to be used when the motor can also be started in the field: MTR-11_HOA is a template used when there is a HAND/OFF/AUTO (HOA) or LOCAL/REMOTE switch wired to a DeltaV discrete input card. The module expects a single discrete input channel to be wired, the AUTO input (1=AUTO) or the LOCAL/REMOTE input (1=REMOTE). When the motor is operated in the field, the TRK_IN_D input of the Device Control block is True, causing OUT_D to track FV_D (that is, the DeltaV output tracks the actual state of the motor and confirm failure alarms do not occur). When the field switch selects DeltaV control, the module functions like a module created from MTR-11. MTR-11_HOA has an additional Quick Config parameter in the discrete input function block (DI_AUTO). IO_IN in this block is used to configure the Device Signal Tag for the AUTO or REMOTE input from the field switch. CAUTION: If interlock conditions are added to a module created from this template, they are only effective when the field switch is in the Auto (or Remote) position. The Device Control function block does not drive outputs based on interlock conditions when TRK_IN_D is True. MTR-21 has optional logic included when there are field stop/start pushbuttons. The module expects two discrete inputs wired to DeltaV input channels: one for the stop pushbutton and one for the start pushbutton. The primary benefit of using this logic is to avoid alarms when the motor is operated in the field. If confirm failure alarms are wanted in this case, do not use this template. When the module detects that a stop or start pushbutton has been pressed, SP_D in the device control block is pulsed by an edge trigger and action block so that confirm failure alarms do not occur. If interlocking in the DeltaV system is required, you can copy this logic into a module created from MTR-21_ILOCK. If field stop/start pushbuttons are not wired to the DeltaV system, remove this logic from the module that was created from MTR-21. When the logic is used, there are two additional Quick Config parameters, DI_START/IO_IN and DI_STOP/IO_IN, that configure the Device Signal Tags for the pushbutton inputs. Make sure that the module execution rate is no slower than 500 msec when field stop/start pushbuttons are used. Subtopics: Device-specific two-state motor module templates

title: Two-way valve module templates
body_text: Two-way valve module templates There are two categories of module templates for two-way valve control, one for normally closed valves (fail closed) and one for normally open (fail open) valves. In each category there are variations for valves with one or two limit switches and valves with or without interlock conditions. The valve module templates are similar to the motor module templates. If you are not familiar with the motor module templates in the Library, read Two-state motor module templates before proceeding. A normally closed valve is closed in the passive state. An interlock condition causes the valve to close. A normally opened valve is open in the passive state, and an interlock condition causes it to open. The two-way valve modules have one or two discrete inputs, depending on the number of limit switches. There is a single latching discrete output to drive the valve open or closed. The STATE_MASKS parameter of the Device Control block is a Quick Config parameter in the valve module templates, which enables the inputs and output to be inverted when necessary. For valves with interlocks, you can optionally configure the valve to automatically return to the active state when the interlock conditions clear. For example, a normally closed valve would be driven closed on an interlock, but could be configured to open when the interlock clears if the previously commanded state was Open. This is done by disabling the SP Track option in DEVICE_OPTS of the Device Control block. Quick Config parameters for the Two-Way Valve module templates Parameter Description IO_IN_1 An I/O Reference parameter that configures the DST for the Open/Close status (1=CLOSED, normally closed valve with one limit switch), Open/Close status (1=OPEN, normally open valve with one limit switch), Close status (1=CLOSED, normally closed valve with two limit switches). IO_IN_2 An I/O Reference parameter that configures the DST for the Open status of the valve (1=OPEN) (two limit switches) (not a Quick Config parameter for valve modules with one limit switch) IO_OUT_1 An I/O Reference parameter that configures the DST for the latching output to the valve (1=OPEN for normally closed valves, 1=CLOSE for normally open valves). CFM_ACT1_TIME The amount of time in seconds for the valve to confirm that it is in the active state (Open for a normally closed valve, Closed for a normally open valve) following a command to that state. If the valve does not confirm within this time, a fail condition occurs. The default is 15 seconds. CFM_PASS_TIME The amount of time in seconds for the valve to confirm that it is in the passive state (Closed for a normally closed valve, Open for a normally open valve) following a command to that state. If the valve does not confirm within this time, a fail condition occurs. The default is 15 seconds. CRACK_TIME The amount of time in seconds for the valve to begin movement to a new state following a command to the new state. The crack time should be less than the confirm times so that a fail condition can occur more quickly when a valve with a long travel time has not cleared the old confirm. The default is 5 seconds. DEVICE_OPTS Configuration options for the Device Control block. The option that defaults to enabled for modules without interlock conditions is SP Track. The options that default to enabled for modules with interlock conditions are SP Track, Permissive, and Interlock. Note: When you want the valve to return to the previously commanded active state when an interlock condition clears, clear the SP Track check box. Reset required is a device option that is not enabled as a default, but is applicable to two-way valves. STATE_MASKS A Quick Config parameter that enables the output to the valve (or feedback from the valve) to be inverted when necessary. Related information Two-state motor module templates

title: Types of field devices
body_text: Types of field devices Be sure to verify that the field devices you intend to connect to the segment are supported by the DeltaV system and account for increased power if they draw more than the assumed 20 mA from the bus.

title: Types of recipes
body_text: Types of recipes S88.01 defines four main types of recipes for process control. They are as follows: General Site Master Control The DeltaV batch applications work with Master recipes and Control recipes only. Subtopics: General recipe Site recipe Master recipe Control recipe

title: Types of Smart Firewall users
body_text: Types of Smart Firewall users There are three types of Smart Firewall users: An Administrator user can set up and configure the firewall, enable traffic protection, and edit all user accounts. An Administrator user can change their first name, last name, and password. In addition, an Administrator user can change the default administrator password, edit all existing user accounts, and create new accounts. When the Administrator user logs in to the web UI for the first time, he should change the default administrator password. It is not possible to change the username or privileges of the default administrator account. If you forget all administrator passwords, including the default administrator password, you can make a serial connection to the firewall to reset the default administrator password. An Engineer user can configure traffic protection and view the same information as a view only user. An Engineer user can change their first name, last name, and password. A View only user can view information about the firewall hardware, the firewall configuration, the firewall firmware, and the enabled traffic protection. A View only user is not able to change any of this information. A View only user can change their first name, last name, and password.

title: Type of data stored
body_text: Type of data stored A database includes everything you can see from the DeltaV Explorer. This includes: the library of control modules and function blocks included with the system the modules you create the workstations and controllers (I/O) in the system (Although they can all be viewed in Explorer, they might not all be physically connected to the network.) system-wide configuration data, such as named sets and alarm preferences

title: Typical Redundant Batch subsystem configuration
body_text: Typical Redundant Batch subsystem configuration Physically, the Application Stations are connected through the ACN (either as a simplex or redundant network) for normal ACN traffic. An additional, direct connection can be established between Application Stations in a redundant subsystem pair by using another network interface card in both Application Stations. This direct connection, or Direct Link, provides an optimized pathway for the synchronization data to use. Redundant Batch Subsystem Workstations in a Typical Configuration Because the Direct Link connection is not physically redundant, the Batch Redundancy Server will redirect the synchronization data traffic to the ACN in the case of a Direct Link failure (or if Direct Link is not configured). The synchronization components in the Batch Redundancy Server are responsible for low-level communications (related to synchronization activities) between the workstations. The Direct Link connection is reflected on the Advanced tab of the Node Properties dialog. The Direct Link's address is formatted the same as the ACN IP address format, resulting in a 10.12.x.x address on the primary (preferred active) workstation and a 10.13.x.x address on the secondary (preferred standby) workstation. During the workstation configuration of the Application Stations in the redundant subsystem pair, the DeltaV system appends the characters _S, by default, to the name of the second Application Station of the pair. Therefore, the pair will be named <nodename> and <nodename_S>. When connecting to or configuring a default connection to the Batch Executive or Campaign Manager (for example, DeltaV Operate Batch Controls, Batch OI Configuration Tool, Campaign Manager Operator Interface, and so on), use the primary Application Station name <nodename>. In Redundant Batch, the first computer in the pair that boots up becomes the active Batch Executive. Therefore, be sure to boot up the primary (preferred active) computer first if you want the designated preferred active to become the active node first. The second machine booted up becomes the standby Batch Executive. Important: There is a condition where both machines run as the Active Batch Executive. While rare, this can occur when communication between the preferred active and the rest of the DeltaV network is disrupted, and the pair is connected to the Plant LAN. When communication between the preferred active and the rest of the DeltaV network is restored, the machine designated as the preferred active becomes the active node and the preferred standby computer (named with the _S) reboots (regardless of the option, Unattended reboot on switchover) and resumes in the standby role. During the time of the 'dual' active Batch Executives, batches on the preferred standby may have started. Any new batch data on the preferred standby will not be updated on the preferred active when the preferred active resumes communications with the DeltaV network. Always running the Batch Executive on the preferred active will negate any discrepancies in the Batch List caused by this dual active condition. Subtopics: Creating new Application Stations for Redundant Batch Adding a new partner Application Station for Redundant Batch Reconfiguring Application Stations for Redundant Batch Demoting an existing Redundant Batch pair to simplex batch

title: Typical redundant DeltaV OPC Data Access Server configuration
main_heading: Typical redundant DeltaV OPC Data Access Server configuration
body_text: Typical redundant DeltaV OPC Data Access Server configuration In the following illustration, an OPC Data Access client is running on a remote workstation. The remote workstation can be either a DeltaV workstation (such as another Application Station) or a non-DeltaV workstation. The client is connected to ROPC. nodename .1, the name of the local proxy server for the active DeltaV OPC Data Access Server on the Application Station named nodename. Redundant DeltaV OPC Data Access Server in a typical configuration During the workstation configuration of an Application Station pair with redundant DeltaV OPC Data Access Server enabled, the DeltaV system appends the characters _S, by default, to the name of the second Application Station of the pair. In this example, therefore, the physical name of the partner Application Station (on the right) would be nodename _S and its DeltaV OPC Data Access Server would become active following a switchover. Important: Technically, the DeltaV OPC Data Access Server on both nodename and nodename_S is named OPC.DeltaV.1. However, to connect an OPC client redundantly, it must always refer to the name of the local proxy server for the redundant DeltaV OPC Data Access Server on the remote workstation, ROPC. nodename .1. Related information Connecting to the redundant DeltaV OPC Data Access Server

title: Understanding active step changes
body_text: Understanding active step changes Operators can perform active step changes to alter the sequence of the steps in a batch. Typically, an active step change is performed to return a batch to a specific step due to a problem in the execution of that particular step. For example, the problem could be an equipment malfunction, or to add a missing ingredient in the batch. In either case, once the problem is corrected, the operator can then rerun the batch at the point of the problematic step by using active step change. The logged in user must have the Batch_Active_Step_Change key to execute an Active Step Change. Important: To perform an active step change the following must be true: The step you are performing the active step change from must be in a terminal state; that is, Complete, Stopped, Aborted, Stopped_NC, or Aborted_NC. The parent steps of the one you are changing from must be in one of the following states: Held, Running or Ready The active step change cannot be performed if the batch or the parent step is in a terminal state (Complete, Stopped, Aborted). However, the operator can reset the batch into an active state if the batch is in a terminal state. If the active step change fails, the state is listed as ASC_Failed. The operator can enter the ASC mode again and either cancel or retry the active step change. Subtopics: Performing an active step change

title: Understanding advanced control capabilities
body_text: Understanding advanced control capabilities While adding a batch, more complex recipes might require the operator to supply additional batch information, such as: Scaling a recipe - The operator provides a value that indicates what percentage of a batch to produce. Entering formula values - The operator enters a value to complete a recipe formula, which is used to override the default value of a phase parameter. The Batch Operator Interface provides the operator with an environment to perform more advanced batch control tasks, such as: Arbitrating equipment - While controlling batches from the Batch Operator Interface, the operator can arbitrate equipment. This allows operators to make decisions and prioritize batches based on the current availability of equipment and ingredients. This information is displayed on the Arbitration screen, through which operators can manually arbitrate resources. Running a segment of a recipe - When controlling a recipe from the Batch Operator Interface, the operator has the option of running an entire recipe procedure, a unit procedure, or even an individual phase. For example, a typical operation that can be run from the Batch Operator Interface is a 'clean in place' operation. This operation is frequently run between batches to clean a piece of equipment, particularly if the next batch to run is a different product or if ingredients used in the first batch are potentially corrosive or dangerous. As another example, a facility defines a phase as ADD_WATER. During the course of producing a batch of cookies, the operator determines additional water is needed. The operator can then run the ADD_WATER phase manually from the Phase Control screen to add water to the batch. After the batch completes, the operator determines whether the mixer used to produce the cookies needs to be soaked before a clean in place operation is initiated. Again, the ADD_WATER phase is run to add water to the mixer. Binding equipment to a step - Recipes built referencing a unit class must have equipment bound to them when the unbound steps activate. Changing the mode of a batch - Related information Scaling batches Recipe Studio Arbitrating equipment Binding equipment Understanding batch modes

title: Understanding batch commands
body_text: Understanding batch commands To control a batch, operators issue batch commands from the Batch Operator Interface screens. These commands include: Start Hold Restart Abort Stop Batch commands apply to the currently selected batch. Operators must assume the responsibility for confirming which batch they are issuing commands to by examining the batch display in the lower-right corner of the Batch Operator Interface screens. Batch commands can be issued from the Batch List screen, the Procedure as PFC screen, or the Procedure as Table screen. For detailed information about the screens and their command buttons, refer to the Batch Operator Interface online help system. The batch only responds to the batch commands that are valid for the batch's current state. For example, an aborted batch will not accept a command to restart. Related information Understanding batch states Starting and controlling batches

title: Understanding batch modes
body_text: Understanding batch modes A batch mode is a state associated with each step of a batch, with rules that apply up and down the recipe hierarchy. Active steps of a recipe are in one of three modes: MANUAL O-AUTO (operator automatic) P-AUTO (program automatic) However, the DeltaV system lets operators control the mode of steps at each level with only two command buttons: Manual Auto The following paragraphs give the characteristics of each mode and the way to arrive at each mode: MANUAL - Placing a step in MANUAL mode puts the selected step and each level of the recipe hierarchy above the selected step in MANUAL mode. Subordinate steps are placed in O-AUTO mode. No command buttons are enabled for a step in MANUAL mode. However, the step must be in MANUAL mode to perform an active step change to the subordinate steps. O-AUTO - The steps subordinate to a step in MANUAL mode are placed in O-AUTO (operator automatic) mode. Command buttons are active for steps in O-AUTO mode, unless the step has reached a terminal state. All steps subordinate to a step in O-AUTO mode are in P-AUTO mode. P-AUTO - Steps in P-AUTO (program automatic) mode are under program control and cannot be modified directly by the operator. Command buttons are not enabled. The top level of a recipe is never in P-AUTO mode. You can consider the batch mode as the mode of the top level of the batch. If the mode is not automatic (that is, O-AUTO or P-AUTO), the batch will not complete automatically. Note, however, that even though the top level is running manually, subordinate parts of the batch may be running automatically. All automatic action is stopped only if all active operations are selected and set to MANUAL. Related information Understanding active step changes Controlling batch modes

title: Understanding batch states
body_text: Understanding batch states As a batch executes, it transitions through various states. The batch state is displayed in several locations within the Batch Operator Interface; every window has either a field or a column where the state information is visible. It is important that the operator always knows the current state of the batch, because the commands available for the operator to issue to the batch are dependent on the batch's current state. When a batch is forced to shut down (from the Administer Batches tab on the Advanced dialog for the Batch Application Manager), it goes to the Lost state. From the Lost state, the batch can be restarted using either a Warm or Cold restart. Subtopics: Understanding batch commands Adding a batch Run commands Interrupt commands Removing a batch Related information Restarting individual batches Forced shutdown of individual batches Appendix B - batch commands and states Starting and controlling batches

title: Understanding equipment configuration
body_text: Understanding equipment configuration The batch equipment is configured using DeltaV Explorer following the same physical and logical structure as found in your P&ID. You create the areas or process cells, units and phases in DeltaV Explorer for use in your control strategy. The equipment-based components are as follows: Areas Process cells Equipment trains Unit modules or units Logic strategies, either unit phases, phase logic modules or external phases for DeltaV Batch Control modules Equipment modules All configuration of the physical equipment and logical groupings of the equipment is defined using the DeltaV Explorer application. Subtopics: Class-based equipment Equipment train classes Process cell classes Areas Unit classes Phase classes Unit phase alarms Implementing external phases Related information Batch control strategy

title: Understanding how a procedural function chart executes
main_heading: Understanding how a procedural function chart executes
body_text: Understanding how a procedural function chart executes Before you create PFCs, it is important to understand how the DeltaV Batch subsystem executes them during production. Because recipes are structured according to the procedural hierarchy, different parts of a recipe can be active at the same time. For example, in the procedure MAKE_PAINT, when the step ADDITIVE runs, it starts the unit procedure ADDITIVE. As a result, the MAKE_PAINT procedure and the ADDITIVE unit procedure are active at the same time. Executing Procedural Function Charts Evaluating parallel recipe transitions However, if parallel recipe transitions become TRUE in the same scan, they are evaluated in ascending alphabetic or numeric order and numeric before alphabetic (that is, A before Z, 1 before 9, and 1 before A). This is different than parallel SFC or phase class transitions which, when parallel transitions that become TRUE in the same scan, are evaluated from left to right regardless of the transition names. Subtopics: Procedural function chart execution flow Or sequence selection and sequence loop execution flow

title: Understanding named sets
body_text: Understanding named sets A named set is a mutually exclusive process variable (string), either user or system defined, that is assigned an ordinal (numeric) value and can be selected from a list. These named set strings become easily understandable choices (displayed in list format) for recipe authors and operators to use when setting values for phase parameters (input, report types, phase algorithm), Boolean operator messages, and phase logic failure messages. The named set string corresponds to the ordinal value that is used by the phase logic in the controller. Typically, you use named sets when the recipe author or operator needs to specify an ingredient type. The operator or recipe author does not need to specify the numeric value required by the phase logic. They only need to select the appropriate ingredient name from the named set list. Example Named Set for Ingredient Types RED DYE 0 BLUE DYE 1 WHITE DYE 2

title: Understanding recipe parameters
body_text: Understanding recipe parameters Recipe parameters are parameters set at the recipe level. That is, they are not specific to a step in the recipe. You can use recipe parameters to defer or refer the value of a step parameter. For example, the phase input parameter, which becomes a step parameter in an operation, can obtain its value from the operation's recipe parameter (that is, the phase input parameter's value is deferred to the operation's recipe parameter). Additionally, a phase report parameter which becomes a step parameter in an operation can pass its value (refer it) to the operation's recipe parameter. This allows you to create formulas for the recipe, set the value during production (which allows you to override a step parameter value and create less specific and more generic recipes), defer the recipe parameter as a step parameter to the next higher recipe level, use parameter values from a lower recipe level in a higher level (useful in unit selection policies). Changes to batch input parameter values made in Control Studio online mode are never uploaded to the Batch Executive. Therefore, these values will be overwritten the next time the phase requests a download of parameter values from the Batch Executive (for example, by phase request code 1000 or 12xx). Changes to batch input parameters (deferred or otherwise) might not be immediately reflected in the online values of their corresponding phase parameters. These values are downloaded to the phase only after the download requests previously mentioned occur. Changes to batch report parameter values are only updated in the batch clients after the phase requests an upload to the Batch Executive (that is, when the phase request code 2000/22xx is issued). Note: Only step parameters of the category Input can be deferred to a recipe parameter. Only step parameters of the category Report can be referred to a recipe parameter. Subtopics: Working with deferred recipe parameters

title: Understanding recipes
body_text: Understanding recipes A recipe is, according to the S88.01 standards, a set of information that uniquely identifies the ingredients, the quantities of ingredients, and the production equipment required to manufacture a product. A recipe defines a sequence of control functions that are started and stopped in a specific order, the variables, and the equipment used to produce a batch. Recipes enable a batch plant to use the same process equipment to produce many different products or product formulations. A recipe is the information that identifies the following manufacturing requirements of a specific product: The necessary ingredients The quantities of each ingredient The production equipment (such as mixers, holding tanks, and ovens) needed to make the product The order in which tasks are performed Subtopics: Types of recipes The recipe hierarchy Recipe strategies Recipe authorization

title: Uninstall a historian
body_text: Uninstall a historian If one of the following scenarios occurs, you may need to uninstall a historian and, in some cases, you may also need to uninstall DeltaV: You need to reinstall the historian on a workstation You decide to run a different historian on a workstation You elect to use the workstation without a historian installed Uninstall the DeltaV Continuous Historian, the Advanced Continuous Historian, or PI Server from an Application Station There is no procedure required to uninstall the DeltaV Continuous Historian from an Application Station. However, if you decide to run the Advanced Continuous Historian or PI Server on the Application Station instead of the DeltaV Continuous Historian, you must uninstall and reinstall DeltaV. If you need to uninstall the Advanced Continuous Historian from an Application Station, refer to the Uninstall the Advanced Continuous Historian topic for step-by-step instructions. After uninstalling the Advanced Continuous Historian, you must also uninstall DeltaV. To uninstall PI Server from an Application Station, refer to the documentation from OSIsoft. After uninstalling PI Server, you must also uninstall DeltaV. Uninstall the DeltaV Continuous Historian from a Professional PLUS workstation or Operator Station There is no procedure required to uninstall the DeltaV Continuous Historian from a Professional PLUS workstation or Operator Station. Uninstall PI Server from a non-DeltaV workstation To uninstall PI Server from a non-DeltaV workstation, refer to the documentation from OSIsoft. Related information Historian installation The Continuous Historian subsystem Uninstall the Advanced Continuous Historian

title: Unintentional disconnects
body_text: Unintentional disconnects If you lose your remote connection while working with DeltaV or Windows software, what happens depends on settings made in a number of places: Server Manager Remote Desktop Session Host Configuration FlexLock DeltaV Autologon feature Depending on the use and settings of these items, if you lose connection anything may happen from being disconnected from your windows session after a timeout to having your Windows and DeltaV sessions re-established when the connection recovers within a time limit. Related information Limiting time for idle, active, or disconnected sessions Recommended maintenance practices

title: Unit
body_text: Unit A unit is a major piece of equipment in a process cell that performs a specific task. It consists of all the equipment and control modules that are needed to perform this task. In the DeltaV system, you define a unit class to set properties that are inherited by all unit instances. A DeltaV unit instance is termed a unit module. Unit modules contain the equipment-specific settings for the unit. When defining the units in your facility, use the following guidelines: A unit should perform one or more major processing tasks. Units should function independently of each other. The unit should be used on only one batch at a time. The following figure demonstrates the unit module for a mixer (in this case, named MIX1). MIX1 is one of three units in the MIXER unit class. Note that the unit consists of several smaller pieces of equipment (equipment modules and control modules).

title: Unit classes
body_text: Unit classes Unit classes are the logical groupings of like equipment. They define common properties of the like equipment, regardless of individual manufacturers (MIXERS, REACTORS, STORAGE TANKS). Using unit classes facilitates the creation of units. Each unit is an instance of one class and inherits the common properties of that class. Individual differences (for example, manufacturer specifications) can be defined at the unit level. An Example of a DeltaV Unit Class Unit classes have the following properties: Unit parameter definitions Phase class associations Alias names Unit modules (that is, the instantiation of the unit class) Unit class definitions are located in the DeltaV system library under the Advanced Definitions category. The names are system wide and are shared with other tagged objects. Therefore, the names must be unique through the system. The following also apply to unit classes: Unit modules are created based on a unit class. Phase classes are associated with a unit class. Control modules are contained by a unit class. Equipment modules are contained by a unit class. A unit module can use the phase algorithm defined by the phase classes that are associated with the module's unit class. Subtopics: Unit parameter definition Fremem parameter Unit parameter names Alias names Unit modules Units

title: Unit module displays
body_text: Unit module displays Note: The recommended display for phase algorithm is the Manual Phase Control screen in the Batch Operator Interface or the Phase Control objects in DeltaV Operate. Using unit module and phase displays as a method of controlling phases is used only in situations where the Batch Executive or other phase control interfaces (the Batch Operator Interface or the Phase Control objects for DeltaV Operate) are not operational or available. The unit module has two displays for use in DeltaV Operate: the faceplate display and the detail display. There is also a unit module dynamo for use in DeltaV Operate. Subtopics: Unit module faceplate display Unit module detail display (UM_DT) Unit module dynamo (Unit_Faceplate)

title: Unit parameter definition
body_text: Unit parameter definition The unit parameter definition contains the name of a class of unit-level parameters for Batch Executive. The unit parameter definition also defines the type of parameter (for example, integer, Boolean, floating point, named set, or parameter reference) that is created in all unit modules based on the unit class. The unit parameters are constants or variables available to all phase algorithm definitions. These unit parameters can be used to define minor differences between units that share the same unit class. For example, a unit parameter can be an integer that defines maximum tank capacity; a Boolean that defines whether or not a secondary agitator is present, or a tag that reads a value of a control module, and so on. The unit parameters are also used to send requests between phases running on the same unit. The names of the unit parameters are not system wide. They are restricted to the parent unit class. The names are shared with the names of the other parameters in the unit modules that are based on the same unit class. Therefore, the name must be unique within this scope. In most cases, the configured initial (downloaded) value for unit parameters is distinct for each unit in a unit class. Therefore, configuring the value at the class level (unit parameter definition) is not recommended. One exception is the use an external reference parameter. When aliasing is used, configuring the external reference parameter to use an alias name is recommended. This technique allows the unit to look up the alias name in the alias resolution table and use that value for the parameter. It is possible to configure default values (appropriate to parameter type) for unit parameters. Configuring with default values allows for class-based configuration of external reference parameters, which permits other parameter types to be configured with safe values by default. However, specifying the default value does not prevent that value from being changed once the parameter is derived from a unit class. Furthermore, if the default value for a unit parameter definition is changed, it does not change the configured values of unit parameters already created.

title: Unit phase alarms
body_text: Unit phase alarms Unit phase alarms can be used to trigger Batch Executive alarms and send a recipe to HOLD. This is accomplished by adding an expression to the Failure_Monitor logic that sets the FAIL_INDEX parameter based on the state of the unit phase alarm.

title: Units
body_text: Units A unit is an instance of a unit class and defines the properties for individual pieces of equipment, taking into consideration the specific characteristics of the equipment such as, manufacturer specifications, plant area, process cell, and so forth. A unit can contain more than one piece of equipment, for example a tank and a value, provided those pieces work together as one unit. Units are created when your batch logic strategy uses phase logic modules. Each unit is an instance of one and only one unit class. Create units in the DeltaV Explorer application. Units are created under process cells in the Explorer hierarchy

title: Unit supervision
body_text: Unit supervision Unit supervision ties the recipe to equipment control. The main control functions performed as part of unit supervision include: Acquiring the required units and execute operations. Managing unit resources for both the acquired unit and services provided by other units. Collecting batch and unit information, including status changes and derived values, for process information management. The DeltaV system uses the equipment requirements defined in the recipe procedure to list the units on which the batch can execute. Prior to starting a batch, the operator binds equipment to the batch by selecting the specific units to use. During batch execution, the DeltaV system allocates the selected units to the batch. The unit operations, defined in the recipe procedure, are run on the allocated units.

title: Unit aliasing
body_text: Unit aliasing You can configure a unit alias for a step in a procedure. Because our example in this tutorial is a simple recipe, we will not be using unit aliasing. However, if we were going to create a recipe that required multiple colors to be charged to one blender, unit aliasing would be useful so that we wouldn't need a separate unit procedure for the charging of color from each each color tank. Instead, unit aliases lets us have one unit procedure that charges color with the unit alias determining the tank unit class to be used. Related information Using unit aliases in recipes

title: Unit classes and unit modules
body_text: Unit classes and unit modules A group of units that share common properties are said to belong to the same unit class . Unit class categories help you to further organize your unit classes. We will create two categories of unit classes, Tanks for the ingredient tanks (both base and color) and Blenders for the blenders. Subtopics: Create unit class categories and unit classes Unit class properties Creating unit parameters Creating alias names in the unit classes Add module classes to unit classes Ownership type for module blocks Variant module substitution Creating unit modules Specifying unit parameter values Bind aliases to the unit parameter Finish the unit modules

title: Unit class properties
body_text: Unit class properties When you create a unit class, you can specify properties for the class. Open the Unit Properties dialog for the COLOR unit class by right-clicking COLOR and selecting Properties from the context menu. On the General page of the Unit Properties dialog, there is a field for entering a description of the unit class and marking it as Work in progress. There are also fields for creating searchable information (types and subtypes), which can be useful when exporting unit modules to a user-defined format. On the Displays page, you can associate unit modules created from this class with a picture file (such as Process.grf). Default displays are defined for unit module detail and faceplate displays. On the Execution page, you can define how frequently the unit module is scanned. Don't make any changes on these dialogs at this time. Click Cancel to close the dialog.

title: Unsuccessful backups
body_text: Unsuccessful backups If the DeltaV Continuous Historian database is unavailable due to access by another applications and does not become available again during the retry period, an error will be logged stating that the retry period was exceeded. The error message is available for viewing in the Windows Event Viewer or the backup log file, if this option was selected. The applications that may lock the DeltaV Continuous Historian database are: The Continuous Historian Administration application, when the Backup , Restore , Export , Create Extended , or Delete options are running The Continuous Historian Server, while performing an Automatic Export or Delete operation If the operation completes with the retry period, the backup will start and complete normally.

title: Download status
body_text: Download status Before downloading a node or subcomponent of a node with a blue triangle ( ) or a blue triangle with a question mark ( ) status indicator beside it, you can review detailed download status information by opening the Pending Download Changes dialog. To open the Pending Download Changes dialog, right-click a node or subcomponent of a node, and then select Download Status > Show Details . If there is a blue triangle ( ) or a blue triangle with a question mark ( ) status indicator beside a node or subcomponent of a node, you can update its download status before downloading by right-clicking the item, and then selecting Download Status > Update . To update the download status of a node or subcomponent of a node and also open the Pending Download Changes dialog, right-click the item, and then select Download Status > Show Details . The Pending Download Changes dialog lists the following detailed download status information: The selected node or subcomponent of a node If a node is selected, any subsystem of the selected node that needs to be downloaded A list of all modified download scripts contributing to the pending download of a selected item The reason that a download is needed: Add, Delete, or Modify Note: All download status information is updated before the Pending Download Changes dialog opens. In the Pending Download Changes dialog, you can copy detailed information about download status to the Clipboard, and then save it as tab-delimited text or as XML-encoded data. Subtopics: Pending Download Changes dialog Download contributors

title: Updating Remote Zone Areas
body_text: Updating Remote Zone Areas If you re-run the auto-sense remote zone areas feature, its response depends on changes made to your Local Shared Areas and Remote Zone Areas configuration. This section outlines the possible changes, their effect on the auto-sense remote zone areas feature, and what actions are required for each type of change. The following table summarizes the actions that may occur in response to an auto-sense request and lists possible reasons for the actions. Action Reason No action. All shared local areas in the remote zone are already in this zone's Remote Shared Areas folder. Remote Zone Area created. A shared local area in the remote zone has not previously been sensed. Remote Zone Area created with a different name. A shared local area in the remote zone has not previously been sensed, but its name conflicts with existing local area or remote shared area. Remote Zone Area name updated. Name of the remote shared area has been changed to match new name of shared local area in remote zone. Popup appears: Remote Zone Area area_name no longer exists as a Local Shared Area. Delete existing area_name and re-scan. An area has been deleted from the Shared Local Areas folder in the remote zone. Popup appears: Conflict with existing Remote Zone Area area_name . Delete existing area_name and Auto-Sense Remote Zone Areas again. Auto-sense cannot identify the shared local area in the remote zone that area_name is mapped to.

title: SLS 1508 Logic Solver and SISNet repeater upgrades
main_heading:
SLS 1508 Logic Solver 
	 and SISNet repeater 
	 upgrades
body_text: SLS 1508 Logic Solver and SISNet repeater upgrades You can upgrade the Logic Solver and SISNet Repeaters using the Controller and I/O Upgrade Utility. Be sure that the Logic Solver is decommissioned and the controller with which it is communicating is commissioned before starting the upgrade process. The controller must be commissioned, not necessarily configured/downloaded before starting the upgrade. If you are upgrading a redundant Logic Solver, be sure to upgrade both cards in the redundant pair to the same revision. Note: Upgrading a single Logic Solver can take between five and ten minutes. Tip: SISNet Repeaters appear in slots 65 and 66 on the screen that lists the available SIS components to upgrade. Scroll the list to find SISNet Repeaters.

title: Uploading recorded parameter changes
body_text: Uploading recorded parameter changes You can change the parameter values in a module online (in a running controller) either through Control Studio or through DeltaV Operate or DeltaV Live. As soon as you make one change to a module online, the database module and the online module no longer match. You could examine the CHANGE records in Event Chronicle to find the changes that have been made, but there is an easier way to assess the online changes that have been made. The configuration host workstation in your system monitors all recorded parameter changes (anything that would appear in any of the Event Chronicle databases in your system) and stores them in a temporary file. The Upload command opens the Upload dialog. This dialog lists recorded parameter changes. All columns can be sorted. The Lock column head enables you to filter the parameters by associated lock. If you are uploading multiple modules, the dialog appears as shown. If you are uploading a single module, the dialog title includes the module name and the Node Name and Modules columns do not appear. The most recent value set for each parameter (and field) and the user who made the change appears in the list. If two or more changes were made to the same parameter and field within 250 milliseconds, the Same Time column includes a question mark (?). The dialog includes the following buttons: OK -- Click this button to upload any selected parameter changes before downloading and remove the temporary file containing parameter change information. Cancel -- Click this button to close this dialog without uploading any parameter changes whether they are selected or not. The temporary file containing parameter changes is retained so subsequent download attempts open an Upload dialog that contains previous changes. Get Online Value -- Click this button to retrieve the current parameter values from the node to which the selected parameters are assigned (this operation supports multi-select). The system displays the read values in the Online Value column of the dialog. This operation supports multi-select. The Online Value will be uploaded in the database if successfully retrieved. Save to XML -- Click this button to generate an XML report that contains the information from the currently displayed dialog. The software displays the Save Parameters to XML dialog. If items were selected in the Upload dialog, you can choose to save only the selected items by clicking Save Selected at the bottom of the Save Parameters to XML dialog. The present controller configuration, operating parameters, and I/O are not necessarily included in the upload process. Any parameter changes made by the control algorithms in the controller, as is done in SFC processing, are not included in the upload. You select which parameter values you want to write to the database modules. The Upload command is available in the DeltaV Explorer and in Control Studio. Note: Upload before download does not capture the present configuration and operating parameters in the controller. By default, only manual operator changes from the workstations are recorded. Any settings automatically performed by the controller are not included in the upload. Use the Get Online Value button to retrieve the current value of parameters online. Use with caution, major process interruption could result from using the upload feature if the specific implementation of the users' configuration is not taken into account. When an upload operation is interrupted before it completes, the values that it uploads before the interruption are retained by the database. CAUTION: Select only the parameter changes that represent desired configuration changes to the module in the database. Normally, changes to operating parameters (setpoints or operating state parameters that are initialized or written by the module and many phase logic module parameters as well) would not be selected for upload. CAUTION: When you request an upload, make sure you select all of the values you want. Parameter changes that are not selected are discarded, and not uploaded to the database. Note: For remote workstations, downloading (total download) the RDS (Remote Data Server) Application Station sends the configuration, setup data, displays, and charts to all the remote workstations (1st and 2nd hop) under that RDS.

title: Uploading DeltaV Operate files when enabling Version Control
main_heading: Uploading DeltaV Operate files when enabling Version Control
body_text: Uploading DeltaV Operate files when enabling Version Control You are prompted to upload files in the following circumstance: when you enable Version Control for Displays and there are multiple DeltaV workstations containing operator graphics and the graphics on the non-ProfessionalPLUS workstations are more recent than the ones existing on the ProfessionalPLUS, or they do not exist on the ProfessionalPLUS The upload process checks the \Graphics-iFIX directories of all workstations on the DeltaV system and compares the files against the ProfessionalPLUS workstation's \Graphics-iFIX directory. The upload process then will take any new files and any existing files that are more recent (than the ProfessionalPLUS' copy) and copy it to the ProfessionalPLUS workstation's \Graphic-iFIX directory. The Version Control for Displays working folder resides on the ProfessionalPLUS and is created from the contents of the ProfessionalPLUS' \Graphics-iFIX directory. Therefore, if you want these files to be included as the VCAT source, upload the files. If you do not want these files to be included as the VCAT source, do not upload them. You must always download the ProfessionalPLUS machine after enabling Version Control for Displays. However, you must also download the other workstations if you have uploaded any files. The download order is important; download the ProfessionalPLUS first and then download the other workstations. You can also download all workstations at one time by downloading the Control Network.

title: Uploading fieldbus devices
body_text: Uploading fieldbus devices You can upload parameter values from function blocks running in a commissioned fieldbus device to the database. This is useful if you want to ensure that factory-set parameter values are maintained in the database or that values modified by a technician in the field are uploaded to the database. Parameter changes to the following function blocks can be uploaded to the database: AI, AO, DI, DO, fieldbus Multiplexed AI, fieldbus Multiple DI, fieldbus Multiple DO. Unlike controllers where the system detects a need to upload changes, the system does not detect a need to upload changes to fieldbus device parameters. To upload a fieldbus device, select the device in the DeltaV Explorer, and select Upload Function Blocks . There is no need to download the device after an upload.

title: Use Logic Solvers with S-series controllers
main_heading: Use Logic Solvers with S-series controllers
body_text: Use Logic Solvers with S-series controllers SIS Adapters are used to connect S-series controllers with Logic Solvers installed on M-series 8-Wide Horizontal I/O Carriers. S-series controllers do not recognize any other M-series I/O. Refer to the Installing Your DeltaV Safety Instrumentation System Hardware manual for information on installing DeltaV SIS hardware. Subtopics: Connect S-series controllers to a small Safety Instrumented System Connect S-series controllers to a large Safety Instrumented System Connect S-series controllers to a Safety Instrumented System on the same DIN rail Connect S-series controllers to a Safety Instrumented System on another DIN rail

title: User-specified macrocyle
body_text: User-specified macrocyle The user-specified Requested macrocycle option runs all blocks on the port at the same scan rate (options are: 150 ms, 250 ms, 500 ms, 1 second, 2 seconds, or 5 seconds). When this option is selected, the Block Scan Rate selection is disabled for fieldbus blocks. Furthermore with this option you must carefully coordinate module execution rates with the macrocycle or scheduling problems can occur. Also, control performance can be impacted when modules with different scan rates run on the same segment. The DeltaV system attempts to run the blocks at the requested rate. However if the requested rate cannot be achieved, the DeltaV system uses the greater of the requested or calculated macrocycle. This is called the actual macrocycle. These guidelines explain how the actual macrocycle is determined: The actual macrocycle is equal to the requested macrocycle if the calculated macrocycle is less than or equal to (<=) the requested macrocycle. The actual macrocycle is equal to the calculated macrocycle if the calculated macrocycle is greater than (>) the requested macrocycle. The following table provides some examples that show how the actual macrocycle is determined: If the requested macrocycle is: and the calculated macrocycle is: then the actual macrocycle is: 1 second 0.6 seconds 1 second 1 second 1.2 seconds 1.2 seconds 0.5 seconds 1 second 1 second 0.5 seconds 0.8 seconds 0.8 seconds Note: Each segment that is connected to a Series 2 H1 card is capable of supporting at least one, 200 ms module by setting the requested macrocycle to 150 ms. To avoid communications problems such as download timeouts and slow AMS Device Manager updates, keep the number of devices on the segment to a minimum if a 150 ms macrocycle is used.

title: User ID Verification in Campaign Manager Operator Interface
main_heading: User ID Verification in Campaign Manager Operator Interface
body_text: User ID Verification in Campaign Manager Operator Interface You can set up confirmation and verification preferences for Campaign Manager Operator Interface commands, such as adding a batch, modifying a batch, modifying a campaign, and so on. The confirmation and verification settings are defined in the Campaign Manager Server Configuration dialog. To access this dialog, open DeltaV Explorer, select and right-click the Campaign Manager node. From the context menu, select Properties . Select the Action Confirmation tab. Configure the actions for each command. The Prompt column is enabled by default. A prompt dialog is displayed when the user selects a command, such as starting a batch (the dialog will prompt the user, "Are you sure you want to start this Batch?"). Campaign Manager Server Action Confirmation Dialog Usually all Campaign Manager operator actions can be performed by users who have been granted a Batch Operate key in the User Manager security scheme. However, to keep a record of which operator confirmed an action, select the Confirmer check box for that action. When the operator attempts to initiate the action, a dialog opens requiring the operator to enter a valid User ID and password. A valid user has the Batch Operate key. In addition, if you select the Verifier check box, the dialog includes the verify fields requiring a user with supervisory privileges to enter a valid user ID and password. Campaign Manager User Verification Dialog Related information The Campaign Manager Server properties

title: User ID Verification in the Batch Operator Interface
main_heading: User ID Verification in the Batch Operator Interface
body_text: User ID Verification in the Batch Operator Interface User ID Verification is defined on the Batch Executive. When configuring the Batch Executive, you have the option of defining settings to require an operator to confirm batch actions such as adding a batch, modifying a batch, aborting a batch, and so on. In addition, you can specify that an action requiring a confirm also requires a verification by a supervisor. As a Batch Operator Interface connects to the Batch Executive, the settings for the Prompts, Confirms, and Verifies are set for that workstation. That is, all Batch Operator Interfaces that connect to the same Batch Executive will have the same Prompt, Confirm, and Verify settings. To view the User ID Verification configuration from the Batch Operator Interface, click the Configuration and Defaults button on the toolbar. Then select the General tab. Batch Operator Interface Confirm and Verify Options Once the confirm and verify functionality has been enabled, a dialog is displayed for the command or prompt requesting the confirmation and verification. For example, when an operator selects a Batch Operator Interface command (such as Start) that includes both a confirm and verify setting, the following dialog is displayed. Dialog Requesting a Confirm and Verify Note: When the confirmer and/or verifier username exists as both a local and a domain account with different passwords, the Batch Operator Interface will validate against the local username only. Therefore, in this case, the local username and password combination must be used. Records containing the user IDs entered to confirm and verify the selected action are saved in the event file (.EVT) for the individual batch. Related information The Batch Executive properties

title: User accounts
body_text: User accounts The first user who logs in to the system (prior to installing DeltaV) starts off with a default user name of either Administrator or Emerson. This person has administration privileges associated with the computer. Once DeltaV is installed, the Windows user logged into the system for the Workstation Configuration step has full access to all DeltaV functions, such as configuring hardware, configuring the process system, downloading the configurations, and so on. Therefore, the Windows user that was logged in for Workstation Configuration must configure the ProfessionalPLUS workstation. Note: You cannot change the default administrator account's privileges unless you have created another user with equal privileges. If you are the first user after the workstation has been configured, log in to Windows as the administrator that ran Workstation Configuration and also log into DeltaV as the same administrator. In a domain environment, this must be a domain administrator because you will be creating domain-level accounts. Some thought should be given to the overall user access scheme. If more than just one or two users will be accessing the system, you might want to limit their ability to change the process configuration or perform downloads. To do this, you need to set up user names and access privileges in the User Manager. Click Start > DeltaV Engineering > User Manager . The DeltaV installation creates default DeltaV interactive user accounts that are disabled by default. Related information DeltaV accounts

title: User account passwords
body_text: User account passwords DeltaV user, application, and service account passwords must comply with the operating system complexity settings. If the same username is going to be used on different workstations in a DeltaV workgroup environment, the password for that particular username must be the same on all workstations. For a domain system, the username and password for all domain users reside on the domain server rather than on each workstation. Each user has only one username and password that apply to all the workstations in the domain. The passwords for the DeltaVAdmin service account and SOFTPHASEUSER accounts are pre-assigned in your DeltaV system. During installation you are prompted to set the password. You can change the password later using DeltaV Security Administration application or, on non-DeltaV computers, the ServPwd utility (located in the \DeltaV\bin directory and copied to the required computer). Several applications that run as Windows services must be re-registered as Windows Services when the password on these accounts is changed. This password is stored only in SAM (the Windows Security Account Manager database). Therefore, you must use this special DeltaV utility to change the password and re-register DeltaV Services. Important: Only change the DeltaVAdmin and SOFTPHASEUSER password using DeltaV Security Administration application or the ServPwd utility (for non-DeltaV computers). Important: Manage the Administrator (or Emerson) account password using DeltaV Security Administration or DeltaV User Manager.

title: User ID Verification
body_text: User ID Verification The DeltaV system provides an additional security feature called User ID Verification. In many batch process environments it is necessary to be able to link certain operator actions to the specific individual who performed the action or who approved the action. For example, modifying a batch can be an action for which you need to record who performed the action as well as who approved it. Tracking of such information is particularly important in environments where multiple batch campaigns are running simultaneously. In industries such as pharmaceutical manufacturing, maintaining electronic batch records could be a regulatory requirement. Confirmation and verification settings are set up for Batch Operator Interface commands and for Campaign Manager Operator Interface commands. If User ID Verification is enabled for adding a batch, a Change User button is available in the Recipe List , Create Batch , and Select Equipment dialogs. This button enables you to temporarily change the user who will be performing the function (adding/creating a batch and binding equipment). Any security checks (area privileges, and so on) are performed on the changed user. Once the function is complete, the logged in user's privileges are checked. Normally the user is changed to a person capable of confirming or verifying the action. Subtopics: User ID Verification in the Batch Operator Interface User ID Verification in Campaign Manager Operator Interface Configuring user ID Verification in phase logic

title: DeltaV User Manager and SIS security
main_heading: DeltaV User Manager and SIS security
body_text: DeltaV User Manager and SIS security The DeltaV User Manager allows you to manage Windows users and DeltaV users without accessing the Windows User Manager application. The procedure for assigning keys to SIS locks is identical to that for DeltaV basic process control system locks. When DeltaV System Preferences for SIS is enabled, an additional set of locks, called SIS locks, appears in a new pane on the main window for DeltaV User Manager. There are three SIS groups (SIS Engineering, SIS Operate, and SIS Supervise). By default, the SIS Engineering group has all SIS keys and the SIS Operate and SIS Supervise groups have some SIS keys. An additional default user account, SIS_Configure, is added when the DeltaV software is installed. You must manually enable this account to use it. This user account belongs to the SIS Engineering group which has all SIS keys except SIS User LockXX and SIS Version Control. Members of the SIS Engineering group have the SIS Can Configure key. Any user with the SIS Can Configure key can assign SIS keys to any other user, including himself. The default system administrator account has no SIS keys assigned; however, the administrator user can assign SIS keys and groups to any user including himself.

title: User Manager application
body_text: User Manager application Security information is defined in terms of users, groups, locks, keys and areas. Users are DeltaV and Windows users. You can assign users to one or more groups. Groups have access to a specific subset of the keys available in a site. Locks prevent users from changing specific module parameters and parameter fields. Locked objects can only be accessed by users who have the appropriate key. Locks are assigned using DeltaV Explorer or Control Studio. Locks and keys are also associated with some user functions. For example, the appropriate keys enable users to: Use AMS Device Manager device configuration and calibration features (calibration requires appropriate AMS Device Manager licenses). Make changes to the configuration database and save Process History View configuration. Download configuration and setup data to system nodes. Use the database administrator tools to create, copy and rename databases. Keys can be held directly by the user or indirectly through association with a group that owns the key. Keys provide permission to access locked parameters or parameter fields. (The granting of keys is done with the DeltaV User Manager.) A user's association with a group or ownership of a key can be global or limited to the scope of a plant area or set of plant areas. Areas - DeltaV system users can be granted different sets of keys in each area. This feature can be used to grant parameter write access to operators for control modules within the operators' responsibility, yet withhold access to other similar modules outside their responsibility. Many of the changes you make in DeltaV User Manager require that you perform a workstation download in DeltaV Explorer. Before you close the DeltaV User Manager, a message appears reminding you to download the workstation to ensure that all security changes take effect. Start User Manager from the taskbar by clicking Start > DeltaV Engineering > User Manager . The User Manager window gives you three views; Users, Locks, and Groups. You can open, close, and resize each pane. These views are available under the View menu. User Manager window Subtopics: User accounts Add a new user

title: User security in domain systems
body_text: User security in domain systems In a domain-based system, "Active Directory" is the Microsoft term used to describe the capabilities for providing and managing user access from the domain controller. In domains, Active Directory provides the advanced, user access security that is available as part of the operating system. Microsoft Active Directory has an extensive built-in structure for implementing Organizational Units and Group Policies. A Group Policy is a set of operating system features that can be turned on and off. Examples of Group Policies are: the ability to enable or disable user access to DVD drives or to the Start menu, to deny run access to specific applications, or to deny or allow access to modify the Internet Explorer configuration. A Group Policy Object (GPO) is a collection of Group Policies. Active Directory allows Group Policies to be applied to Organization Units only; not to users or groups. Organizational Units are containers for GPOs and are configured to be logical representations of an organization. They can be configured in a hierarchy of levels to divide users and computers into manageable segments that represent your organization. The DeltaV software has preconfigured OUs and GPOs so that you can easily use the user access control features of Active Directory. It is not necessary for you to completely understand the user access control features of Active Directory; however, if you want to learn more about Organizational Units, NTFS, and Group Policy Objects, refer to your Windows documentation. Related information DeltaV Organizational Units GPO settings applied to user roles

title: SLS 1508 SIS Simulation parameters
body_text: SLS 1508 SIS Simulation parameters During preliminary design of SIS modules you may want to download a module to test a piece of the logic before you have completely configured the module. Enable the simulation parameter in LSDI and LSAI blocks in SIS modules downloaded to the simulated Logic Solver card. You cannot enable the simulation parameters in modules that are running in physical Logic Solver cards. You must completely configure the LSDI and LSAI blocks to successfully download and use simulation: Create an SIS module in Control Studio. Assign the module to a simulated Logic Solver card. Enable a channel in the Logic Solver. Define the channel type for the correct input type (Analog Input or Discrete Input). Assign the channel to the input block's IO_IN parameter. From the SIMULATE or SIMULATE_D properties dialog, enable simulation and enter a simulate value. Save the module. In DeltaV Explorer, download the Logic Solver. Note: If you restart the workstation you must re-download the simulated Logic Solver. Note: After you complete your simulation configuration and before you export the configuration, make sure simulation parameters in the configuration are disabled. If you do not disable the simulation parameters, the CRCs of the simulated system do not match the CRCs of the system downloaded to the runtime system.

title: Using Bussed Field Power with VerticalPLUS Carriers
main_heading: Using Bussed Field Power with VerticalPLUS Carriers
body_text: Using Bussed Field Power with VerticalPLUS Carriers The bussed field power connectors on the VerticalPLUS carriers differ from those on the horizontal and Legacy Vertical carriers; however, some basic principles apply to all carrier types. Before connecting or extending bussed field power to VerticalPLUS carriers, read the important information in "Connecting Bussed Field Power". Subtopics: Extending Bussed Field Power to VerticalPLUS Carriers Related information Connecting Bussed Field Power

title: Using DeltaV Diagnostics
body_text: Using DeltaV Diagnostics The DeltaV Explorer allows you to launch the DeltaV Diagnostics application and view diagnostics data for any selected DeltaV Explorer object. This provides useful diagnostic information for nodes that have good status or show the indicator. To investigate integrity problems for a node or subsystem, select its icon, click the right mouse button, and then click Diagnose. Information about DeltaV Diagnostics is located in online help.

title: Using DeltaV Diagnostics
body_text: Using DeltaV Diagnostics The DeltaV Explorer allows you to launch the DeltaV Diagnostics application and view diagnostics data for any selected DeltaV Explorer object. This provides useful diagnostic information for nodes that have good status or show the indicator. To investigate integrity problems for a node or subsystem, select its icon, click the right mouse button, and then click Diagnose. Information about DeltaV Diagnostics is located in online help.

title: Using the DeltaV Explorer
body_text: Using the DeltaV Explorer The DeltaV Explorer presents a view of the overall structure and layout of your system. The tree view shows your control strategies and the hierarchy of the nodes on your Control Network. These nodes can be physically connected to the system, or they can be placeholders configured prior to the installation of the actual hardware. When you check out your system, remember that the DeltaV Explorer gives you a view of your database, but this may not necessarily match what is actually installed on the network. For example, before connecting controllers, you can define them as controller placeholders in the Control Network. The icons for the placeholders appear in the DeltaV Explorer but are not bound to any device. Then, when the controllers are available and connected, you drag and drop them from the Decommissioned Controllers section to the controller placeholder icons in the Control Network. Resolving system problems is often a matter of making sure the database and the network match and making sure all the nodes on the network have information about all other nodes. The Download commands in the DeltaV Explorer provide the nodes with all the information they need to operate and interact with other nodes. See the manual Getting Started with Your DeltaV Software for information on: Downloading Setup Data Downloading Controllers and Installing Workstations Dragging decommissioned controllers to the Control Network Subtopics: Status Indicators
