title: Version Control for documents
body_text: Version Control for documents DeltaV Version Control and Audit Trail (VCAT) for documents makes it possible to use the DeltaV database to manage changes to any type of document or file by retaining previous versions of these files. Version Control for documents is similar in functionality to Version Control for configuration and user security. The topics in this section describe any specific information or instructions regarding Version Control for documents. To use VCAT for documents you must set working folders (directories on a hard drive accessible from the workstation) to hold documents while you are working on them. After setting working folders you do not need to use Windows Explorer to navigate to the documents to work on them. Because the documents are also in the DeltaV database, you can access all documents from DeltaV Explorer. That is, from DeltaV Explorer you can check documents out of VCAT, edit the documents, save the documents, and check them back in to VCAT. Note: You cannot save documents larger than 25 megabytes. An error message appears if you attempt to save documents larger than this limit. Subtopics: Set working folders Edit documents Related information Setting up and disabling Version Control

title: Version Control functions and locks
body_text: Version Control functions and locks Keys are required for various version control functions: VC_ADMINISTRATOR - Enables a user to undo the check out of items checked out by other users. VC_CHECKOUT_CHECKIN - Enables a user to check configuration items in and out of the Version Control database VC_DOWNLOAD_CHECKEDOUT - Enables a user to download configuration items that are checked out VC_PURGE_RECOVER_ITEMS - Enables a user to permanently remove an item from the Version Control database VC_ROLLBACK_ITEMS - Enables a user to restore an item from the Version Control database VC_SET_LABEL - Enables a user to label configuration items so that they can be easily restored at a later date Related information Parameter, field, and function security

title: Version Control history and library objects
main_heading: Version Control history and library objects
body_text: Version Control history and library objects The following sections describe the behavior of version control history for items that are linked to objects in the library. Subtopics: History for class-based modules and linked composites History for library function blocks

title: Version Control history for batch and recipe objects
main_heading: Version Control history for batch and recipe objects
body_text: Version Control history for batch and recipe objects Recipe parameters in the Version Control database only appear in the history of the recipe when the default value has been overridden. Understanding this is helpful when viewing the Version Control history for a recipe parameter. When the recipe is created (either as a procedure, unit procedure, or operation) with a default recipe parameter value, the parameter does not appear in the version control history of that recipe. Once the recipe parameter value is modified, the parameter appears in the history of the recipe. Additional changes are also recorded in Version Control history.

title: Version Control labels
body_text: Version Control labels Labels mark a configuration or a specific item for later reference. There are two main types of labels: user-created labels download labels In addition to these two types of labels, DeltaV software automatically labels all of the initial configuration items in the configuration database when you enable Version Control. User-created labels The Version Control database enables you to mark either an entire configuration or a specific configuration for later reference or use. This mark is called a label . For example, you might want to label a configuration prior to a significant change or a shutdown. The label can be attached to all the configuration items, which makes it easy to restore that configuration at a later date using DeltaV Explorer. Download labels The system labels downloaded configuration items. For example, when a module is downloaded to the controller, a download label is added to the module. This allows you to track which configuration version is currently in the controller as well as which configuration version was in the controller on a given date.

title: Version Control messages
body_text: Version Control messages The Version Control - Messages dialog pops up to inform you of changes in the version control database. The changes monitored include: An item has been checked out. An item has been checked in. An item has been added or deleted. A label has been applied to an item. An item has been purged, recovered, or rolled back to a previous version. An item's version number changed during DeltaV upgrade. The dialog has the following buttons: Clear - Use the Clear button to remove all messages from the dialog. Cancel - Use the Cancel button to stop long operations such as recursive check ins. Canceling an operation interrupts it at the point at which you click the button. Any portion of the operation that has already occurred is not undone by clicking the Cancel button. Copy - After you select one or more messages, the Copy button is available. Use the button to copy selected messages to the clipboard. You can then paste the messages into another application. Click the minimize (-) button in the upper right to hide the message dialog. When you perform an action that affects the Version Control database, the message window pops up automatically. Right-click the Control menu (the application icon in the upper-left corner) to define other behaviors of the dialog: Always on Top - places the messages dialog on top of all other windows so that it is always visible Keep Minimized - keeps the messages dialog minimized even during Version Control operations Auto Minimize - minimizes the messages dialog when you select another window Related information Version Control and DeltaV Upgrade

title: Version Control Snapshot tool
body_text: Version Control Snapshot tool Snapshot is a Database Administrator tool that captures a complete copy of your present configuration database and adds it to the Version Control database. Unlike a check in or an add, snapshot does not affect the current versions of items in the Version Control database. Instead, it makes the captured configuration database available to you at any time. This is useful since a rollback of an individual item to a previous version might fail if it depends upon a library item, such as a composite block that has been deleted. Snapshots are only visible when you select History from the DeltaV Explorer root. You can replace the existing configuration with a snapshot by selecting the Version Control Snapshot tool in the Database Administrator. Select the Snapshot tool, and use the Restore option, and select the desired snapshot. All items must be checked in before you can restore a snapshot. When you restore a snapshot, the DeltaV system: deletes your current configuration database replaces your current configuration database with the snapshot synchronizes the configuration database with the Version Control database. Snapshot items that differ from those in the previous configuration database are added to the Version Control database and marked as the most current version. labels the Version Control database

title: VerticalPLUS Carriers
body_text: VerticalPLUS Carriers DeltaV VerticalPLUS carriers can be used for DeltaV Safety Instrumented Systems (SIS) and DeltaV basic process control systems. The Installing Your DeltaV SIS™ Process Safety System Hardware manual provides instructions for installing SLS 1508 hardware. VerticalPLUS carriers mount on standard 35 mm. (1.38 in.) T-type DIN rails. There are several types of VerticalPLUS carriers: 4-wide power/controller carrier 4-wide SISNet Repeater carrier 4-wide power carrier left and right 8-wide I/O interface carriers left and right 1-wide carrier extenders Related information DIN Rail Recommendations

title: 4-Wide VerticalPLUS Power/Controller Carriers
body_text: 4-Wide VerticalPLUS Power/Controller Carriers The 4-wide VerticalPLUS power/controller carrier holds up to two controllers (primary and secondary) and two system power supplies. The 4-wide VerticalPLUS power/controller carriers install on the top left of a vertical system. The 96 pin connector on the bottom of the carrier connects to the top of a left, 8-wide VerticalPLUS I/O interface carrier. 4-Wide VerticalPLUS Power/Controller Carrier

title: Video port setup for DeltaV multiple monitor workstations
main_heading: Video port setup for DeltaV multiple monitor workstations
body_text: Video port setup for DeltaV multiple monitor workstations This topic defines the recommended setup for an Emerson DeltaV 4 (quad) monitor (multiple monitor) workstation using the Dell T5810, R7910, or R5500-based computers. These platforms are currently supported as DeltaV multiple monitor (4-head or quad head) workstations. R7910XL platform The R7910XL quad-monitor workstation has one AMD FirePro W5100 graphic card with four DisplayPort (DP) outputs. If purchased directly from Emerson, the DeltaV Quad-Monitor Workstation package includes four DP-to-DVI adapters. Note: Early packages of R7910XL were shipped with four passive DP-to-DVI adapters. Using these adapters may cause an issue wherein only three monitors can be detected. As a workaround, at least one Visiontek active DP-to-DVI adapter (Manufacturer Part Number 900639, Dell Part Number A7102180) must be purchased and used on the fourth port. Newer R7910XLs are being shipped with four active DP-to-DVI adapters. Recommended connections for R7910XL with AMD FirePro W5100 T5810 platform The T5810 quad-monitor workstation has two AMD FirePro W2100 graphic cards. Each graphic card has two DisplayPort (DP) outputs. If purchased directly from Emerson, the DeltaV Quad-Monitor Workstation package includes four DP-to-DVI adapters. Recommended connections for T5810 with AMD FirePro W2100 R5500-based platform The R5500-based platform comes with two ATI FirePro 2270 graphics cards installed. Each video card ships with a DS59 to dual DVI 'Y cable' assembly. Note: There are no direct-connect DVI or VGA outputs available on the ATI FirePro 2270. The following image shows the recommended way of connecting quad head (4-head) monitors using a R5500 machine. The picture is of the R5500's back panel. Notice that there are two ports. As such, the R5500 systems with a quad monitor configuration have two (2) Y connectors that come with the package. Note: The Y connector labeled "1" is for monitor 2 or 4, while the connector labeled "2" is for monitor 1 or 3. Recommended connections for R5500 platform with ATI FirePro 2270 with DVI output

title: Viewing all resources
body_text: Viewing all resources Once the device focus is established, the ownership information for that resource is visible in the Arbitration screen. This information is visible in two sections of the screen, each of which contain two windows: Current Profile Owns - Lists what, if any, resources the current device focus entity owns. Owned By - Lists current owner of the resource. Priority List Needs - The resource that is required by the device focus entity. Needed By - The name of the process or operator requesting the resource.

title: Viewing the active phase summary
body_text: Viewing the active phase summary The Active Phase Summary screen displays an overview of the active phases (phases that are not in the IDLE or UNKNOWN states are displayed) configured in the area model. From this screen, operators can quickly identify units and their related phases. Operators can selectively filter which columns of information are visible by configuring the Active Phase Summary screen from the System Configuration and Defaults screen. The data displayed in the columns of the screen can include the following: Phase - a listing of all phases in the area model. State - the current state of the phase. Mode - the current mode of the phase, either MANUAL or AUTOMATIC. Unit - the unit to which the phase belongs. Step index - the current step of the active phase, displayed as a number on the Select Phase button. Owner - the current controller of the phase. Batch ID - the name of the batch to which the phase belongs. Operator Message - informational message sent to the operator. Failures - any instances where the phase did not function properly. The Active Phase Summary screen functions as a display screen only. Interaction with the batch at the phase level must be done from the Phase Control screen. Related information Understanding batch states

title: Viewing alarms and recording events between zones
main_heading: Viewing alarms and recording events between zones
body_text: Viewing alarms and recording events between zones To view alarms and record events from the remote zone in the local zone, assign Remote Zone Areas to the Alarms and Events subsystem of workstations in the local system. Doing so: Adds the alarms from the Remote Zone Area to the alarm scope of the workstation (defines what alarms are eligible to show in active/suppressed alarm lists, alarm banner, and so on). Includes all events from the Remote Zone Area in the Event Chronicle (should one be enabled) on that workstation. Note: The DeltaV OPC Alarms and Events Server does not support Inter-Zone alarms and events. Alarms and events from remote zones appear in the Event Chronicle of a workstation (if the remote zone area is assigned to the workstation's Alarms and Events subsystem), but are not seen by OPC Alarms and Events clients (Plant Event Historian, for example) connected to the workstation. The alarms and events that are recorded in a workstation's Event Chronicle (if it is enabled) depend on the following: The workstation's alarm scope — The local plant areas and Remote Zone Areas assigned to the workstation's Alarm and Events subsystem. The shared areas in the remote zone — Areas in the remote zone must be shared for alarms and events from the remote area to appear in the local zone's Event Chronicle. The alarms that appear in a workstation's alarm banner and alarm displays depend on the following: The areas shared in the remote zone — Areas in remote zones must be shared with the local zone for alarms to appear. Alarms from remote zone areas that are shared as read only cannot be acknowledged from the local zone. The workstation's alarm scope — The local plant areas and Remote Zone Areas assigned to the workstation's Alarm and Events subsystem. The alarm scope of the currently logged in user — The local plant areas and Remote Zone areas for which the currently logged in user has been granted any security key from the DeltaV User Manager. Only those alarms and events that meet these criteria appear in the alarm banner and alarm displays. Related information Hardware alarm messages

title: Viewing DeltaV Operate file differences with Version Control enabled
main_heading:
Viewing DeltaV Operate file differences with Version Control
	 enabled
body_text: Viewing DeltaV Operate file differences with Version Control enabled You can compare files two ways; between the configuration database and the VCAT database, and, between two versions of a file within the VCAT database. To show differences between the configuration database and VCAT, right-click a file in DeltaV Explorer, and then select Version Control > Differences . To show differences of two files within the VCAT database, right-click the file, and then select Show History . From the History dialog, select two versions of the file by using CTRL+click and clicking Differences .

title: View differences as text
body_text: View differences as text To see the differences in text, click the Text button. The Textual Differences dialog opens. The view shows the unchanged items in gray, added items highlighted with green, changed items highlighted with red, and deleted items highlighted with blue. The text above each pane of text indicates the versions of the item being compared.

title: View differences graphically
body_text: View differences graphically For graphics, the system displays a diagram view containing a combination of all the elements in the two configuration items. The most current version appears on top by default. The view shows the unchanged items without highlights, added items highlighted with green, changed items highlighted with red, and deleted items highlighted with blue. The text above the graphics view indicates the two versions of the item being compared. The difference display enables you to transpose the graphic view of differences. This places the older version on top. Note that Added elements such as function blocks (those that appeared in green when the newer version of the item was on top), will be highlighted in blue when the older item is on top. Strictly speaking, these items have not been deleted. However when the system compares the two versions, it recognizes that this item is absent from the older version and highlights the item in blue.

title: SIS module on-line in Control Studio
main_heading: SIS module on-line in Control Studio
body_text: SIS module on-line in Control Studio You can view any SIS module downloaded to a logic solver (CSLS or SLS 1508) in Control Studio on-line mode. In SLS 1508 simulation systems, you can open an SIS module downloaded to a workstation (simulated SLS 1508 logic solver) in on-line mode. The Logic Solver must be unlocked for a module to be opened in on-line mode. In on-line mode you can change only writeable parameters to a module downloaded to a physical logic solver. If you are viewing a module downloaded to a simulated Logic Solver, you can also manipulate SIMULATE parameters of input blocks.

title: Viewing history data
body_text: Viewing history data Now that you have defined the data you want collected and told the system to start collecting it, you can create a chart to plot the module trends and show events. There are three types of Process History documents: E +Chart - shows module trends plotted on a graph and historical events displayed in a grid Chart - shows only module trends plotted on a graph Event - shows only historical events displayed in a grid Subtopics: Open the Process History View application

title: VIM configuration overview
body_text: VIM configuration overview The general steps to configure the VIM are: Install the VIMs and other hardware as needed. Each VIM requires a DeltaV 2-wide carrier and power supply. Install the VIMNet Explorer software on a workstation connected to the plant Ethernet network. Launch the VIMNet Explorer software. In the VIMNet Explorer the VIM is called VIM. If the VIMNet Explorer is installed on the DeltaV workstation, you can launch the VIMNet Explorer software from DeltaV Explorer from the Applications menu. The first time VIMNet Explorer is launched, a dialog appears from which you enter the IP Address of the plant Ethernet network. You can also open this dialog from the Physical Network context menu. Refer to the VIMNet documentation for information on completing the dialog. In VIMNet Explorer, the VIMs installed appear as decommissioned VIMs. From the I/O Net folder context menu, select New Controller . Rename the controller to match an existing controller in the DeltaV database. From the controller node context menu, select New I/O VIM . A dialog appears from which you specify information about the VIM you are creating. Refer to the VIMNet Explorer documentation for information on completing the dialog. The VIM created contains four simulated simplex or redundant DeltaV serial cards in the slots you specify. (57 through 60 and 61 through 64 for simplex VIMs; 57 through 64 for redundant VIMs). From the VIM context menu, commission the VIM by selecting the appropriate decommissioned VIM. Select a Serial Card. Select a Port (P01 or P02). From the Port's context menu, select Add Device . From the Add Device dialog, specify the device address and IP address of the device. Refer to the VIMNet Explorer documentation for more information on completing this dialog. For generic Ethernet devices: Add or Import a Connection Definition (available VIM definition files (VDF) are in the folder where VIMNet Explorer was installed). Add the Connection Definition of the newly added Ethernet device. The Connection Definition defines the messaging type and data to retrieve from a field device. When a Connection Definition exists, auto-sensing the VIMs from DeltaV explorer creates datasets automatically. From the VIM context menu, upload the VIM configuration. Use DeltaV Explorer to auto-sense the VIMs you configured in the VIMNet Explorer software. Use DeltaV Explorer to configure the serial card ports. Use DeltaV Explorer to add and configure the serial I/O devices. Use DeltaV Explorer to add and configure the serial card datasets. Step 1 is explained in the DeltaV Hardware manual . This topic explains steps 2, 3, and 12 through 15. For information on steps 4 through 11, refer to the VIMNet software documentation . Related information Install and launch VIMNet software

title: VIM implementation overview
body_text: VIM implementation overview The following figure is a simple example of a VIM implementation. The S-series VIM is shown in the figure. Simplex Virtual I/O Module (VIM) Installation On the DeltaV Network the minimum requirement is to have enough VIMs to simulate your I/O needs. Each VIM simulates four DeltaV serial cards.

title: DeltaV Virtualization host alerts
body_text: DeltaV Virtualization host alerts DeltaV Virtual Studio media provides a module class (VIRTHOST_STDCFG) that allows virtual machines to detect health issues occurring on the host machine and generate abnormal condition indicators. DeltaV Virtual Studio is an integrated DeltaV application environment designed for easy implementation and management of both off-line and on-line DeltaV production control systems. Highly available virtualization systems allow for failures to the hardware without interrupting the virtual machines such that your operator is unaware of the failure and DeltaV continues to run as expected. For more information on using the VIRTHOST_STDCFG module class, refer to DeltaV Virtualization host alerts , located on any virtual machine at c:\EmersonVirtualization\config .

title: Virtual EIOC
body_text: Virtual EIOC The virtual Ethernet I/O Card (vEIOC) is a virtual machine image of the physical Ethernet I/O card. Like the physical EIOC, the vEIOC supports the following protocols: Modbus TCP Ethernet/IP IEC 61850 OPC UA Ethernet/IP Control Tag Integration You configure a vEIOC in the same manner as a physical EIOC. The vEIOC supports the same function blocks as the EIOC. The same configuration can be used for both the vEIOC and the physical EIOC. The vEIOC supports a redundant Area Control Network and a redundant device network. A template is used to simplify the management of the vEIOC in DeltaV Virtual Studio. After the vEIOC is configured and set up in DeltaV Virtual Studio it appears in DeltaV Explorer in the same way as the EIOC; however, it uses a different model number. The vEIOC is simplex but supports high availability options such as failover clusters and replication in DeltaV Virtual Studio. Note: The host's time must be set to UTC time and not local time. This is because the virtual machines (vEIOCs) get their initial time from the host when the virtual machine starts. For more information on the vEIOC, visit the DeltaV website and refer to the DeltaV Virtual EIOC product data sheet. For more information on DeltaV Virtual Studio refer to the DeltaV Virtualization media. Related information Manually decommission a virtual EIOC

title: Virtual I/O Modules (VIM)
body_text: Virtual I/O Modules (VIM) The DeltaV Virtual I/O Module (VIM) provides an interface to plant Ethernet networks and devices that use the Modbus TCP/IP or Ethernet/IP protocols. DeltaV controllers can read and write signals from plant floor devices such as PLC's, Motor Control Centers, and Weigh Scales that are connected to these plant Ethernet networks. The DeltaV system supports the S-series VIM and the M-series and S-series VIM 2. The S-series VIM operates with S-series controllers, the M-series VIM 2 is an upgraded model that operates with M-series controllers (MD Plus, MX, and MQ), and the S-series VIM 2 is an upgraded model that operates with S-series controllers (SD Plus, SX, SQ). The VIM has a single 10Base-T Ethernet network for field communications and a serial port for redundant VIM to VIM communications. The VIM 2 has two 10/100Base-T Ethernet networks. One network is for field communications and the other for redundant VIM to VIM communications. The VIM represents the integration of the Mynah Technologies Virtual I/O Module (VIM) with the DeltaV system hardware. Each VIM is seen by the DeltaV controller as four DeltaV Serial Cards, allowing up to 128 serial datasets (with 100 registers per dataset) over 32 TCP/IP addresses and 128 Modbus addresses per VIM. Commissioned VIMs are auto-sensed by the DeltaV controller just as other DeltaV I/O Cards. I/O signals can be used in DeltaV Control Modules and displayed on DeltaV Operate graphics. Each DeltaV controller can have one redundant or two simplex VIMs. Use the Mynah VIMNet Explorer to configure the plant Ethernet network. Graphical, drag-and-drop functionality makes setting up the plant Ethernet network quick and easy. VIMNet Explorer is integrated with DeltaV Explorer to make setup of the VIM easy and intuitive. With a DeltaV workstation connected to the plant Ethernet network, you can configure the VIM and the VIM interface to the plant Ethernet network and store the device configuration files in the DeltaV Version Control and Audit Trail database. Configure the devices from the PLC engineering workstation connected to the plant Ethernet network. Subtopics: VIM implementation overview VIM configuration overview Install and launch VIMNet software Configure VIM serial cards and ports Configure VIM Modbus TCP/IP Create datasets for VIM diagnostics Configure VIM Ethernet devices Autosense VIMs

title: Scenario: Add SIS CSLS hardware that does not interact with existing hardware
main_heading:
Scenario: Add SIS CSLS hardware that does not interact with existing
	 hardware
body_text: Scenario: Add SIS CSLS hardware that does not interact with existing hardware In this scenario An existing system is being expanded. There is no interaction between the existing system and the new hardware. The strategy to implement this expansion is: Export the entire existing DeltaV system configuration from the production system. Ensure that the ProfessionalPLUS workstation of the virtual system matches that of the production system. Import the system configuration into the virtual system. Add new safety system hardware to the virtual system. Check out the logic. Disable all SIMULATE_IN parameters and turn off Debug mode for all modules. Record the module CRCs. Decommission and unassign all virtual hardware. Export the entire system configuration from the virtual system. Import the configuration into the production system. On the import dialog that asks "Would like to update the existing object in the database…" click No to All . Assign, commission, and download the physical hardware in the production system. Verify that module CRCs are the same as they were in the virtual system. After the import the configuration of the original production system is unaffected because it was not changed.

title: Scenario: Add SIS CSLS hardware that interacts with existing hardware
main_heading:
Scenario: Add SIS CSLS hardware that interacts with existing
	 hardware
body_text: Scenario: Add SIS CSLS hardware that interacts with existing hardware In this scenario An existing system is being expanded. The new safety system hardware interacts with the existing safety system requiring some reconfiguration and downloading of existing hardware. Note: The configuration changes and download of the existing hardware in this scenario requires that the production system be shut down before exporting the configuration for use in the virtual system. The strategy to implement this expansion is: Shutdown the existing system. Decommission and unassign the hardware that will be affected by the updated configuration. Export the entire existing DeltaV system configuration from the production system. Ensure that the ProfessionalPLUS of the virtual system matches that of the production system. Import the system configuration into the virtual system. Add the new safety system hardware to the virtual system. Check out the logic. Disable all SIMULATE_IN parameters and turn off Debug mode for all modules. Record module CRCs. Decommission and unassign all virtual hardware. Export the entire DeltaV virtual system. Import the configuration into the production system. On the import dialogs that ask "Would like to update the existing object in the database…" click Yes only for the new physical hardware and the existing physical hardware affected by the configuration changes. Click No for all other objects. Assign, commission, download the physical hardware. Verify that module CRCs are the same as in the virtual system.

title: Configure virtual system, test, and move configuration to production system
main_heading:
Configure virtual system, test, and move configuration to production
	 system
body_text: Configure virtual system, test, and move configuration to production system After you have defined and populated the virtual system with the required hardware, configure the system, check the logic, and when satisfied with the configuration, move it to the production system. Configure the virtual safety system Configure modules, CHARMs, and DST assignments. You must completely configure these items in the virtual system so that no additional configuration is required after you import the virtual system into the production system. This ensures that module CRCs do not change from the virtual system to the production system. Examine and test the configuration Perform all tests and logic checkout your situation requires. You cannot simulate I/O at the CHARM level but you can use the SIMULATE_IN parameter on function blocks and Debug mode in DeltaV Explorer. You can examine the virtual hardware in DeltaV Diagnostics. The virtual hardware appears nearly identical to physical hardware with a few exceptions. For example, the revision numbers of the virtual hardware and software do not match those of physical hardware. Note: If a yellow triangle download indicator appears on a running virtual CSLS or LSNB and an attempt to download the node results in the following messages in the download dialog: SISCTLR : CSLS_NAME SISCTLR :1:ERROR: An error occurred (error code 2097172,LS_SLS_IN_REDUCED_OPERATION). You can recover and download the LSNB or CSLS by following these steps: Open DeltaV Diagnostics. Select the CSLS or LSNB. From the context menu select Force Reset On Active . A secure write confirmation dialog box appears. Confirm the secure write. Ignore or dismiss any messages that appear related to the secure write request. Download the CSLS or LSNB from DeltaV Explorer. The download should complete without errors. Move virtual configuration to production system After you have completed your logic check, follow the instructions to export the configuration from the virtual system and import it into the production system. Related information SIS CSLS VM scenarios and strategies Scenario: Create a new SIS CSLS system Scenario: Add SIS CSLS hardware that does not interact with existing hardware Scenario: Add SIS CSLS hardware that interacts with existing hardware

title: Create virtual hardware from templates
body_text: Create virtual hardware from templates After the virtual networks are defined, create the virtual machines (controllers, CSLSs, and so on) your system requires. Follow the instructions in the DeltaV Virtual Studio online help. For each virtual machine you create you specify the following: The DeltaV Version or Release Independent. The node type (SZ controller, CSLS, LSNB, etc.). The node name. The network assignments for the virtual machine. CAUTION: Allow the creation of each virtual machine to finish before creating another virtual machine. Create all virtual machines before assigning and downloading modules and testing configuration logic. Attempting to create multiple virtual machines simultaneously may cause virtual CSLSs into reduced operations mode. The DeltaV Virtual Studio online help for the dialog contains detailed information about creating virtual machines.

title: Set up Virtual Networks
body_text: Set up Virtual Networks Remember, the naming convention used in this example is not required. If you have not already done so, in DeltaV Virtual Studio create and name the networks that your situation requires. Refer to the DeltaV Virtual Studio documentation for detailed information on creating virtual networks. For the example system the networks are: ACN Primary ACN Secondary LSN01 Primary LSN01 Secondary LSN02 Primary LSN02 Secondary GSN Primary GSN Secondary

title: Scenario: Create a new SIS CSLS system
main_heading: Scenario: Create a new SIS CSLS system
body_text: Scenario: Create a new SIS CSLS system In this scenario there is no existing SIS CSLS system. A new system is being created. The strategy required to implement this scenario includes the following: Create the virtual safety system. Check out the logic. Disable all SIMULATE_IN parameters and turn off Debug mode for all modules. Record the module CRCs. Decommission and unassign all virtual hardware. Export the entire DeltaV system configuration. Import the configuration into the production system. Assign, commission, and download physical hardware in the production system.

title: Create the SIS CSLS virtual system
main_heading: Create the SIS CSLS virtual system
body_text: Create the SIS CSLS virtual system This document uses an example SIS CSLS DeltaV system to explain how to use DeltaV Virtual Studio (DVS) and DeltaV Explorer to create a DeltaV virtual system for logic checkout. The figure shows the example system used in this document. To simplify the diagram redundant networks are not shown. Example SIS CSLS virtual system Note: The names used in the virtual system for hardware items must match exactly with the names used in the production system or CRCs in the virtual and production systems will differ. The names inside the blocks of the diagram (SZ01, CSLS0101, and so on) are the hardware names that will appear in the DeltaV Explorer configuration for the virtual system and the production system. The names in parentheses in the example diagram (LSN01, ACN) are the names of the virtual networks. These names do not appear in DeltaV Explorer but are created and used in DeltaV Virtual Studio to define the virtual networks. Note: This example system includes the use of Local Safety Network Bridges to create a Global Safety Network. If your system does not include LSNBs, you can ignore their mention in the remainder of this document. The numbers in the names define the location of the item in the example system. The first pair in a name defines the LSN the item is in. The second pair of numbers in the CSLS names indicates which CSLS it is in the LSN. For example, CSLS0101 is the first CSLS on LSN01. In this example there is only one CSLS per LSN. Note: The host's time must be set to UTC time and not local time. This is because the virtual CSLSs get their initial time from the Host when the virtual machine starts. Subtopics: Set up Virtual Networks Create virtual hardware from templates Relate virtual hardware to items in DeltaV Explorer

title: SIS CSLS logic checkout using virtual machines
main_heading: SIS CSLS logic checkout using virtual machines
body_text: SIS CSLS logic checkout using virtual machines You can test the configuration and logic of a SIS CSLS system without physical hardware by creating a test DeltaV system using the DeltaV virtual machine (VM) templates of the SZ controller, the CHARMs Smart Logic Solver (CSLS), and the Local Safety Network Bridge (LSNB). Use these templates with DeltaV Virtual Studio (DVS) to create test systems. All of the SIS CSLS hardware in a test system using VMs must be virtual machines, but depending on your requirements and situation, you may need or want some physical hardware in your system, for example, Global Safety Networks, ACNs, and the ProfessionalPLUS workstation. The information in this document applies whether these items are physical or virtual. This document uses the term virtual system to refer to the test system that is a collection of physical and virtual items used for logic checkout. The following are necessary to use virtual machines to check out SIS CSLS logic: An adequate number of Virtual Machine host computers to support the virtual machines to be configured in the virtual system are available. DeltaV Virtual Studio is available. The virtual system is not connected to a production system. The VM templates you need are accessible from DeltaV Virtual Studio. The use of SIS CSLS VMs as described in this document is constrained by the following: A virtual system supports checking of configuration logic only. It does not support simulation systems or operator training systems. If you are using the recommended and supported computers, each VM host supports as many as 18 virtual machines. For example, one VM host can contain an entire virtual Local Safety Network (one SZ controller, 16 CSLSs, and one LSNB) or any combination of SZ controllers, CSLSs and LSNBs as long as the total number of VMs does not exceed 18. You cannot combine virtual and physical SIS CSLS hardware in a system. Simulated I/O is not supported but you can use the SIMULATE_IN parameter at the function block level. You can also use Debug mode. The entire DeltaV system must be exported and imported to ensure module CRCs are unchanged. Note: If the same ProfessionalPLUS workstation is used in the virtual system and the physical system you do not need to export and import the DeltaV system. You need only to unassign the CSLSs and SZs from the virtual nodes to the physical nodes. The ProfessionalPlus workstation name should be the same in the virtual system and the production system. (This is not an absolute requirement but if the names are the same there is less clean up required after importing to the production system.) Only if the instructions in this document are followed will module CRCs remain unchanged when the configuration is moved from the virtual system to the production DeltaV system. title: Relate virtual hardware to items in DeltaV Explorer

title: SIS CSLS VM scenarios and strategies
main_heading: SIS CSLS VM scenarios and strategies
body_text: SIS CSLS VM scenarios and strategies This document cannot explain every possible situation in which a virtual SIS CSLS system can be created and then downloaded to a production system. However, there are three main scenarios in which virtual SIS CSLS systems can be used to configure and check out logic for safety systems, after which the configuration can be imported and downloaded to the production DeltaV safety system. Note: Before you export the virtual system configuration you must : Disable all SIMILATE_IN parameters. Decommission and unassign all virtual hardware in the configuration. Any virtual hardware that you fail to decommission and unassign appears with red Xs in DeltaV Explorer (to indicate they are not communicating) after being imported into the production system. You cannot correct this but must re-export and import again. The scenarios do not show every step but are an overview of the tasks required. title: Visual C++ tips
body_text: Visual C++ tips Creating a custom COM client in Visual C++ requires a knowledge of COM programming. The following is a very brief set of steps required to get started with an MFC-based OPC client application. Adding OLE support to the project In the pre-compiled header, add: #include "afxole.h" Adding OPC support to the project In the pre-compiled header, add: #include "opc.h" In the main application CPP file, add: #include "opc_i.c" Opc.h and opc_i.c can be generated from files included at the OPC ftp site (zilker.net/pub/opc). Adding UNICODE to the project Change the preprocessor symbol _MBCS to _UNICODE to the preprocessor symbols. An unresolved external on _WinMain@16 will also occur if you fail to add wWinMainCRTStartup into the EntryPointSymbol section of the link output category after adding _UNICODE to the preprocessor symbols. Adding DCOM support If you plan to use DCOM, you will also need to define the symbol _WIN32_DCOM. Handling messages Any OLE thread must dispatch messages in order to function correctly. OLE threads that do not dispatch messages can cause message broadcasters to hang. For more details on this subject, refer to article Q136885 - OLE Threads Must Dispatch Messages in Microsoft's OLE knowledge base. Writing a client for redundant DeltaV OPC Data Access Server A redundant DeltaV OPC Data Access Server is an in-process server, implemented by a dynamic-link library (DLL) module. If the design of your OPC client explicitly excludes interfacing with an in-process server, the client will fail if it attempts to connect to a redundant DeltaV OPC Data Access Server. In an OPC client that does not exclude interfacing with an in-process server, the third parameter of its call to CoCreateInstance or CoCreateInstanceEx must resolve to CLSCTX_INPROC_SERVER, by referencing CLSCTX_SERVER or CLSCTX_ALL, as in the following example: CoCreateInstanceEx(CLSID_OPCServer, NULL, CLSCTX_SERVER, pServerInfo, cmq, queue); where CLSCTX_SERVER and CLSCTX_ALL are defined as follows: #define CLSCTX_SERVER (CLSCTX_INPROC_SERVER | CLSCTX_LOCAL_SERVER | CLSCTX_REMOTE_SERVER) #define CLSCTX_ALL (CLSCTX_INPROC_SERVER | CLSCTX_INPROC_HANDLER | CLSCTX_LOCAL_SERVER) Note: If you use an OPC client that you acquired from an outside vendor, you should contact the author to verify that the client is not written to exclude interfacing with an in-process server before using it with redundant DeltaV OPC Data Access Server. For more information about interfacing with in-process servers, refer to the Microsoft Developer Network Library articles on Component Object Model (COM) programming at http://msdn2.microsoft.com/en-us/library/ms687205.aspx.

title: Warning when downloading a fieldbus port
main_heading: Warning when downloading a fieldbus port
body_text: Warning when downloading a fieldbus port When the Module-driven macrocycle option is used, it is possible to receive a warning during a controller or port download that a fieldbus segment requires a longer macrocycle than that configured for the port. This warning does not prevent you from downloading the port; however, your modules will not run at the specified rate if you download with this warning. This problem can occur when too many blocks are scheduled at the same block scan rate and the total time to sequentially execute the blocks exceeds the configured macrocycle. In this case, the DeltaV system increases the macrocycle to accommodate the blocks. If you get this warning, try reducing the number of blocks and/or slowing down the module execution rates. If your configuration requires module execution rates faster than 0.5 seconds, use the User-specified macrocycle option rather than the Module-driven macrocycle option. Related information DeltaV fieldbus function blocks in the control strategy

title: Water Enthalpy function block application information
main_heading: Water Enthalpy function block application information
body_text: Water Enthalpy function block application information The WTH function block calculates the enthalpy of water for a specified temperature. The calculation is limited to a temperature range of 32 °F to 704 °F ( 0 °C to 373.3 °C ).

title: Water Enthalpy function block status handling
main_heading: Water Enthalpy function block status handling
body_text: Water Enthalpy function block status handling The status of the output parameter (ENTHALPY) is decided by the status of the input parameter (TEMP). It is set to be the status of the input parameter. If the input value is out of the range of 32 °F to 704 °F ( 0 °C to 373.3 °C ), the status is set to Uncertain.

title: What happens during a download
body_text: What happens during a download When you select a download option, the system evaluates the data in the database for possible errors or omissions to determine if it can be downloaded. For example, if you have a module referencing I/O from a different controller node, the system displays a dialog that informs you of that fact. In the same way, the system displays a dialog if function blocks in a fieldbus module have not been assigned to fieldbus devices. The dialog has the following buttons: Download Anyway , Print , Cancel . The user selects one of these in order to cancel or proceed with the download. Note: If any online parameter changes have been made since the previous download, the DeltaV system stores these changes in a temporary file. When you download a controller or a module for a controller, the DeltaV system compares the temporary file with DeltaV database and presents these changed parameters in an Upload dialog. Note: It is possible for a DeltaV user to make online changes between the time a user requests the download and the time the system transfers the data. Online changes made within this window of time are not displayed as uploadable parameter changes. For this reason, it is important for users performing downloads to coordinate the downloads with those who have permission to make online parameter changes. If you decide to continue downloading, the system downloads the data to the appropriate nodes and stores a copy of the data on the ProfessionalPLUS workstation in the DeltaV\DVData\POWERUP directory. If the download includes controllers (partial or total), the system also transfers the downloaded information to controller flash memory. This enables the controller to perform a cold restart and download itself if power fails and is restored. The download progress log is saved to DeltaV\DVData by default for workstations in the control network. It is saved to DeltaV\DVData\RemoteSystems\ identifier for Remote Operator Stations. CAUTION: For blocks assigned to non-bus I/O cards (excluding Provox and RS3 I/O) , only the channels that have been modified will be affected by a download. All other channels will hold their values and status during the download to prevent disruption to the I/O. For blocks tied to bus cards (AS-I, DeviceNet, H1 fieldbus, Profibus DP, Serial), a download can potentially bump the I/O and cause the controller to hold values. To prevent bumped I/O or held values during a download, place the block producing the output in Manual mode before downloading. Be sure to determine if the process can withstand this temporary disruption. To ensure the safety of the process, it might be necessary to delay the download of the configuration changes until the process can be shut down. Alarm parameter fields all get initialized to their default (or configured) value as is appropriate, the first execution cycle of the module establishes the initial alarm state for it's alarms. In practice, this means that inactive, unacknowledged alarms appearing in the alarm list prior to a download will not be in the list after the download because they are initialized to acknowledged by the download. Downloading large modules to a controller can use a large amount of system resources. Exact amounts vary depending on the module being currently run by the controller and the size of the module being downloaded. To ensure that you do not have a problem with system resources, place the running block in manual mode before you download. Large databases require significant amounts of free disk space in order to download successfully. Make sure that there is a least half the size of the database in free disk space before downloading the database. Related information Uploading recorded parameter changes Preserving configuration and controller data during power loss

title: What is the 2.5 network?
body_text: What is the 2.5 network? The 2.5 network is between the external Network Interface Card (NIC) and the firewall or other security or network device separating the DeltaV system from any external network. The 2.5 designation refers to the ISA S95 architecture model where the control system is designated as level 2 and the level above the control system as level 3. Level 3 is typically a process information network or a DMZ (demilitarized zone). The 2.5 network is not shared with other systems and communications that are not specifically targeted to DeltaV workstations are not allowed on this network. Only network traffic from the DeltaV workstations' third Network Interface Cards (NICs) are allowed on this network. It is expected that the 2.5 network is segmented from non DeltaV traffic by a firewall or router properly configured to allow only DeltaV inbound and outbound communications. 2.5 network

title: What to download
body_text: What to download Controller and I/O To minimize process disruption, download I/O components at the lowest level that downloads the desired changes. For example, if you add or modify a card, download only the card rather than downloading the whole I/O subsystem or the whole controller. By referencing the hierarchy in DeltaV Explorer, you can determine the lowest level object to download. Expand the hierarchy (click the + next to an object) and download the lowest level object with a blue triangle ( ) next to it. To preserve outputs during a download, a module-level download that includes AO, DO, Loop, and Device Control is partial. CAUTION: For blocks assigned to non-bus I/O cards (excluding Provox and RS3 I/O) , only the channels that have been modified will be affected by a download. All other channels will hold their values and status during the download to prevent disruption to the I/O. For blocks tied to bus cards (AS-I, DeviceNet, H1 fieldbus, Profibus DP, Serial), a download can potentially bump the I/O and cause the controller to hold values. To prevent bumped I/O or held values during a download, place the block producing the output in Manual mode before downloading. Be sure to determine if the process can withstand this temporary disruption. To ensure the safety of the process, it might be necessary to delay the download of the configuration changes until the process can be shut down. Downloading loaded Phases or an SFC that has undergone a structural change can cause the controller memory to fragment. In this situation FREMEM remains constant but the largest contiguous portion of memory decreases. Typically, controller performance is not significantly affected unless several downloads of this type are performed. To prevent any impact on controller performance, do not download to loaded phases. Workstation When downloading a node, the other workstations on the network must wait until the download is complete. The DeltaV system attaches application locks and does not permit any other workstation to modify the data.

title: What are CHARMs?
body_text: What are CHARMs? When a CIOC is added to the I/O Network, a collapsed container called CHARMs appears under the CIOC in the Explorer hierarchy as shown in the following image. CHARMs can be thought of as single I/O channels under a CIOC that processes the CHARMs' signals and communications. When the CHARMs container is expanded, all 96 CHARMs that can be supported by the CIOC are visible. The 96 CHARMs are organized in eight banks of 12 CHARMs under the CIOC: bank one is CHM1-01 through CHM1-12 , bank 2 is CHM2-01 through CHM2-12 , bank 3 is CHM3-01 through CHM3-12 , and so on. In the hardware, each bank of 12 CHARMs is installed on a carrier called a CHARM Baseplate. The CHARM Baseplate consists of 12 I/O channels with terminals for connecting field wiring and an Address Plug. Each channel is undefined until a CHARM is inserted into that terminal. That is, the installation of the CHARM defines the physical channel type and makes the signal available to the DeltaV system over the redundant bus. In the software, CHARM placeholders are defined according to class and type and then assigned to controllers.The CHARM placeholders can be defined offline or when the CIOC is autosensed. Note: For information on Logic Solver CHARMs (LS CHARMs) refer to CHARMs Smart Logic Solver (CSLS) SIS Systems in the DeltaV Safety Instrumented System manual in Books Online. title: What are parameter tagnames?
body_text: What are parameter tagnames? Parameter values are defined by their tagnames (tags, for short) in the form: module/function block/parameter When identifying parameter tags, you can build the tags from scratch by typing them in or you can use the parameter browser to search the database.

title: What happens in CIOC simulate mode?
main_heading: What happens in CIOC simulate mode?
body_text: What happens in CIOC simulate mode? The following occurs in the process when a CIOC is in simulate mode: AO and DO CHARMs' outputs go to Fail Action Mode in which the last value or user-defined configured value is held AI and DI CHARMs do not receive data from the field In DeltaV Diagnostics, the icon appears at the Controller, Assigned I/O, CIOC, and CHARMs levels when a CIOC is in simulate mode. CIOC redundancy is not supported in simulate mode. When a CIOC is taken out of simulate mode: AO and DO CHARMs' outputs go from Fail Action Mode to the user-defined values and the outputs go live AI and DI CHARMs resume receiving data from the field

title: What happens to control on the segment when the controller fails?
main_heading: What happens to control on the segment when the controller fails?
body_text: What happens to control on the segment when the controller fails? If the control loop is running completely on the fieldbus segment (that is, the control is running in the devices and not in the controller), the loop keeps running. However, if the loop is getting input from the controller, the loop performs its configured error processing. To recover from a controller failure, replace the controller and then commission and download it. If the controller failure affected the fieldbus loop, startup of the loop depends on how the loop is configured.

title: What happens to control on the segment when the H1 card fails?
main_heading: What happens to control on the segment when the H1 card fails?
body_text: What happens to control on the segment when the H1 card fails? On a segment that does not support backup Link Active Scheduler (LAS), if the PCMCIA card goes down, all communication on the fieldbus segment stops. Depending on the configuration, output blocks might go to a Fault State state.

title: What is a CIOC?
body_text: What is a CIOC? CHARM I/O Cards (CIOCs) are simplex or redundant cards that process signals from up to 96 configurable channels called CHARMs and make the CHARMs' signals available to multiple S-series controllers over the DeltaV Control Network. A CIOC is connected to the control network through a CIOC Carrier that also provides power distribution to the CIOCs for signal processing and communications. CHARMs are installed on carriers called CHARM Baseplates. Up to eight CHARM Baseplates can be connected to one CIOC Carrier holding redundant CIOCs. The connected CIOC Carrier and CHARM Baseplates form a continuous redundant power and communications bus. In the DeltaV Explorer, you can create a CIOC placeholder to configure the CIOC offline before it is connected and then commission a physical CIOC to the placeholder. When you commission the CIOC, the system can autosense the CIOC's CHARMs and reconcile the installed CHARMs to the configured channels. main_heading: Who uses the Database Administrator Tools?

title: Windows Firewall
body_text: Windows Firewall The Windows firewall service is enabled by default on all DeltaV workstations. The Windows firewall profiles are off by default. Important: The Windows firewall profiles should not be enabled without fully understanding the potential impact on communications between DeltaV and any applications external to DeltaV on the either the DeltaV 2.5 network or applications in networks above the 2.5 network. Always refer to the Windows help system for more information about the Windows firewall. The information provided here is designed as an overview of the features you need to enable the Windows firewall profiles and to apply any rules pertinent to the DeltaV system. Important: Do not enable the Windows firewall profiles for any dedicated DeltaV networks; for example, the DeltaV Primary and Secondary ACNs , DLINK for Redundant Batch, and the Thin Client Primary and Secondary networks . Doing so could disrupt communications between DeltaV nodes. Networks used to connect to the DeltaV system that are outside of the DeltaV network need to be evaluated for the Windows firewall. If any non-DeltaV traffic is allowed on the network connecting to DeltaV, then enable the Windows firewall on that NIC and use DeltaV Security Administration to select the correct rule to open the necessary ports.

title: The Windows firewall and a DeltaV workstation
main_heading: The Windows firewall and a DeltaV workstation
body_text: The Windows firewall and a DeltaV workstation The Windows firewall service is enabled by default on all DeltaV workstations. The Windows firewall profiles are off by default. To control which network has the Windows firewall applied to it, you must enable the Windows firewall profile and select the specific network interface cards (NICs) for that profile. To allow incoming communications through the enabled firewall, rules are created and applied that specify the port to be opened for communication. The Windows firewall has a default set of rules opening specific ports. These default Windows firewall rules are applied when the Windows firewall is enabled. DeltaV Security Administration contains additional rules that open communication ports needed for certain Emerson-approved applications. Important: The Windows firewall profiles should not be enabled without fully understanding the potential impact on communications between DeltaV and any applications external to DeltaV on the either the DeltaV 2.5 network or applications in networks above the 2.5 network. Always refer to the Windows help system for more information about the Windows firewall. The information provided here is designed as an overview of the features you need to enable the Windows firewall profiles and to apply any rules pertinent to the DeltaV system. Important: Do not enable the Windows firewall profiles for any dedicated DeltaV networks; for example, the DeltaV Primary and Secondary ACNs , DLINK for Redundant Batch, and the Thin Client Primary and Secondary networks . Doing so could disrupt communications between DeltaV nodes. Networks used to connect to the DeltaV system that are outside of the DeltaV network need to be evaluated for the Windows firewall. If any non-DeltaV traffic is allowed on the network connecting to DeltaV, then enable the Windows firewall on that NIC and use DeltaV Security Administration to select the correct rule to open the necessary ports. The Windows firewall profile types are as follows: ( All definitions are from the Windows firewall help. ) Domain Profile The domain profile applies to a network when a domain controller is detected for the domain to which the local computer is joined. If you select this box, then the rule applies to network traffic passing through a network adapter connected to this network. When DeltaV is in its own private domain, you do not need to enable this profile. However, if DeltaV is in a child domain, then you should enable this profile for the NICs that are the parent/child domain connection. Private Profile The private profile applies to a network when it is marked private by the computer administrator and it is not a domain network. Newly detected networks are not marked private by default. A network should be marked private only when there is some kind of security device, such as a network address translator or perimeter firewall, between the computer and the Internet. The private profile settings should be more restrictive than the domain profile settings. DeltaV itself is a private network. Other networks connected to the DeltaV system can also be private networks (such as the Remote Client and Thin Client networks). You can apply the firewall to the non-DeltaV ACN NICs in the private profile. Public Profile The public profile applies to a network when the computer is connected directly to a public network, such as one available in airports and coffee shops. The public profile settings should be the most restrictive because the computer is connected to a public network where the security cannot be as tightly controlled as it is in an IT environment. DeltaV should never be connected to a public network. Enabling this profile for the non-DeltaV ACN NICs protects DeltaV in the unusual event that it is connected to a public network. Subtopics: Configure Windows firewall profiles on a DeltaV workstation Firewall rules for DeltaV Manage the firewall application rules

title: Windows logon and DeltaV logon
body_text: Windows logon and DeltaV logon There are two different logons for your system: the Windows logon and the DeltaV logon. The Windows logon logs the user on to the workstation to access the computer system. Access to specific Windows system resources and the type of access the user has depends upon the Windows user privileges (that is, Windows group memberships and assigned user roles). User privileges are set using the DeltaV User Manager. When a user logs on to the system, the DeltaV Logon window appears. The DeltaV logon allows the user to access DeltaV resources and applications. Access to specific DeltaV system applications and resources and the type of access the user has depends upon user privileges (that is, Windows and DeltaV group memberships and assigned user roles). User privileges are set using the DeltaV User Manager. Important: When you log off of the DeltaV system, be sure to log off of Windows as well, especially if you are logged on to the system with Windows Administrator privileges. Until you log off of Windows, subsequent users logging on to the DeltaV system are operating under the Windows Administrator account. The Windows Administrator account grants the user the right to perform actions that could interfere with the operation of the DeltaV system. Important: When setting up the DeltaV system, make sure that Autoswitch Desktop is enabled. Doing so helps protect against operators and maintenance personnel having unrestricted access to the system if a user with administrator privileges is logged on to the underlying Windows system. Make sure that all users with Windows administrator privileges log off of the Windows system after have finished using a workstation. Do not allow non-administrative users to log on to the DeltaV system on top of an underlying Windows Administrator logon. Related information DeltaV FlexLock DeltaV User Manager and DeltaV security

title: DeltaV Wireless I/O Card configuration options
main_heading: DeltaV Wireless I/O Card configuration options
body_text: DeltaV Wireless I/O Card configuration options Like the CIOC, the WIOC can be configured to support hardware alarms and redundancy, to show integrity errors when its time is not synchronized with other nodes, and to enable the use of cascade ports to connect multiple WIOCs together in series. Following are some additional configuration options for WirelessHART I/O cards. Note: After changing any of the following properties: Network ID, Common Join Key, or Rotation Period, wait until all devices have rejoined the network before attempting to change these properties again. The rejoining process can take an hour or even more to complete. If devices do not rejoin the network, it may be necessary to restore Network ID and Join Keys using AMS Device Manager or a HART handheld device. Note: There may be a temporary loss of data after making changes to any of the following: Network ID Common Join Key Enable Network Key Rotation Change the Network ID and Common Join Keys online The DeltaV system generates a default Network ID of 01 and a unique Common Join Key when a WIOC is created. All wireless devices in the network must be configured with the Network ID and Common Join Key to participate in the network. Users with the key to the Wireless Provisioning Lock can modify the Network ID and Common Join Key. The Network ID and Common Join Key can be modified when the WIOC is commissioned or decommissioned. Any online changes to the Network ID or Common Join Key are automatically propagated to all wireless devices after a download of the WIOC (including a Changed Setup Data download). Online changes are changes made to a commissioned, downloaded WIOC with reporting devices. Valid ranges for the Network ID are 1 through 32767 and 32767 through 36863. These options are available through the WIOC Properties dialog in DeltaV Explorer. Enable active advertising When Active Advertising is enabled, the server polls the wireless network looking for new or unreachable devices to join the network. Users with the key to the Wireless Provisioning Lock can specify the number of minutes that Active Advertising runs. Changes to the active advertising setting take effect immediately without a download. Rotate the network key When Network Key Rotation is enabled and downloaded for the WIOC, the WIOC generates a new random network key on a periodic basis to enhance network security. The network key is used to authenticate wireless devices on the network. Users with the key to the Wireless Provisioning Lock can rotate the network key. The key is rotated immediately after the command is issued. The key can be rotated when the WIOC is commissioned. This option is available from the WIOC's context menu in DeltaV Explorer. Supports HART-IP The WIOC HART server supports HART-IP which allows the integration of steam trap and machinery health applications into the DeltaV system.

To enable the Wireless I/O Network, click Start > DeltaV Engineering > System Preferences . After the Wireless I/O Network is enabled, it appears under the Control Network in the DeltaV Explorer. WIOCs and Wireless Gateways are added to the Wireless I/O Network from DeltaV Explorer. The following image shows a DeltaV Explorer hierarchy with a Wireless I/O Network containing one WIOC and one Wireless Gateway. The Assigned Wireless I/O container holds a WIOC and a Wireless Gateway (WG1). title: Wireless I/O troubleshooting
body_text: Wireless I/O troubleshooting There are several ways to troubleshoot Wireless I/O: The controller's COMM_ALM hardware alarm condition becomes active if the controller cannot communicate with an assigned Gateway. For redundant controllers, the COMM_ALM hardware alarm condition becomes active if it cannot communicate with an assigned Gateway on both networks. If device alarms are enabled on a wireless device, alarms under the device tag become active when there are active alert conditions in the device. If a Wireless Gateway loses communication with the DeltaV system, a red X appears on the Gateway's icon in DeltaV Explorer and in DeltaV Diagnostics. Use the Gateway's web interface to gather diagnostic information about the network. To launch the Web Interface, select a commissioned Wireless Gateway node and select 1420 Web Interface from the context menu. Use the DeltaV Diagnostics application. To launch Diagnostics click Start > DeltaV Operator > Diagnostics . Use the troubleshooting information provided in the 1420 documentation. Related information Alarms and events

title: Wiring components
body_text: Wiring components Emerson recommends a family of connection blocks and cable components for use in installing your fieldbus segment. These components include standard junction blocks, junction blocks with short circuit protection, and terminators. These components can be used with fieldbus cable that you can purchase from recommended suppliers. All of these components are selected to not degrade the communications between devices.

title: Wiring Guidelines
body_text: Wiring Guidelines The power and grounding terminals and field termination points on the I/O subsystem and the system power supplies are designed to accept 2.5 mm 2 (14 AWG) stranded or solid wire. To select wire, calculate the maximum current limit expected for each wire. Local electrical codes define the wire size required for a specific current. Shielded twisted pair wiring is recommended for low-level signal wiring to reduce susceptibility to noise. You can order an I/O carrier with a shield bar (to terminate the shields from field wiring) or without a shield bar (where termination is not necessary).
